Generating synthetic cell shapes realistically can contribute to developing training datasets to enhance cell tracking and segmentation capabilities in biomedical imaging. For effective cell shape synthesis, a compact yet flexible representation is required, however current methods involving voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches have limitations for high-resolution and topology changes such as growth and cell division. Our proposal utilizes level sets of signed distance functions to represent cell shapes. By training a neural network to implicitly generate signed distance function values at any point in three-dimensional space over time, conditioned on latent vectors that can be sampled randomly or controlled programmatically, we achieve the required synthetic cell shape synthesis capability. The resulting network was evaluated based on its ability to produce new cell shape sequences that match existing ones, and our experiments demonstrate the significant benefits of this compact and flexible level set representation in synthetic cell shape generation. The generated cell shapes also featured improved realism over voxel-based and polygon mesh approaches, and facilitated the creation of a small training dataset for cell tracking that can serve as a foundation for future growth. Researchers in neuroscience hypothesize the brain utilizes diverse coordinate systems, such as body-centric, world-based, and others, to represent 3D environments. Conversely, advancements in reinforcement learning present a novel approach that might serve as a more plausible model for spatial perception and navigation in biology. Focusing on reinforcement learning methods that encourage agents to achieve target images without creating a 3D map, we examine this type of representation's capability to facilitate spatial tasks involving geometric consistency, like decoding location features. To demonstrate this, we design a hand-crafted representation ensuring high geometric consistency, and show that retaining information on persisting visual features during camera movement can improve performance in these tasks. Our findings provide a significant stimulus for neuroscientists to explore non-Cartesian spatial representations as an alternative to cognitive mapping. Moreover, they suggest that persistent visual content may play a crucial role in facilitating learning in reinforcement-based agents with a focus on spatial tasks. Our research, including related code and relevant papers, can be accessed at https://github.com/alexrame/Reinforcement-Based-Place-Representation. To evaluate the efficiency of event-chain Monte Carlo algorithms for complex simulations, specifically in two-dimensional models of hard-disk dipoles tethered together, researchers assess their suitability for future use in molecular water models. They analyze the rotational motion of these dipoles through measurements of their polarization's autocorrelation times. Four distinct event-driven algorithms are examined: straight, reflective, forward, and Newtonian ECMC, all differing in their updating methods at specific times. These non-reversible methods exhibit considerable performance gains over traditional local Metropolis algorithms. Additionally, there are notable speed disparities among the ECMC variations, with the Newtonian variant showing exceptional potential in overcoming the dynamic stagnation often encountered in 3D dipolar models with electrostatic interactions. Based on this assessment, the 2D tethered dipole model may serve as a suitable precursor for developing more advanced ECMC strategies for 3D dipolar water models. Further simulation details can be adjusted to optimize the effectiveness of these techniques. Finally, a comparison of Newtonian ECMC's theoretical limitations with actual simulation results reveals a favorable outlook for its applicability in this context. Given its promising potential, a detailed derivation of the theoretical scaling of its autocorrelation times is presented for the tethered dipole model. Nonetheless, replacing electrostatic interactions with a Coulomb law may jeopardize the effectiveness of the Newtonian variant. To combat this challenge, an alternative variant utilizing Newtonian ECMC for short, dipole-based steps and ECMC at times is proposed, demonstrating excellent performance and theoretical scalability up to the Ornstein-Zernike level. To verify the applicability of this strategy in water models, its application to 3D dipolar liquids is examined through simulations with various dipole concentrations and sizes, results comparable to those obtained with a 3D dipolar protein model. Finally, a groundbreaking 3D dipolar protein model is introduced, incorporating a comprehensive protein structure and multi-scale analysis of polarization autocorrelation times, revealing excellent performance and theoretical scalability up to the level of dynamic cluster approximation for moderate protein sizes and ECMC parameters. Consequently, a promising outlook emerges for the widespread adoption of Newtonian ECMC algorithms in complex simulation models. These findings will soon be extended to the realm of water with dipole potentials modeling polar fluids. In conclusion, the proposed 3D dipolar protein model and accompanying multi-scale analysis of polarization autocorrelation times provide a valuable framework for optimizing Metropolitan area transport algorithms and evaluating future simulation strategies in this context. We present a novel universal method for detecting multiple types of dynamic behavior,
including stable and traveling chimera states using a dynamically adjusted measure of
coherence. This method automatically identifies and differentiates between synchronized
clusters, traveling wave patterns, chimera states, and asynchronous states. Additionally,
it is capable of determining the number of clusters present in cluster synchronization
situations. To further enhance our method, we developed a new technique for measuring the
speed of traveling chimera states. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method using a
specific example of a ring network composed of type II Morris-Lecar neurons with asymmetric
nonlocal inhibitory connections, where a diverse range of coherent and wave states are
identified. Notably, we propose that our method is robust for networks of phase oscillators and
generalizable to a broader class of relaxation oscillator networks. The presented approach
can be utilized for the reliable detection of coherent and wave states in various network types.

Our analysis shows distinct regional influences, with East Pacific events strongly linked to significant global precipitation impacts, whereas Central Pacific events exhibit less effect and more variable effects. Notably, the effects of Central Pacific events can sometimes mirror those of East Pacific events for certain global precipitation patterns. This suggests that East Pacific and Central Pacific events should be considered as varying phases of a single phenomenon rather than as distinct flavors. Our findings can inform decision-making strategies by highlighting the heightened risks associated with East Pacific events and suggesting East Pacific and La Ni\~na events can lead to comparable global precipitation outcomes. We also find that East Pacific and Central Pacific events can share similar regional impacts on global precipitation patterns. Our analysis shows that East Pacific events are likely to occur when strong tropical forcing interacts with a particular type of atmospheric variability, whereas Central Pacific events are more likely when another type of atmospheric variability is active. This suggests a physical link between these flavors of ENSO and their respective atmospheric conditions. Our study provides a non-conditioning, probabilistic look at ENSO's impact on global precipitation and highlights the distinct characteristics and effects of El Ni\~no and La Ni\~na on the world's precipitation patterns. Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, multi-source satellite data streams often have varying missing data
rates and errors, making precise AOD estimation and prediction challenging.
Therefore, a practical need exists to develop a physics-based statistical method
for wildfire AOD forecasting by integrating heterogeneous satellite data streams.
By incorporating spectral analysis, the proposed method merges multiple satellite
datasets with an underlying advection-diffusion equation driving AOD propagation,
including bias correction to compensate for model biases and Fourier series errors.
This approach was tested using California wildfire AOD data provided by the NOAA,
along with numerical examples demonstrating its predictive capabilities and
model transparency. Moreover, the corresponding code has been made accessible on GitHub.

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce systematic biases in connectivity measures. In this research, we studied how site-to-site effects impact our ability to detect individual and group differences, and our analysis suggests that multisite studies are feasible when utilizing large sample sizes. Our data collection was based on actual, rather than simulated, fMRI datasets from N=345 young, healthy subjects, acquired across eight scanning sites, all of which utilized 3T scanners and varied scanning protocols. Our findings demonstrate that commonly observed functional networks are consistently present across all sites, and inter-site effects were relatively minor. Through Monte-Carlo simulations, we evaluated the effects of multisite data on our ability to detect changes and predict group labels, revealing that our ability to detect changes increased slightly when data from multiple sites were combined, but remained comparable to that of single-site studies with larger sample sizes. Our results imply that large sample sizes can make multisite research in rs-fMRI feasible and potentially increase our ability to detect individual and group differences. Our multisite dataset is now available for further analysis. DOI: 10.1038/s41592-021-00396-1, https://osf.io/7chcd/ (JRS, 2021).

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. A major obstacle in achieving this goal is 
overcoming the limitations imposed by language switch points. Statistical models 
are unable to efficiently capture the characteristics of these transition points 
due to the variability in where they occur in any given sentence. To address 
this challenge, we propose FastText-GLM, a character-based language model that 
utilizes character n-grams as input. This model is capable of learning representations 
for words in code-mixed languages that are robust to language switch points. Our 
results demonstrate that FastText-GLM outperforms other models in zero-shot 
classification tasks involving multiple languages. FastText-GLM also facilitates 
the development of word embeddings for code-mixed languages that accurately 
reflect their linguistic structure. Additionally, we employ it to create monolingual 
word embeddings for languages that appear in code-mixed form, and our results 
reveal that these embeddings compare favorably to those generated using state-of-
the-art monolingual pre-training methods. Having established its effectiveness, 
we apply FastText-GLM to address two significant NLP challenges in code-mixed 
languages: language switch point detection and part-of-speech tagging. Our experiments 
demonstrate that FastText-GLM enables successful implementation of these tasks. 
Notably, it surpasses the performance of a recently proposed model that leverages 
self-attention for part-of-speech tagging in code-mixed languages. Based on these 
findings, we conclude that FastText-GLM represents a valuable tool for a broad 
range of NLP tasks involving code-mixed languages. Our associated repository

Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted to obtain a comprehensive picture of the inspiral, merger, and post-merger stages.  The analysis across various initial and computational configurations reveals universally similar evolution processes, regardless of setup variations.  The disruption of the neutron star leads to mass ejection accompanied by a massive accretion disk formation; the magnetic field within this disk then undergoes amplification due to various instabilities and turbulent forces, inducing the dynamo and angular momentum transfer.  The subsequent mass ejection by viscous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence begins roughly 300-500 milliseconds post-merger, persists for several hundred milliseconds; meanwhile, a magnetosphere is formed around the black hole, producing a focused strong electromagnetic outflow lasting about 0.5-2 seconds.  The model without equatorial-plane symmetry shows inverted magnetic polarity in the magnetosphere, caused by a magnetorotational instability dynamo, whereas a model initially comprising toroidal fields demonstrates a late post-merger stage characterized by a tilted disk and magnetosphere, due to anisotropic mass ejection effects, potentially shortening the Poynting-luminosity phase to 0.5-2 seconds.  The late stage Poynting-luminosity phase duration variation remains a model-dependent issue; however, a general agreement exists that a late stage thermal radiation phase duration could be significantly shorter (on the order of tens of milliseconds) and heavily dependent on an initial neutron star radius and central engine duration.  The model with an initial neutron star radius of 40 km indicates a late stage thermal radiation phase duration could be approximately 10-100 milliseconds. for compact Riemann surfaces $C$ of genus $g \geq 1$ is presented, exploring
its connections to the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class $e_1 = \kappa_1$ on the
moduli space and its relation to the traditional Kawazumi-Zhang invariant. The
given $\varphi(C)$ can be represented as a division of the volume of the
moduli space by the leading coefficient of its canonical principal partial
polarization, and its structure allows for an explicit calculation that
incorporates the intersection numbers of the Chow ring of $A_{g,1}$. The
presented $\varphi(C)$ can also be manipulated to recover the original
Kawazumi-Zhang invariant, and its properties enable the exploration of its
behavior for specific Riemann surfaces, such as those derived from boundary
strata of the Torelli space. The study of this $\varphi(C)$ provides a entry
point for more extensive research aimed at understanding the Mumford-Morita-Miller
classes $\kappa_i$ for $i = 2, \ldots, g-1$. The introduced notation of
$\varphi(C)$ (''second Kawazumi-Zhang invariant'') serves as a mirror to the
Mumford-Morris invariant, highlighting the symmetry in the moduli space of
one boundary point. The presented work is an expansion on the original

This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process also attains a distinct quasi-stationary equilibrium, which it converges toward at an exponential rate across all initial distributions. Furthermore, we illustrate a corollary ergodic theorem under specific conditions. Moreover, we apply two common techniques for analyzing upper bounds to quasi-stationary ergodic theorems, before applying these insights to a variety of examples, including (i) a random walk on an inflated Cayley graph, (ii) a time-changed Brownian motion, and (iii) revival in reversible communication systems. The study of quasi-stationary distributions has significant implications in the fields of biology, communications, and probability. The issue of sequencing tasks optimally for a robot is a long-established concern in manufacturing, yet most solutions proposed to date are tailored to specific environments and fail to account for the robot's real-time performance needs. In this research, we introduce a multi-objective optimization approach that determines the optimal sequence of tasks by minimizing both the machine's utilization and the robot's transit times. These improvements enable the rapid completion of tasks to a high standard, thus facilitating the efficient execution of robot-based services in a timely manner. Our study examines the existence of domain-level source diversity bias in video search outcomes by utilizing a virtual agent-based method. The approach entails comparing the outputs of five prominent search engines, comprising four Western and one non-Western search engines, for both English and Russian language queries. This study is the first to analyze the average local transmission delay experienced by a user when data packets are transmitted at a fixed rate over a wireless Rayleigh fading channel in the presence of multiple interfering signals. A systematic approach allows the derivation of an exact mathematical expression for the average local delay, which indicates that interference correlation has a significant impact on local transmission efficiency. By contrast, when interference does not correlate with each other, the average local delay is found to be directly proportional to the number of interfering signals, and this relationship is shown to be invalid when interference correlation exists. Furthermore, when a form of control is applied to packetize data, which is commonly known as delay-bounded packetization, the average local delay can be expressed as the sum of the queuing delay and the transmission delay, which are proportional to $1/(2\sigma^2)$ and $2/(2\sigma^2)$ respectively, where $\sigma^2$ represents the variance of the combined interference signal. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed in node classification to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in an unsupervised manner. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely slow down the label leakage. Secondly, they separate label acquisition from model training, leading to inefficient exploration of pseudo-labels and suboptimal model performance. To address these limitations, this study proposes an innovative pseudo-labeling framework called Informed Label Acquisition and Sharing (ILAS). ILAS seamlessly integrates label acquisition and sharing into model training and encourages informed pseudo-labeling by assigning a larger weight to nodes with mixed model and ground-truth predictions. As a result, ILAS not only accelerates pseudo-label leakage but also significantly enhances model performance and expands the label set with more informative nodes. The proposed method is evaluated on three graph classification tasks and outperforms current state-of-the-art pseudo-labeling techniques on multiple datasets. The code for ILAS can be found at https://github.com/J-You/ILAS. The empirical findings and code in the paper's supplement can be accessed at https://jyou2020.github.io/ILAS/.

In video processing tasks, precise identification of recognizable objects at a low computational cost enables real-time performance even on devices limited by memory. We address this challenge by designing PatchNet, a highly efficient framework for object detection and classification in videos. Unlike traditional pixel-based approaches, PatchNet leverages patchwise features that are more adaptable and robust. We also introduce patch grouping, a novel technique for generating recognizable objects at a low computational cost. Through extensive experimentation on various videos, we demonstrate PatchNet's remarkable performance in both object detection and classification tasks, achieving remarkable accuracy on small datasets and comparable results on larger datasets. Notably, PatchNet's computational efficiency enables seamless operation on devices limited by memory, enabling real-time performance even at high resolution. Analytical derivations are developed, incorporating fundamental aspects like the back-action force, input-output relationships, and corresponding spectral densities, all situated within a purely classical framework. This study investigates how basic autonomous entities akin to Braitenberg vehicles can manifest complex, unpredictable movements. Employing a robot design proposed by Steve Mesburger and Alfred Hubler in "Chaos in Wall Following Robots", the autonomous entities use a straightforward distance sensor to navigate, with the added limitation of a narrow "phi" field of view. As these agents maintain a consistent forward velocity, they rely on the sensor to adjust their path accordingly: rightward when close to obstacles and leftward when distant from them. In a linear environment, the autonomous entities maintain a consistent distance from their surroundings and proceed along a fixed path. However, when faced with periodic patterns in the environment, such as square, triangular, or sawtooth shapes, and the field of view is narrowed, these agents follow a recurring path. But as their field of view expands, their movements become increasingly chaotic. A thorough examination, using numerical methods with these shapes, led to identifying key points of transition and analyzing various bifurcation types including border collision and period doubling, with further detailed results to be presented in a separate report. Numerical simulations were carried out over an extended duration of 200,000 seconds, with the results confirming observations from earlier studies of Braitenberg vehicle-like creatures. Furthermore, a thorough analysis of the autonomous entities' behavior in a triangular environment has yielded significant insights into their movement patterns. In a related study, the autonomous entities were tested in a rotating wave and categorization was achieved based on their behavior, along with a detailed examination of their movement patterns in a series of periodic patterns in the environment. The conclusions drawn from this study confirm that the autonomous entities exhibit a range of behavior from simple, predictable movements to complex, unpredictable chaos, all in line with the original robot design's capabilities. The study successfully bridges the original robot design's behavior with mathematical modeling, offering valuable insights into its movement patterns. This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.  The study shows the generated theory on this geometric space is a factor theory of the full pAQFT, with its sections representing chiral fields.  The theory is then applied to analyze a model of a chiral particle interacting with a quantum field.  The analysis involves solving for the particle's associated null geodesic equation of motion and observing how its trajectory divides the spacetime into a left and right half, influencing the particle's state in a way that varies depending on the spacetime's direction and the far distant future.  Consequently, this study gives rise to a set of non-trivial inequalities that must be satisfied by any chiral field's covariant relation with a geometric space.  Ultimately, the theory is tested by examining its chiral content in a diverse range of spacetime scenarios, including both globally hyperbolic and non-globally hyperbolic cases, covering various geometries such as cones, hypercones, and the Luders state in the former category, and the Baysian faithful in the latter.  The assessment involves analyzing and graphically presenting the associated null geodesics in these spacetimes.  The findings indicate that the given physical models possess chiral content for all the mentioned spacetimes except the hypercone, where the situation remains undetermined.  The study concludes by summarizing the learned outcomes.  The final section provides an overview and discussion of the study's results and proposes potential future directions and research topics.  The appendix contains two additional sections, the first addressing technical inaccuracies in a previously published article and the second examining the relationship between chiral and anti-chiral observables under the conditions of spatial homogeneity and isotropy, including a discussion of the associated null geodesics. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation in such operations obstructs the surgeon's visibility, highlighting the need for smoke removal to ensure a clear view. To apply smoke removal effectively, it's essential to accurately distinguish between smoke and non-smoke images, which poses a challenge as current methods are incomplete. To overcome this issue, we have developed an image enhancement technique that extracts crucial information from RGB images to differentiate between smoke and non-smoke content. Leveraging a weighted least squares optimization framework, we employ statistical features derived from bivariate histograms and specific image characteristics, which are then used to train a classifier for binary classification of smoke or non-smoke content. We have tested our approach on the Cholec80 dataset and achieved notable results, demonstrating a 4% improvement in accuracy and F1-score over standard RGB image performance, as well as enhanced performance compared to existing methods. Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into equivalent versions that utilize the fewest number of gates possible. To achieve
this, researchers have developed a new approach, the Opaque Path Compiler, which uses
program analysis to efficiently convert quantum algorithms into a optimized form.
This compiler system, based on source-to-source translation, replaces critical
program sections with stable versions, addressing errors and gate optimization issues.
The key components of the compiler framework include a stable version of the quantum
algorithm translator and an error-constrained parser for the Z quantum assembly language.
The Opaque Path Compiler has demonstrated improved performance, reducing the number of
gate operations by a factor of 10 to 100 times, and it is now available for public
use at [www.qcsem.com/opc/](http://www.qcsem.com/opc/). The project is hosted at

Recent breakthroughs in producing two-dimensional materials with specific patterns of layered structures have paved the way for achieving unique states known as excitonic insulators, in which certain inherent electronic characteristics spontaneously emerge within the layers. A novel concept has been introduced where an intralayer particle (formed through light exposure) interacts with particles that can leave the excitonic state to form interlayer charged entities called polarons. Utilizing complex computational methods, our study begins with calculating the strength of bonds between particles composed of those from different and the same layers, crucial in the understanding of charged entities' behavior. To model excitements within the primary state, we rely on a specific theory describing paired entities and, for analyzing interactions with optical stimuli, adopt a simplified representation of these interactions to predict optical behaviors. Predicted features match known patterns for this type of layered material state, indicating changes in these interactions when layers are spaced farther apart will alter their corresponding light response patterns. This fundamental study sets the ground for analyzing charged entities' behavior in these types of layered materials and their potential applications in optical technology. We have developed a message-passing algorithm designed to accurately determine the location and track of mobile objects within areas with multiple signal paths that may experience blocked or obstructed visibility. The proposed adaptive probabilistic algorithm estimates a mobile device's position by leveraging data from multiple anchors, taking into account the timing and amplitude variations in signal components and associated uncertainties. Utilizing an adaptable noise model, the algorithm calculates a covariance matrix on the fly to weigh signal components according to their reliability. Numerical results demonstrate significantly improved estimation accuracy when the algorithm accounts for multi-path components and uncertainties, even in scenarios with limited visibility. We have tested the algorithm's performance in diverse environments and scenarios, such as narrow corridors, dense forests, and urban areas with high building interference. The outcomes indicate superior minimization of location estimation error in comparison to conventional methods. The efficiency of the algorithm is also evaluated in terms of computational complexity. The findings indicate that the proposed adaptive algorithm offers rapid solution times, thereby enabling its implementation for real-time location tracking applications. We verify this capability through the implementation of a live demo using Android devices in outdoor settings. The study showcases the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in achieving high accuracy and rapid solution times, thereby addressing critical localization challenges in complex and hidden areas. The associated code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/APOGEE-UIUC/MPLT. For real-time tracking purposes, please refer to the live demo in the attached document. Measurements of joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ bosons in $W^{\pm}Z$ production processes have been reported. These measurements were derived from $139$ fb$^{-1}$ worth of data from proton-proton collisions at a $13$ TeV center-of-mass energy, obtained with the ATLAS detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.  $W^{\pm}Z$ candidate events, resulting from the decay of these bosons into electrons and muons, have been used to quantify longitudinally polarized vector boson pair production, an event that is here reported for the first time, occurring at a statistical significance of $7.1$ standard deviations.  Fiducially-integrated joint helicity fractions for these events are $f_{\mathrm{00}} = 0.067 \pm 0.010$, $f_{\mathrm{0T}} = 0.110 \pm 0.029$, $f_{\mathrm{T0}} = 0.179 \pm 0.023$ and $f_{\mathrm{TT}} = 0.644 \pm 0.032$, in concordance with the next-to-leading order predictions from the Standard Model of physics.  Additionally, joint helicity fractions for individual $W$ and $Z$ bosons were computed, revealing no substantial disparity between these quantities and standard model predictions.  These measurements expand upon work from $8$ TeV data, addressing uncertainties associated with parton distribution functions and model-dependent corrections.  Finally, cross-sections for multiple $W$ and $Z$ boson interactions were quantified, ranging between $18.2$ pb and $0.048$ pb for various $W$ and $Z$ boson configurations.  Observed values for these interactions align with standard model predictions.  These measurements constitute the first quantitative assessment of joint polarization states for $W$ and $Z$ boson pair production. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof terms into dot language nodes and edges, allowing for the visualization of a Coq proof within the Isabelle proof assistant environment. This system enables teaching strategy-based proof development with the aid of visual representations, which can be visualized at specific proof steps. Consequently, by combining these visual and computational tools, students can acquire essential skills in both computer-aided and human-based proof methods. Furthermore, our findings imply that the Riemann Hypothesis is linked to a specific inequality involving the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, and we establish a sharper bound on this moment that surpasses previous estimates by a significant factor, while also providing the first explicit lower limit on this moment. Moreover, under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis, we derive a condition that precludes the existence of certain patterns of nonconjectural zeros in the L-functions of degree 2, and this condition has far-reaching implications for the study of gaps between zeros of L-functions and prime numbers. Lastly, our work enables the computation of the second moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms, yielding results that exceed the predictions made by Shanks in 1979 and settle a conjecture proposed by Darmon and Rotger in 2015. Established industries such as aviation gather real-life mistakes in centralized databases to facilitate safer practices. Conversely, emerging technologies like intelligent systems frequently result in real-world setbacks despite a lack of record of their failures. Consequently, businesses repeatedly replicate mistakes when designing, developing, and deploying intelligent systems, leading to unintended harm. A central database of intelligent system failures experienced in real-life scenarios (i.e., incidents) is required to ensure these systems genuinely contribute to societal well-being. The AI Incident Database, spearheaded by a joint venture between industry and non-profit sectors, aims to prevent and mitigate intelligent system failures. It supports a wide range of research and development applications through search functions for over 1,000 documented incident reports to date. Each incident report includes details of the failure, the system being developed, and the methodologies employed. By providing full control of their data to contributors, the AI Incident Database promotes a culture of responsibility within the intelligent system community. Moreover, the database serves as a resource for developing safer versions of intelligent systems, similar to those in established industries. You can access the AI Incident Database at https://incident.ai and contribute your knowledge to make intelligent systems safer.

Researchers have introduced an innovative technique for accurately measuring the masses of extremely short-lived, unusual atomic isotopes over a wide range of frequencies. This method utilizes the principle of isochronous mass spectrometry, combining real-time ion velocity and trajectory analysis at the Lanzhou CSRe particle storage facility. Dubbed Bρ-defined isochronous mass spectrometry, or Bρ-IMS, this technique enhances precision and sensitivity, paving the way for new mass measurements. Specifically, in a single test setting, precise mass readings were obtained for $^{46}$Cr, $^{50}$Fe, and $^{54}$Ni with exceptionally low margins of error. This breakthrough technique will serve as a crucial tool for evaluating the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa quark interaction matrix and for further refining the measurements of highly rare, shortest-lived atomic isotopes. This approach is expected to significantly expand the scope of one-proton, one-neutron nucleus studies. Additionally, precise mass readings for $^{54}$Fe and $^{54}$Co have enabled researchers to calculate the nuclear binding energy difference between the isobaric pairs $^{54}$Ca and $^{54}$Co, and $^{54}$Fe and $^{54}$Co, yielding values of 1234 keV and 932 keV, respectively. This study represents the first report of a nuclear mass difference measured using the mass spectrometry technique. Overall, the Bρ-IMS method has shown exceptional promise for opening up new avenues of research in the field of exotic nucleus physics. This approach is particularly suited for accurately measuring the masses of very short-lived, unusual atomic isotopes with a range of frequencies from a few tens of thousands to several million, and with a variety of atomic mass values up to 80. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the cross-sectional measurement for isolated electrons or muons in association with high transverse momentum jets was found to be 26 nanobarns with a 4-nanobarn uncertainty, matching theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. The study represents the first reporting of isolated electron or muon production in association with four or more jets from proton-lead data. Furthermore, the isolation of top quark pairs in association with high transverse momentum jets was found to be within theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics, with the isolation effect measured as 1.07 ± 0.09, within the 68% confidence interval, factorizing the contributions from underlying event and single-parton scattering. The study's results are crucial for understanding quark and antiquark scattering and confirming that top quark pairs can be effectively separated from background events in proton-lead data. The findings open the door for further top quark and vector boson investigations in proton-lead data with higher luminosity. The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDR Lasso) model offers a computationally efficient solution to handle complex data analysis. Introduced as a parameter-free and adaptive alternative to traditional Lasso methods, HDR Lasso has been shown to outperform other models in adaptive and model-agnostic settings, such as multiple testing and change-point detection. Mathematically, HDR Lasso is a nonconvex optimization problem that converges to the global optimum due to an established convex convexification method. In this paper, an accelerated HDR Lasso algorithm is proposed by capitalizing on nonconvex characteristics. Drawing inspiration from nonconvex optimization techniques, this faster HDR Lasso algorithm leverages the first-order stationary point property, achieving convergence to the global optimum at a reduced computational cost. In particular, the new method requires only n/2 iterations of the convex convexification procedure, leading to faster solution times, particularly for large data sets. The enhanced algorithm retains the adaptive and model-agnostic features of HDR Lasso, making it suitable for a broad range of applications, including multiple testing and change-point detection, where the underlying parameters are unknown. Empirical evaluations confirm that the accelerated algorithm emulates the statistical performance of HDR Lasso across various statistical challenges, such as false discovery rates and prediction losses, while significantly decreasing computational costs by 50%. The research code can be accessed at https://github.com/arkhshl/Accelerated-HDR-Lasso. In particular, the multiple testing application in Figure 1 shows that the faster algorithm emits relevant signals earlier in the iterations, enhancing its practical usefulness. In line with the blind algorithm nature of HDR Lasso, the advantages of the accelerated algorithm are automatically achieved, necessitating no additional adjustments from the user. In conclusion, the study presents an HDR Lasso algorithm that balances statistical performance and computational efficiency, paving the way for broader HDR Lasso applications in high-dimensional data analysis. In particular, the faster algorithm has promising implications for large-scale empirical research and data analysis tasks. We have developed a model that captures how individuals with limited confidence in their judgments form opinions based on their personal relationships. We considered scenarios with both balanced and uneven numbers of agents, who are influenced by the opinions of their friends or enemies within a confined boundary. Our findings reveal the intricate effects of mutual friendships and antagonism, leading to system breakdown or the emergence of stable, polarized states. However, the outcome depends on the initial conditions and the parameters that govern interpersonal relationships. Our analysis delves into the dynamics of friendship dynamics, enemy formation, and opinion segmentation within the framework of our model. The model blends a mechanistic approach with a flexible statistical method, incorporating uncertainty into the calculations through Bayesian estimation. Chiral SU(N) gauge theories, consisting of Weyl fermions and additional fermions, are examined to analyze their dynamics. An older suggestion by Bars and Yankielowicz to match the theory's 't Hooft anomalies with those of free fermions is revisited, resulting in novel constraints for the large N limit of SU(N) theories. Specifically, this leads to an anomaly equivalence with fundamental SU(N) theories, consisting of N chiral Weyl fermions and additional fermions. We introduce a new efficient framework for representing functions in graphical models, which serves as a foundation for a variety of computational tasks. Our method involves expressing functions as deterministic finite state automata (DFAs) and proposing DFA-based approaches for tasks such as marginalization, belief propagation, and factorization. The visual appearance and auditory qualities of an object provide dual insights into its material properties.  In everyday situations, information from vision and hearing arrive simultaneously, but the integration of asynchronous cues is essential, as seen when we locate an object dropped on the ground after hearing its fall.  In this paper, a multi-sensory system is proposed to identify and locate objects based on auditory cues and visual object characteristics gathered from a database of objects.  The system comprises three modules.  First, 3D sound localization algorithms are used to estimate the position of the object dropped.  Then, a multi-view retrieval module is applied to object images gathered from various viewpoints to pinpoint the object's visual appearance.  Finally, a multi-modal object localization module integrates the object's position from both the auditory and visual systems to produce a precise estimation of its location.  The performance of this system was evaluated using simulated and real recordings of objects dropped, yielding an average localization error of less than 0.5 meters in simulated environments and approximately 1.1 meters in real recordings.  The proposed method provides an innovative solution for object localization in complex environments.  The code is available at https://github.com/ashishsharma25/Object_Loc, along with related data at https://drive.google.com/drive/folderview/1sV9T_tOoQG4Y7QY7pQG4Y7QY7PQG4Y7QY7PQG4Y7PQG4Y7PQG4Y7PQG4Y7P?usp=sharing. Compositional data analysis is a technique that deals with complex datasets, which consist of several interdependent components summing to a constant value. Common constant values are 1 and 100%. This type of data is commonly found in disciplines such as biochemistry, geochemistry, and the social sciences. Researchers often examine compositional data in "omics" studies with extremely large dimensions. The method involves performing standard transformations on the data to achieve uniformly distributed variances on each dimension. The most well-known of these transformations is the Simple Ratios Transformation (SRT), which yields a metric space with desirable properties. However, the SRT has some drawbacks: it can cannot handle extremely large data sets due to computational limitations, and the results it yields are difficult to interpret. To address these issues, we present the Advanced Ratios Transformation (ART), which is based on the generalized Simple Ratios formula. The study confirms that ART produces a metric space with useful characteristics, such as positive definiteness and the Laplace distribution. Additionally, ART facilitates the creation of profiles, or focused compositions, which are easily interpretable and useful for dimensionality reduction in complex datasets. To illustrate its effectiveness, we apply ART to a real-world biochemistry dataset in a supervised setting. The results show that ART's use leads to improved classification accuracy and more reliable predictive models. Artificial intelligence models, modeled after biological agents, can regulate their awareness by restricting their input from the environment to minimize information overload. A new method we put forth learns control of a focused "spotlight" in the artificial intelligence by boosting its comprehension of correlations between the external world and its focus, at each step of processing.  To achieve this, an internal mental map of its condition is developed which makes predictions about where it may need more information. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires considerable effort,
so many researchers opt for pre-training their model on a different task before
further refining it using a smaller annotated dataset. Top-notch approaches
traditionally rely on image classification for pre-training, a method which can
be marred by uncontrollable biases. To investigate a more effective method, we
proposed that depth estimation using untagged videos might be a better choice
for pre-training. Although this method lacks any meaningful scene details, we
assert that calculating the three-dimensional geometry of scenes is closer to
the goal of semantic segmentation than assigning broad image classifications.
Lacking an analytical method for validating our hypothesis, we conducted an
experimental evaluation that demonstrated our pre-training scheme produced an
improvement of 5.7% mean intersection over union and 4.1% pixel accuracy in
comparison to classification-based pre-training. Notably, although we were able
to bypass annotation during pre-training, it is indispensable for assessing our
proposed scheme's effectiveness. To validate our findings, we employed the
popular KITTI (outdoor) and NYU-V2 (indoor) benchmarking datasets, where
lacking annotations would render the evaluation unreliable. By manually
countering potential bias in deep neural network training, we confirmed our
findings could be replicated, and our proposed pre-training scheme became the
state-of-the-art in deep semantic segmentation, according to the evaluated
datasets. Moreover, calculating three-dimensional geometries significantly
enhanced the segmentation performance in comparison to the classification-
based method. When used in conjunction with recurrent neural networks, our
method produced an additional improvement of 6.9% mean intersection over union
and 4.9% pixel accuracy in comparison to the classification-based pre-training
scheme. Finally, we note that our pre-training scheme can be applied to a wide
variety of other computer vision tasks. To facilitate the replication of our
study, we made our source code available at github.com/fatemehkarimrezi.

The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is extremely important in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, trade analysis, stock market monitoring, and sales forecasting. Currently, domain-specific time-series narration methods rely on predefined templates that ensure consistency but often produce mechanical, uninspired narratives. In contrast, we introduce TCube, a neural framework that can describe time-series data in a universal way without being tied to a particular domain. TCube represents essential time-series elements using a knowledge graph, which is then translated into coherent, engaging stories by leveraging the strengths of pre-trained language models. Since there's a scarcity of labeled data for time-series, TCube incorporates a knowledge graph to make the translation process feasible. This innovative approach opens the door for exploring new applications in fields where tailored solutions exist, such as personalized narratives and interactive, story-driven data analysis. Furthermore, TCube offers various options to control the level of formality in the generated stories, thereby providing high quality, accurate descriptions. Extensive experiments were conducted across multiple domains to validate TCube's effectiveness, and the system is live on github, ready to use. TCube generates stories about the COVID-19 pandemic, stock market trends, and seismic activity that can be found at: https://github.com/ai4sm/TCube. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort involves repeated link sharing activities, where 82.5% of all links are external and 57.0% consist of frequently shared resources. To streamline users' knowledge management, this study delves into the characteristics of these shared links to identify common patterns in external resources that are repeatedly disseminated. Our research focuses on Stack Overflow, where analysis reveals that links to text-based documentation, tutorials, and other reference materials are most often reshared. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Additionally, we have computed the mass and radius of spin-polarized strange quark stars under distinct conditions. Moreover, we have plotted the dimensionless curvature scalar and the magnetic field strength within the framework of the Hartle-Thawley theory for spin-polarized strange quark stars. Our analysis shows that the application of the strong magnetic field has a significant impact on the thermodynamic characteristics, mass, radius, curvature scalar, and the behavior of spin-polarized strange quark stars across temperatures. Our results suggest that the maximum mass of spin-polarized strange quark stars under the influence of a strong magnetic field is significantly higher compared to the mass in the absence of a strong magnetic field. We have observed the maximum mass of spin-polarized strange quark stars to be 7.881 times higher than the Chandrasekhar limit. We have also derived the adiabatic index for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and our results indicate that it is predominantly determined by the magnetic field strength. A surge in personal device ownership offers an immense, yet largely underutilized resource of computational power, making it feasible to utilize it. To harness this potential, we developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system based on declarative concurrent programming, and powered by JavaScript, WebRTC, and WebSockets. By employing a dynamic network of unreliable, volunteer-sourced personal devices and their browsers, Pando facilitates parallel execution of a function on multiple values, thus enhancing efficiency on compute-intensive applications like animation rendering and image processing. Furthermore, our approach's adaptability is demonstrated through Pando's deployment across a range of platforms, encompassing local networks, Grid5000, and PlanetLab's distributed nodes spanning across Europe. Although focused primarily on numerical computation, Pando's design excels in being modular, user-friendly, and adaptable, with potential for extension to other application domains in the future. Declarative programming's inherent simplicity, in particular, reduces the risk of coding-related errors, encompassing issues like volatility, node imbalance, and data transfer, which Pando addresses through innovative techniques, such as data partitioning and checkpointing. To showcase Pando's full feature set, we describe its implementation of an additive blend, a characteristic example of operations suitable for parallel execution in the volunteer computing context. Our evaluation, encompassing over 150 nodes and across various application domains, reveals a substantial speedup in computation time. For instance, a 30-frame animation typically takes around 10 seconds to generate on a single node. When distributed across 8-10 nodes, the same task completes in under 2 seconds. Our analysis spots opportunities for further improvement, including the integration of load balancing, more efficient transport of large data, and the implementation of a dynamic node management strategy to match the structure of the computation task with the topology of the volunteer node network more closely. Future enhancements to Pando could also involve the handling of user-driven parallel computation, the expansion to support streaming-based applications, and the exploration of other concurrent program patterns, such as dataflow or pipeline, to further boost performance and efficiency. To facilitate this advancement, the associated source code is available under the permissive Berkeley Software Distribution license, providing full accessibility to the Pando framework. Our research on Pando contributes to the field of volunteer computing by introducing innovative concepts, like the dynamic creation of a volunteer computing system from a network of personal devices, and novel high-level parallel computation patterns, leading to significant speedups and more efficient volunteer usage. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results, such as a comprehensive formula for the Hausdorff dimension of the set that arises when a hole is placed at zero in an interval. Our analysis also covers various other properties, including asymptotic distances, occurence frequencies, and the structure of its non-flat parts of a given point's beta-transformative image. Moreover, we establish a connection between the shift maps on one-sided shifts defined by sequences related to these beta-transformations and the set of double sequences that are 'in standard position' as per Arztone's classification, while also showing that the associated Hausdorff dimensions can be matched through a specific mapping. Furthermore, we extend Kudinov's result from 1972, which concerned the number of distinct values produced by iterating a non-degenerate interval with a beta-transformation, to our specific case of incorporating a hole at zero. Lastly, we address a question posed by Trivizilla in 2017 regarding the uniqueness of any given greedy beta-transformation that has a hole at zero that is similar to a non-degenerate interval beta-transformation. Our analysis shows that such uniqueness holds when the corresponding beta-transformation does not have a flat image, specifically when its first iteration does not equal the original interval. However, we found that flat images do exist for certain beta-transformations with holes at zero, which in turn led us to identify a set of sequences, denoted as $\mathscr{R}$, where the first iteration of a beta-transformation with a hole at zero and sequence in $\mathscr{R}$ is always the original interval, with the added condition that its image is flat. One of the key properties in this set $\mathscr{R}$ is that the sequence that corresponds to the shift map on one-sided shifts defined by sequences related to beta-transformations with a hole at zero is a double sequence in'standard position' as per Arztone's classification, with additional properties, specifically that its third component is consistently zero, while its eighth component is non-zero. Our findings also reveal that there are an infinite number of distinct elements present in set $\mathscr{R}$. Lastly, we address a more general property, specifically that beta-transformations with a hole at zero that are flat and non-degenerate over a non-degenerate interval

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee - an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both training and communication times, while remaining robust against adversarial manipulation. Evaluations confirm that Flatee outperforms existing solutions, with only negligible effects on model privacy. The framework is accessible on our website. \href{https://github.com/Cheng-Li/Flatee}{GitHub} \href{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8v1HnVRLrEw}{YouTube}. Trust has driven significant advancements in developing zero-trust networks, but - surprisingly - it has not been leveraged for mitigating privacy breaches in machine learning applications. This study rectifies this disparity by harnessing the privacy safeguards offered by Trusted Execution Environments (TEE), to establish a private and efficient federated learning system called Flatee. This novel system relies on TEEs to protect both data and model, specificially designed for parallel hardware architectures (e.g. Xeon Phi, GPUs), to safeguard against unauthorized access, while enabling secure data sharing towards developing shared machine learning models. Unlike current end-to-end encryption based solutions that result in high computational overhead due to cipher-decipher operations, Flatee takes a different approach by integrating with computing platforms that support hardware-based security. By combining both data and model encryption, Flatee offers an efficient and scalable solution for private federated learning that minimizes both training time and data transmission delays. The framework has been validated on several public datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Fashion MNIST for various models including CNN, ResNet, and MobileNet, with an accelerated training speed of up to 38 times the existing solutions. The proposed Flatee has been made available on an online repository \href{https://github.com/Cheng-Li/Flatee}{GitHub}. The embedded systems industry is massive and ubiquitous, as evidenced by its presence in most of the world's produced processors. Interactions between drivers and external components like sensors and actuators pose significant challenges to embedded software development and testing. Failing to simulate these interactions effectively can lead to delayed discoveries of software errors, making them harder to identify and fix. Existing solutions often require extensive modifications to the software and/or the testing environment, which is both laborious and costly. Alternatively, a more practical approach involves using a simulation framework to mimic the behavior of external peripherals in real-time within the device's firmware. This allows software testing to take place sooner, be more efficient, and save resources. And, as an added bonus, such a framework can also facilitate rapid prototyping of control algorithms before the hardware is available. By mimicking the behavior of sensors and actuators, a software simulator can enable real-time traffic, including periodic and aperiodic transactions, to flow between the test code and the simulator. This traffic can be generated by the real-time operating system itself, which can be configured to correspond to the target system's operational conditions. Furthermore, the simulator can also produce dynamic scenes, such as trajectories within an game engine like Unity, to simulate scenarios like vehicle driving. By using this approach, even small systems can run sophisticated applications that were previously only feasible on larger systems. We have used this method to test a remote control driver on a tiny system, consisting of a Raspberry Pi and a Flight Simulator HU, where the driver had to interact with the Flight Simulator via a Bluetooth connection. This involved using the Bluetooth HCI socket interface to exchange data with a Bluetooth module. Our results show that this method can successfully detect and highlight software errors, which in turn enable the development of a working driver for remote control systems. For example, we found that when testing the driver's connection establishment process on the Raspberry Pi, a software error caused a system crash. This means that while the driver was able to connect to the Flight Simulator, the connection was lost as soon as we started the testing process. This kind of issue is typical of the type of software interactions being tested here. We were able to verify that the cause of this bug was a incorrect implementation of the driver's code responsible for handling data traffic from the Flight Simulator. By fixing this error, we were able to successfully test the driver's ability to establish a connection to the Flight Simulator, which in turn enabled the remote control driver to work seamlessly with the Flight Simulator. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls required by an application, and block any system calls deviating from these norms. In comparison to existing static analysis-based methods, Timeloops yields more accurate results by reducing false positives. Additionally, Timeloops supports dynamic learning rules and can adapt to changes in application behavior. The author's evaluation reveals that Timeloops can determine an accurate set of system calls for 88% of applications without human intervention, and achieves significant performance gains over static analysis-based methods. Furthermore, Timeloops can detect security threats such as RCE and SQL injection more effectively. Advanced techniques for representing complex data in compact forms involve the embedding of product spaces. We have found that linear classifiers can effectively capture complex patterns in not only Euclidean (e.g. 2D, 3D) but also non-Euclidean geometries, such as spherical surfaces. Our galactic center, located at a distance of only 15 parsecs from the heart of the Milky Way, is exceptional in its proximity to a supermassive black hole. After decades of observation, the area surrounding this black hole has been populated by a vast array of stars originating from multiple early formations. However, the number of these stars has been found to decline significantly near the center due to gravitational force from the black hole, as if they were avoiding it. Researchers have now used years' worth of motion tracking for over 140 stars located within a distance of about 1 parsec from the center to distinguish the effect of the black hole's gravity from other factors. Their analysis took into consideration various disturbances caused by the presence of an unseen, disk-shaped structure of unmixed star populations as well as uneven illumination from both nearby and distant regions. They discovered that both factors played a significant role and initially masked the black hole's gravity's effect, but once these other disturbances were accounted for, the stars' motion showed clear evidence of being impacted by the black hole's gravity alone. This breakthrough has significant implications for the study of similar supermassive black holes in the far distant past. If similar systems exist in the center of our galaxy and other galaxies, they can no longer be hidden, and the process by which supermassive black holes formed can be better understood. Additionally, the study provides valuable insights regarding the early development of the galaxy and the mixing of its star populations. It suggests that these stars were initially arranged in specific, spiral patterns and underwent an extensive mixing process about 7 billion years ago. Their analysis further reveals an unexpected uneven distribution of star light in the galaxy, which varies in specific patterns at different wavelengths and scales. When considering all these factors together, the researchers discovered an unexpected, unevenly mixed structure of unmixed star populations extending out to a significant distance from the center of the galaxy. This complex pattern shows a gradual, continuous change and repeated patterns at varying distances from the center, which may be connected to an unevenly distributed, rotating disk of unmixed star populations. Despite initial expectations, the researchers discovered no evidence of a previously proposed "bar" structure in the center of the galaxy. However, the presence of an unevenly distributed, rotating disk of unmixed star populations is thought to be responsible for the galaxy's characteristic shape and can easily be confused with other structures. For example, the shape of the galaxy's stellar structure appears to be primarily determined by an unevenly distributed, rotating disk of unmixed star populations

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, coexistence of both species, or an abrupt transition between these states depending on immigration parameters. The model also exhibits a complex life cycle where the dominant species' temporary success can trigger a switch to another species' dominance in a noisy environment, which can be slowed down by increasing the distance over which the underdog species can immigrate. The critical distance for this underdog advantage was found to increase with the strength of external noise. The model was also applied to studies of species coexistence and the evolution of migratory behavior in real ecosystems, such as the coexistence of babbling brook crickets and the possible benefits of long-distance migration in red deer. The theoretical framework of the model can be generalized for any pair of species with different colonization abilities. The underdog advantage dynamics in this model can be visualized using time-series data and explained using mean-field theory, which provides a fundamental concept for the analysis of species competition and the development of more realistic species competition models in biology. The model can be simulated using the Python package PySTEMSim, which is included in the supplementary materials of this study. The package can be applied to various biological systems, such as the colonization of species in the invasion of a new environment by a superior species driving others to extinction. The model can be extended to studies of species that switch between different types of migration using time and frequency analyses, such as the annual migration patterns of red deer, which can be investigated using real data from deer studies. The model can be modified to examine the impact of environmental factors, such as the availability of resources, on species competition and the evolution of migratory behavior in those species. The model can be simulated for different biological systems, such as the species mentioned above, using different parameters to describe their unique colonizations behaviors. The model can be used to investigate the role of genetic factors in species competition and the evolution of migratory behavior in real ecosystems, such as the coexistence of two species with different colonization abilities in an ecosystem. The model can be applied to studies of species extinctions and the importance of dispersal in preserving species diversity.

To resolve this complex problem, we utilize a two-stage approach: first, we determine optimal D2D transmission power and IRS reflection coefficients through a proposed iterative method. This two-stage approach enables us to efficiently solve the power control problem despite the non-convex nature of the resulting optimization problem. The cardinalities of finite models for sentences with at least three variables and binary relations are examined in this study.  Specifically, we demonstrate that any such sentence, denoted as $\Phi$, has a corresponding sentence, denoted as $\Phi'$, utilizing the same number of variables and one symmetric binary relation, whose set of model cardinalities increases linearly with $\Phi$'s model cardinalities. Furthermore, we observe that the models of sentence $\Phi'$ are all bipartite graph representations.  Consequently, we deduce that, in order to resolve Asser's conjecture regarding the class's closure under complement, we may focus solely on examining sentences with at most three variables whose models consist of undirected bipartite graphs.  We also establish an algorithm as well as determine a lower bound for the complexity of determining if a given sentence, $\Phi$, and its complementary sentence, $\Phi'$, have models of the same cardinality.  Finally, we prove that determining if the complementary sentence, $\Phi'$$, has a model of the same cardinality and at most the same number of variables, is indeed harder than resolving Asser's conjecture.  In contrast, we demonstrate that, when the number of variables is fixed and greater than 3, deciding whether the complementary sentence, $\Phi'$, has a model of the same cardinality and at most the same number of variables, is relatively easier and can be resolved through a fixed-point approach in polynomial time. Drawing inspiration from Feynman's and Deutsch's groundbreaking work, we introduce a theoretical framework that assesses computational capability across diverse physical platforms and complexity scales. This framework is utilized to analyze the fundamental principles of quantum computation. Furthermore, this study serves as a precursor to investigating more universal computation models by examining additional physical mechanisms exemplified throughout the paper. The central idea behind this framework is the concept of Computational Complexity Theory applied to fundamental physical relationships governed by the Schrödinger equation. In this context, a physical system can be viewed as a computational device capable of performing operations on input states to produce output states. The number of distinct output states it can generate, along with its ability to vary the probabilities between them, can be regarded as a measure of its computational capacity. This concept aligns with the idea of simulating the behavior of other physical systems. Based on this idea, we examine the role of physical parameters in relation to the capabilities of computational systems. The approach of analyzing the computational capacity of physical systems also enables the comparison of fundamental principles underlying the operation of these systems. The study of these physical mechanisms contributes to the evolution of complexity theory, which in turn informs the development of more universal computation models. Ultimately, this research aims to understand the physical limitations of computational systems by generalizing the principles of quantum computation and applying them to other physical mechanisms. The general strategy is to start with the most complex physical mechanisms, such as quantum computation, and then work backwards to less complex mechanisms, such as the fundamental principles of classical computation. The ultimate goal is to identify the most essential features of computational systems and to explore the physical reality that gives rise to these fundamental principles. The key to this framework lies in the relationship between the complexity of physical mechanisms and the complexity of the computations they can perform. The development of this framework is crucial for the ongoing project of analyzing the computational capacity of fundamental physical parameters. The project aims to identify the most essential features of computational systems and the physical parameters that give rise to these fundamental principles. The approach is similar to how physicists identify the most essential features of physical systems by experimenting with weaker versions of fundamental parameters. This study focused on determining the general formula for calculating the potential positions of an $n$ step random walk in a $d$ dimensional space with a single unit step size. The general formula specifically counts the number of distinct random walk paths starting from the origin within an $n$ step process in a $d$ dimensional space. The given formula is generally considered to be the most flexible and applicable solution to this problem. Furthermore, this study verified that the given formula is indeed the correct representation by proving it through mathematical induction. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. Additionally, the isothermal compressibility reveals a temperature-independent behavior. These results are also relevant to other two-dimensional systems of massless Dirac fermions. Furthermore, we use the thermal capacity to determine the thermal screening length of these Dirac electrons at finite temperatures. Our predictions can be verified through experiments utilizing x-ray scattering, low-field magnetometry, and calculations involving Raman scattering. This research also paves the way for similar studies of other 2D Dirac fermions in materials such as surface states of topological insulators and ultra-thin layers of transition metal compounds. Additionally, the work may contribute to advancements in the understanding of massless Weyl fermions that may emerge in certain materials. Lastly, the study is relevant to recent proposals for using graphene in quantum thermal states and matter-wave interferometry with graphene. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware speech synthesis system that incorporates contextual features. It employs a contextual encoder which extracts contextual audio, a contextual classifier that identifies speech status in paragraphs, and a contextual editor that adapts phoneme production based on paragraph context and speech status. During training, contextual information is masked and replaced with special tokens. While base models rely on context during inference time, we introduce a novel training method - Optimal Masking - that trains contextual models to choose the most relevant context for each utterance. Evaluations reveal that MaskedSpeech yields significant improvements over standard speech synthesis models. Optimal Masking further boosts its performance, achieving an average decrease of 12.5% in sentence-level variance in acoustic parameters compared to baseline models. The contextual editor achieves an average reduction of 14.6% in sentence-level variance in acoustic parameters after incorporating context. An external listener assessment confirms the relevance of contextual information for paragraph-level variation in acoustic parameters, supporting the claim that contextual information contributes substantially to paragraph-level speech synthesis. In addition, we identified the relevant contextual information through analysis of prior works and an external listener assessment. Prior works have demonstrated the relevance of sentence-level contextual information for basic speech parameters and mel-frequency cepstral coefficients. An external listener assessment revealed the significance of sentence-level contextual information for spectral tensor characteristics, but not for basic speech parameters or mel-frequency cepstral coefficients. These findings align with the system's designed objective, stressing the need for more sophisticated features like spectral tensor characteristics for paragraph-level speech synthesis.
