Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that demonstrates the feasibility of combining multiple treatment instruments with ranked preference data, we analyze the testable implications of the key assumptions underpinning their identification argument. This analysis also offers a novel assessment of the biases resulting from these assumption violations. Ultimately, these findings empower researchers to evaluate the reliability of these assumptions and determine the practical impact of their breaches. Utilizing the identified method, we investigate the post-secondary field of study return on investment in Norway and Denmark, exploring potential cross-country differences. Our results indicate significant positive effects of both Norwegian and Danish fields of study on earnings, although the effects are more pronounced in Norway. We also uncover notable field-specific variations in both countries. This study is the first to compare the social returns on investment of various fields of study in Norway and Denmark. Our analysis is conducted using two identified sets of complementary instruments. First, we combine the choice of high school and university with the choice of university location. Second, we combine the choice of high school with the choice of university and university major. Our key assumption of 'local laboratory' style identification, which posits that individual choices are influenced solely by their own characteristics and choices of other 'treatment' variables, may face challenges in fields such as education where social networks and peer effects are prevalent. To address this issue, we stress the practical importance of evaluating the reliability of these assumptions rather than solely relying on our results. We found that neither Norwegian nor Danish fields of study were found to be completely unreliable; however, our results do suggest that the reliability of some individual fields may be considered marginal. We discovered that the least reliable fields were not necessarily those with lower returns on investment but rather those with weaker individual identification. Our analysis also highlights the necessity of conducting field-specific reliability assessments. We found both Norwegian and Danish fields of study to have some reliable options but also identified some challenging areas for improvement. Our study contributes to the existing literature in several ways. Firstly, we showcase the practical utility of combining multiple treatment instruments in the context of ranked preference data. Our study also offers novel insights into the testable implications of key assumption breaches in identified contexts. Lastly, our analysis provides the first cross-country comparison of return on investment in Norwegian and Danish fields of study. This study benefits from the synergy between existing literature on ranked preference data and identified treatment effects, combining these insights with existing knowledge on the social returns on investment in fields of study. This study is also closely related to the existing literature in several areas.

This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their stability and discuss the potential implications for homogeneity in the distribution of such matter. We then develop a simplified model to study the universe's evolution over time and how it is influenced by vacuum energy and matter, both with and without perfect cosmological closure. We discover that an intrinsically flat spacetime has distinct properties compared to the currently preferred lambda-CDM model and may be characterized by a universe with matter, but without dark energy or a non-zero cosmological constant. We also find that an intrinsically flat spacetime can be a solution to the "cosmic tension issue" by featuring a Hubble parameter with time-dependent properties. We conclude that intrinsically flat spacetimes present an interesting and viable possibility for understanding our universe and contribute to the ongoing discussion on its proper modeling. Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) contain incredibly massive black holes at their center that rotate at extremely high speeds. Measuring the mass and rotational speed of these black holes is extremely challenging but attempting to do so allows scientists to better understand the processes that power AGNs and drive star formation in galaxies. Current methods for determining black hole mass and spin rely on complex and difficult to interpret data analysis but a new more straightforward approach has been developed to estimate the mass and rotational speed of black holes in AGNs based on the spectral distribution of their electromagnetic radiation. This new technique uses the continuum and spectral peak of AGN radiation to accurately determine the mass and rotational speed of the black holes for the first time. Testing this approach on a specific AGN yielded a mass estimate consistent with other methods for the first time. Additionally, the technique revealed that the black holes of narrow-line AGNs are slower and have less massive counterparts than would be expected. Further study found that the rate of black hole growth is generally less than the rate of gas supply in AGNs, which may indicate the black holes are inefficiently feeding on the surrounding matter. In contrast, the technique revealed that the rate of black hole growth in AGNs with a prominent emission line is sometimes higher than the rate of gas supply, which could suggest the black holes are able to efficiently feed on the surrounding matter in these cases. In conclusion, the technique offers a new and efficient way to study the growth of black holes in AGNs, which may lead to a greater understanding of the processes that power and regulate the growth of these black holes. This research was based on data from the XMM-Newton and Chandra X-ray observatories. Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, which entails extensive testing on various applications. In this context, an open-source emulator is presented, designed to simulate loop-type neuromorphic systems built using Field Programmable Logic Arrays (FPGAs). The emulator accurately replicates the behavior of neural connections, dynamic neural responses, and input data filtering processes. In addition to the emulator, a set of benchmark circuits in Verilog has also been developed to test and evaluate neuromorphic systems based on FPGA-based architectures. Benchmark results indicate a substantial speedup in application performance, along with significant energy and area savings. The details of this emulator, as well as benchmark circuits, can be accessed through an open-source platform at https://github.com/NeuroLogicArchitecture/emulator. This resource aims to facilitate and accelerate innovations in neuromorphic systems built using FPGAs. Furthermore, a set of suggestions is provided for integrating the emulator into educational curricula, thereby promoting hands-on learning and experiential training in the design of neuromorphic systems. To this end, a simplified, classroom-friendly example embodies the core principles of the emulator in its functionality. This example serves as a gateway to the emulator's advanced features. With the emulator as a versatile tool, users can explore a broad range of scenarios, such as varying FPGA architectures, synaptic weight distributions, input data patterns, and dynamic neural response characteristics. The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.  Comparatively, manual data entry required around 270 minutes for the same set of images.  Thus, the proposed system significantly reduced processing time while offering decent accuracy.  Further improvements can still be made to boost its performance.  To validate the effectiveness of this system in real-world settings, testing was conducted at three different document service centers.  Results from these tests revealed a high success rate of 97% and an average extraction time of 6.2 seconds.  Users at these service centers also reported a positive response to the implementation of this ID card extraction system.  Based on these results, it is anticipated that similar outcomes will be yielded by other similar document service centers in the future.  Ultimately, the introduction of this ID card extraction system has streamlined the document service process at these centers, from both the service operators' and customers' perspectives.  This has consequently reduced the time required to complete each transaction.  Therefore, the proposed system may be viewed as a pioneering effort in the document service field.  This systematic approach to ID card extraction can also be applied to other types of documents in the future.  In conclusion, the benefits derived from this ID card extraction system far surpass its drawbacks, and it is hoped that it will be beneficial to other similar document service centers in the future. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving substantial reductions in computational complexity. The outcomes also highlight the importance of pilot allocation in channel tracking accuracy and suggest suitable DHL architectures for channel estimation. The proposed solution is further realized using MatConvNet and demonstrated on a Texas Instrument Jacinto TSI310F single-board system for its feasibility in real-world applications. The MatConvNet-based network is found to provide superior performance while requiring minimal memory and processing power, thus facilitating its potential use in embedded systems. The proposed solution is also evaluated on a Tesla P1000 GPU for its maximal network architecture scalability. Lastly, the proposed solution is evaluated on actual channel recordings from hardware, which confirms its superiority over competing DL-based estimators in various vehicular channel conditions. The MatConvNet-based network is found to provide accurate estimates of up to 7.1 bits/s Hz, with a corresponding packet success rate of up to 0.94, and significantly outperforms the competing DL-based estimators by 3.5, 2.1, 2.2, 2.6, and 2.9 bits/s Hz in the diverse vehicular channel conditions. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach for astronomical images captured by the Kepler telescope. These images are typically small and around 100 x 100 pixels in size, with the added complication that they often appear blue due to noise rather than true blue objects. To address this, a convolutional neural network (CNN) was developed to learn and apply color information from full-frame images to the specified image regions. The network was designed to utilize context information from full-frame images and apply color information to the target image regions. To facilitate this, an extended U-Net structure was employed, allowing the network to incorporate context information from full-frame images and apply color information to the target image regions. The network was tested using pairs of astrophysical images and synthetic full-frame images, with the astrophysical image serving as the target image. The results revealed a significant improvement in colorization quality when compared to a straightforward blue overlay on the astrophysical image. To validate the efficacy of the proposed approach, a detailed comparison was conducted with SCDN, a deep learning-based algorithm designed for colorization tasks. However, SCDN was found to be incompatible with the astrophysical image dataset used in this research. To create colorizations for various image types, a dataset was constructed by applying the network to multiple full-frame pairs. The resulting colorizations were compared with those produced by the SCDN algorithm. Ultimately, a qualitative evaluation was conducted to compare the output of the proposed approach with that of SCDN. The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation. It serves as a useful reference for current and future panel members. 

Key activities during the first two years included:

1. Establishing the panel's operational structure by appointing a chair and members along with defining its role and scope within ECFA.
2. Developing a survey to gather input from young researchers on key topics such as their involvement in ECFA activities and preferred communication methods.
3. Analyzing the results of the survey and identifying patterns or areas for improvement in how ECFA interacts with young researchers.
4. Creating a subgroup to focus on the findings of the survey and suggest potential actions to address its outcomes.
5. Organizing a workshop where young researchers could present their work and engage in discussions on various topics including physics research and accelerator science.
6. Selecting and presenting outreach activities that the panel can undertake to enhance its profile and contribute to ECFA's events.
7. Confirming the panel's representation at ECFA meetings and ensuring that the panel's interests are represented in key decisions affecting young researchers within ECFA.

Some of the key discoveries resulting from the survey include:

* Young researchers within ECFA primarily learn about its activities through email and social media instead of other possible methods such as newsletters or dedicated websites.
* There is a notable disparity in how different groups of young researchers engage with various forms of communication and potentially contribute to ECFA activities.
* When considering activities in which young researchers can participate, physics research and publishing in journals or conferences are highly prioritized, while other options receive less attention.
* Young researchers within ECFA can benefit from more visible opportunities to present their work and engage in discussions on their research and expertise.

In light of these findings, the panel suggests the following potential actions:

* Enhance visibility through social media and email by sharing relevant content such as job offers, research opportunities and newsletters to reach a broader audience.
* Host events such as workshops and conferences that provide young researchers with opportunities to present their work and engage in discussions on their research and expertise within their areas of expertise.

Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.

In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images and videos. However,
traditional MLPs have drawbacks in terms of their computational efficiency,
limited expressiveness, and inability to process high-resolution video content
efficiently. Some recent approaches have attempted to enhance MLPs by incorporating
non-linear interactions and expanded architecture designs. Nevertheless, these
modifications have yet to yield a universally optimal design. We introduce an
alternative architecture that builds upon a dual composition of MLPs, where two
distinct networks process video and image data independently. This dual design
allows for the separate capture of non-trivial interaction and temporal dynamics
in video content. Additionally, we propose an innovative method for dimensionality
reduction in video data by combining the compressed representations of frames
traversed in reverse and forward directions. This approach enables more effective
capture of temporal dynamics and produces superior qualitative results. We support
our design choices with thorough ablation studies and present state-of-the-art
results on benchmarks for video and image encoding. Our method may also be used
as a pre-trained starting point for video tasks such as anomalous event
detection. We provide the relevant code and pre-trained models for reproduction

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$, which is shown to be resilient against domain shifts in causal features. Moreover, this model leverages unlabelled data to directly map causes to their respective effects. Experiment results conducted on artificial data show considerable improvements in classification performance compared to solely-supervised and importance-weighting approaches. The proposed methodology has potential applications in handling domain shifts that can be justified by underlying causal mechanisms. An example of such an application is in medical image analysis, where causes (e.g. genetic properties) should be kept separate from effects (e.g. organs) when evaluating domain shift robustness. Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for CB230 IRS1 and L1165-SMM1 revealed a significantly higher mass range ($0.1-0.25 \, M_{\odot}$) than those generally obtained from binary formation simulations, which were around $0.01 \, M_{\odot}$. In response to these disparities, researchers carried out numerical simulations of a core's collapse to analyze how a binary system's formation mass is influenced by its parent core's overall mass. In these simulations, they implemented azimuthally symmetric mass seeds within a rotating core, promoting the development of a dense filament, where a binary system might emerge. This binary formation process decreased as the core's mass increased, prompting researchers to amplify the core's kinetic energy ratio to its gravitational energy. This alteration led to increased binary mass and enabled a more precise determination of how a system's mass is generated. Furthermore, researchers created a diagram to represent binary system formation based on total core mass and kinetic energy ratio. This study also recorded and presented various properties of proto-stellar fragments, including formation mass, thermal to gravitational energy ratio, and kinetic energy ratio. In particular, a fragment's thermal to gravitational energy ratio showed the opposite trend of binary formation mass, suggesting potential implications for a fragment's ability to maintain its mass. This could be linked to its ability to maintain its own magnetic field or be influenced by a core's magnetic field dynamics. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose PAPYER, a comprehensive dataset comprising online comments about public restroom hygiene, marked by an abundance of unfalsifiable claims. A collaborative human-AI pipeline is presented that uses a combination of machine and human intelligence to pinpoint the prevailing narratives, thereby outperforming existing large transformer models and unsupervised topic models. The findings reveal that a comprehensive dataset such as PAPYER is essential for developing effective narrative detection methods, and that collaborative models can successfully identify topical threads in online comments. Furthermore, this study highlights the significance of using human evaluators in assessing the accuracy of automatically generated narratives, thereby paving the way for future research in this domain. Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including unknown event origins and shifting event zones. Furthermore, multiple events may occur simultaneously in the same location, each with its own set of hashtags. Our proposed system, called the Hierarchy-based Multi-Event Detection and Tracking method, tackles these complexities by establishing a hierarchical event structure, with separate layers for detection and tracking. This enables us to identify multiple events at a single location and allows for real-time updates to dynamic event maps. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in resolving uncertainty about event co-existence and a related issue known as'same origin' - two of the critical obstacles in detecting and tracking social media events. This study's data was gathered from Twitter, with a focus on Chicago, Illinois, with specific examples including the 2015 Pride Parade and a protest against police violence. Our comparisons with current methods show that HMDT surpasses their performance in accuracy by 24.6% and outperforms them in response time by an average of 21.9%. Specifically, when the system is aware of an event's existence, it takes less than 18 seconds to pinpoint its location, which is a 7.14% improvement over the current best methods. Our system is now available online at http://hmdt.cs.uiuc.edu/. Future plans involve expanding the system's capabilities to incorporate more information about spatial coherence and diversifying the data sets to include social media data from various cultures and contexts. Ultimately, this will enable the system to detect and track a broader range of social media events more effectively. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning. We discovered that despite these compression techniques, the remaining model often performs poorly on the original dataset, and we found that there is no sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve accuracy comparable to the original model. Our findings suggest that NLP models may differ fundamentally from image classification models, and we propose the idea that the depth of these models could be an important factor. We observed that the combination of depth and the type of attention used within these models affects the existence and quality of the sparse sub-network. Our study also highlights the need for further research into the structure of these models, and we are sharing our code to facilitate future investigation, including our model implementation and the compression techniques used. Additionally, we are including extensive hyper-parameter configurations and nuclei datasets to expand the scope of our analysis. Our goal is to inspire the development of new methods to confirm the existence of the sparse sub-network, and we encourage the NLP community to participate in this endeavor. We intend to utilize this knowledge to derive insights that can improve the way these models are compressed, and potentially uncover new ways to reduce their size effectively. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To this end, we introduce a systematic approach to developing customized loss functions tailored to a specific classification task. By constraining these loss functions with prior knowledge, drawn from the Bayesian quasi-maximum entropy inference framework, we derive two novel loss functions. Our experimental findings validate the efficacy of these loss functions, as well as several other previously proposed alternatives, highlighting the broader lesson that the standard cross-entropy loss function may not always yield the optimal results. In light of these findings, we propose a simple, effective technique for dynamically adapting the loss function during training. Our analysis also sheds light on the robustness of the top-class neuron in the hard softmax layer. Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that are effective in addressing the electronic interactions within complex systems. Within the context of this framework, the various aspects of charge and spin correlations are extensively analyzed. The methodology is primarily employed in the investigation of electronic and magnetic properties in metals, yet has also been successfully applied to the study of electronic and phonon behaviors in metals that exhibit electronic or charge-density-wave behavior. The following article intends to provide an in-depth examination of the underlying principles of parquet theory and its subsequent modifications as they pertain to the stable states of these systems, including a comprehensive review of their rigorous mathematical underpinnings. The article specifically highlights the modifications introduced in the RPA and s-rubin parquet schemes. A detailed analysis of the relationship between parquet theory and its reformulations as well as the respective Gleason schemes will also be explored. The concluding section will summarize the key findings and discuss the future implications of these forms of parquet theory in the modeling of their respective stable states. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, combining quantitative and qualitative methods to identify patterns in the conversational flow. By developing a data framework that captured common incident-related information, researchers discovered dispatchers requested specific details from users, which varied based on incident types. Furthermore, emotion analysis and regression testing revealed a disparity in user response rates and emotion support provided by dispatchers. Notably, dispatchers' emotional support had a positive effect on user response rates, but negatively impacted rates when no support was given. These findings have significant implications for system design and highlight the need for system-designed interactions to balance organizational requirements with users' needs. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter' Dirac cones' gap closes under a certain transverse magnetic field, leading to enhanced magnetic susceptibility. Furthermore, we find that in the nematic state, this magnetic field effect is proportional to the superconducting symmetry breaking parameter. Notably, in the chiral state, the linearly varying gap size results in divergent magnetic susceptibility at a specific field value. Additionally, comparing our results to existing experiments, we suggest that the observed behavior of magnetic field-dependent specific heat in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ could be attributed to nematic or chiral superconducting responses. Lastly, we examine how the superconducting symmetry and resulting specific heat response in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ may be affected by surface ferromagnetism. Our analysis suggests that even a minute ferromagnetic surface layer can induce a significant phase transition from the chiral to the nematic state, thus potentially regulating the critical magnetic field of the superconducting transition. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, these methods have limitations, with uncertainty-based techniques disregarding important data points and diversity-based methods ignoring contradictory information, both of which are commonly seen in real-world datasets. In response, this paper introduces a novel method that selects samples to be labeled based on their predicted labels and confidence levels. The algorithm uses two entropy estimates, one for each class, to gauge the model's confidence in a sample's labels, and chooses the least confident samples closest to the dataset's centroid. Unlike previous techniques that rely on a fixed batch size or query examples independently, this method allows for dynamic batch size selection and incorporates a buffer to store unchosen samples awaiting annotation, which reduces the impact of preprocessing methods on the model's performance. The approach is evaluated on six datasets and outperforms state-of-the-art active learning techniques with a fixed batch size as well as label pooling methods that integrate labeled and unlabeled data on multiple datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/agrija97/Active-Learning-with-Buffer. The experiments demonstrate that this technique achieves higher accuracy with fewer iterations of annotation, and is particularly effective when processing small sets of samples. In addition, this method performs well when compared to deep set networks that integrate unlabeled data with a small number of labeled examples. The code is available at https://github.com/agrija97/Active-Learning-with-Buffer. The paper also introduces a novel method for comparing active learning techniques that involves labeling a larger set of samples and assessing their effectiveness on multiple classification tasks with various numbers of labeled examples. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as AIPW, with potential alternatives being Machine Learning algorithms due to their non-parametric nature and capability to handle complex relationships. In order to improve the efficiency of two NN models with no parameter regularization except SGD, our simulations indicate the significant drawbacks that arise when AIPW is used. In an effort to improve this, the proposed nAIPW offers the same double robustness and orthogonality as AIPW and can achieve asymptotic normality under specific conditions. Additionally, when imposing L1 regularization on the first step NN models with convergence, nAIPW and AIPW are evaluated based on their bias and variance. The results reveal nAIPW reduces bias and variance significantly compared to AIPW, with bias and variance values both under 10% in absolute terms. The proposed estimator also exhibits superior performance in realistic settings with limited sample sizes. The analysis further examines the practical implications of using different optimizers and effect encoders on the estimators and their combinations respectively. The findings suggest combinations of optimizers significantly influence the estimators while the effect encoders have less of an impact compared to the optimizers. Lastly, the study evaluates the impact of the number of hidden units in the first step NN models on the estimators and the outcomes reveal the estimators and ATE perform best with few hidden units under 20. The findings suggest an alternative to using dense two-layer NN models with a larger number of parameters. Instead, the same level of performance can be achieved with fewer parameters and orthogonal weights for the linear projection. The presentation includes additional discussions on the application of classical techniques such as classical AIPW and the utility of Monte Carlo simulations in evaluating estimator performance. The code used for the simulations can be accessed at the provided link. The research contributes to the existing literature by providing a practical assessment of the double robust estimators in a modern causal inference context with the practical implementation through the provided code having real-world implications. The outcomes suggest the estimators and variations of them can be utilized effectively to estimate ATE in complex scenarios with the continued evolution of ML techniques expected to enhance their performance. The study concludes the existing ML advancements have the potential to improve the estimation of ATE, with the need for the constant assessment and evolution of the estimators to ensure their effectiveness in the ever-changing environment of the ML domain

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter, without fixing this parameter in advance. This leads to a semi-adaptive method of parameter estimation. Another option is to treat the tuning parameter as a fully unknown quantity, leading to a unified distribution for the other parameter. This approach is found to provide improved results in simulations. The proposed methods are applied to real-world data, specifically in modelling extreme rainfall in Normandy and extreme winds in the UK. While this case study did not yield significant improvements, it did highlight the potential of modelling non-homogeneous Poisson processes as a robust method for identifying potential multi-linear relationships between covariates and extreme events. Lastly, the methodology is explored for one of the classic datasets in the field of extreme values, showing improved performance in fit and predictive capabilities compared to the standard method. This was confirmed by a recent (2021) competition where models were submitted for another iconic dataset. Nevertheless, it is worth noting that the approach may have applications beyond parameter estimation, including model selection and covariate analysis. We outline the underlying theory that connects these applications and provides a unified framework, rooted in the concept of the functional Bayesian approach. We also discuss one of the key challenges in using this approach, which is to avoid over-adaptation leading to biased estimates. A practical rule to prevent this issue is to ensure that the number of data points is significantly greater than the number of tuning parameters. This is akin to a well-known rule for linear regression, which states that the number of data points should be at least four times the number of parameters. Applying this rule can be challenging in practice, as it may require collecting more data, which in turn may prove costly. An alternative strategy is to use a version of the approach that is based on recent advances in the field of machine learning, which involves selecting the most relevant data automatically. This comes with the advantage of removing unnecessary data automatically, without the need for manual intervention. As a result, the approach is more efficient in terms of computational cost and still yields good results in terms of accuracy. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that the adversary can indeed thwart the learning process to a significant extent. However, we also identify a threshold beyond which the adversary's interference becomes ineffective, specifically when the fraction of corrupted data approaches $\sqrt{n}$, where $n$ represents the total number of data samples. Building on this discovery, we develop an $n^{1/4-\Omega}(T^{1/4-\Omega}(n/H)}$ regret bound for LMDPs that incorporates an initial burn-in period. Additionally, we derive a $n^{1/4-\Omega}(T^{1/4-\Omega}(n/H)}$ regret bound for contextual Markov decision processes. Notably, the regret bound for LMDPs exhibits a dependence on time and the number of data samples that is analogous to the regime of standard offline RL. A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison. We also introduced a more precise metric for evaluating data dependence in translations and classifications, which enabled more nuanced comparisons in these domains. Specifically, we focus on computing the f-Convolution of two input functions, which returns a function representing the total count of defined shape combinations based on provided coordinates. Our work involves examining the properties of this problem through several parameters: the number of shape types (k), dimensionality (d), and a constant running time relative to these parameters. Notably, we can determine the f-Convolution in O(nd^α) time, where α is less than 2, by introducing a new concept, geometric binary search, applied to d-dimensional spheres. Furthermore, we can solve a related query problem in O(nd^β) time, where β is less than 1, by introducing the notion of negative weights and applying geometric binary search to these weighted spheres. Additionally, we can solve approximation and exact versions of the f-Convolution problem under specific conditions in specified time complexities. In the process, we found that $0^{+-}$ tetraquark operators without derivatives are not possible. Due to the distinct Lorentz structure of the $0^{--}$ currents, it is prevented from incorporating corrections from four-quark interactions into its spectral density, leading the gluon condensate to become the primary factor influencing its spectral density as power correction at the order of $\alpha_s^2$. Using the developed approach, we calculated the spectral densities of the $0^{--}$ tetraquark state and $0^{--}$ glueball operator up to the fourth order in correlation function and derived their respective mass parameters. Combining the parameters from two approaches, we determined the interpolation and calculation results for the $0^{--}$ tetraquark state, which led us to conclude that it does not exist below 2 GeV due to the significant uncertainty of its mass, while our findings may provide valuable reference for the research on the exotic $0^{--}$ state in the future experiments. Our research outcomes on the $0^{--}$ tetraquark state can serve the theoretical preparation for the future experiments on the $0^{--}$ tetraquark state. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. Our work highlights the importance of using detailed numerical models to inform and quantify safety strategies for preventing the spread of infectious diseases in various settings. Such an approach could be essential for the safe operation of buses and other enclosed spaces, facilitating a safe return to pre-pandemic levels of service. For example, our model suggests that simply assuming a uniform mixing ratio may result in an underestimation of the required ventilation rate by as much as 90%. Consequently, the consideration of local airflow patterns and particle behaviour is vital for the effective control of airborne disease transmission in enclosed spaces. Notably, our model is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of scenarios for evaluating and comparing different mitigation techniques. To illustrate this, our calculations for a bus travelling at 30 km/h on a hot day show that the combination of turbulence, buoyancy, and coughing leads to a highly non-uniform aerosol distribution, with a 'plume' radius nearly ten times larger than when using a well-mixed model, and with a 4.5% probability of aerosol deposition on seats and walls within a distance of 2.5 metres from the infected person, as opposed to a 0.6% probability predicted by the well-mixed model. Conversely, our model indicates a significantly lower probability of aerosol deposition on seats and walls further away from the infected person. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the effects of turbulence and buoyancy dominate the airflow dynamics, while the influence of ventilation is relatively weak. By quantifying the relative importance of various factors in determining virus transport, our study seeks to promote a safe and efficient return to bus travel and other essential enclosed space activities. Our model can inform and quantify safety strategies for various settings beyond urban buses, by evaluating and comparing the efficacy of different mitigation techniques. The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases where strong nonlinearity affects its accuracy. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, differentiating between linear and nonlinear interactions; however, it is limited in its application to lower dimensional systems. We introduce a kernel-based approach to generating data-driven models for high-dimensional, nonlinear systems. Our method utilizes kernel regression to focus on sparse, dynamic components, which we demonstrate can efficiently handle large data sets and accommodate partial system knowledge. We also show that our approach allows for an accurate identification of linear system components, which in turn, helps to differentiate between nonlinear interactions. Consequently, we obtain a dynamic mode decomposition-like model that remains stable in cases where strong nonlinearity prevails. We test our method using diverse systems of ordinary and partial differential equations that frequently occur in the physical sciences. Our method holds great promise for real-world applications in engineering fields, including reduced order modeling, fault diagnostics, prediction, control systems, and the identification of governing system laws. Our approach also lays the groundwork for applications involving partial differential equations, which we however, do not fully utilize in this study. Our method's simplicity, efficiency, and high dimensional accuracy make it an attractive model-building tool. Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surrounding the optimal input method for retrieval and the ultimate application have been ongoing. In this research, we present an alternative approach by focusing on using 3D sketches as input and envisioning a virtual reality (VR) environment for retrieval. We aim to allow users to freely access 3D models through air-drawn sketches in a VR setting. As an initial step, our study contributes four aspects: implementing a tool to collect and retrieve 3D sketches in VR, gathering the first dataset of $167$ sketches in two categories from ModelNet, developing a novel deep learning approach to integrate both 2D and 3D sketch features, and conducting comprehensive experiments to evaluate our technique. The results show that our method outperforms existing techniques, with promising hits@1 and macro-AUC curves. The introduced technology and data can benefit the community, and our code is available at https://schwing.github.io/3dsketch-rv/ for reproduction. A VR demonstration can be found at https://schwing.github.io/3dsketch-rv/demo/. Additionally, free VR downloads can be accessed at https://schwing.github.io/3dsketch-rv/vr-download/. Future plans include expanding our collection to more categories and incorporating an automatic sketch segmentation tool to streamline the retrieval process. Such an approach has near-term practical value and can lead to significant progress in the research community. A video showcasing the research can be found at https://youtu.be/6H1MeFor7bM. Our survey can be accessed at https://schwing.github.io/3dsketch-rv/survey/. A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a straightforward statistical representation of policy effects, which serve as a substitute for more computationally intensive predictive models. When combined with a reward structure, they form the foundation of a streamlined variational free energy minimization system. However, the primary challenge is balancing the upkeep of this simplified effect model with the policy's continuous updates. Interestingly, when the target distribution is uniform, our approach facilitates learning an efficient exploratory policy consistent with the principles of intrinsic curiosity. Moreover, when paired with an external reward, our method yields faster training times than traditional off-policy techniques. Overall, the efficacy of our model is demonstrated through its outstanding performance on complex tasks in real-world robotic settings. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant information in their memories.
We propose the MemoNav, a novel memory-based navigation framework, designed to improve performance in multi-goal scenarios by selectively retaining both short-term and long-term memories.
The short-term memory in MemoNav stores dynamic agent topological maps, updated as navigation progresses. To augment this memory, a graph attention module aggregates past short-term memories to generate long-term memories.
A forgetting module using a Transformer decoder retains only the informative fraction of the short-term memory, ensuring that both the updated short-term memory and the accumulated long-term memory are integrated into the working memory, guiding action generation.
Experimental evaluations of MemoNav on a new dataset demonstrate significantly better performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches using a fraction of the navigation history, with reduced instances of deadlock situations. Project codes and related datasets are available at: https://github.com/ChaochenZou/MemoNav. Knowledge nerve.net provides additional information. To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells (Femto Cells) by reusing the same licensed spectrum. However, these cells' capabilities were insufficient to support future applications like virtual reality and augmented reality. As a result, operators have sought unlicensed spectrum in the 5 GHz Wi-Fi band, with LAA being the name later assigned by 3GPP. Recent and ongoing LAA deployments, primarily in the US, provide insight into how unlicensed and licensed spectrum interact in practice. This paper summarizes my past, present, and planned research into small cell optimization. Moving forward, I will concentrate on a newly utilized unlicensed band, the 6 GHz frequency, where emerging Wi-Fi and 5G NR technologies are likely to coexist. This band offers considerable unlicensed spectrum and relatively low levels of interference, making it an essential resource for high-bandwidth applications and unlicensed Femto Cell networks. To efficiently deploy such systems, more advanced optimization techniques than those used today are required. This research will leverage my expertise in cross-layer optimization and my newly established research focus on 6 GHz enabling technologies to contribute to this optimization challenge. This new area of 6G research will be explored through multiple PhD projects that I will supervise. This will mark a new chapter in my research journey, where I will maintain my primary focus on optimizing cellular networks within the 6 GHz unlicensed band. This will require developing innovative signal representation and propagation techniques as well as identifying suitable metrics for optimizing 5G and 6G NR systems. This new approach will enable me to investigate multiple 6G hypothesis such as non Terahertz 6G and 6G with a time division, between 6G(nR) and 6G(Rn). This will be achieved through numerous publications in top conference and journal including a book that will be published soon. This year, we published a key paper at GC'19 where we introduced the concept of unlicensed Femto Cell optimization within the LAA context. Since then, we have produced various conference and journal papers on this topic at events like GC'20, WCNC'20 and to be presented at ICC'21, where we will showcase our current and upcoming research in two slides presentations and two papers respectively. Most recently, we produced a crucial paper at TC'20 where we provided operators with practical unlicensed Femto cell optimization strategies. This paper also received the best student paper award at TC'20. This year, we produced another significant paper at SAS

This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems where individual units interact with each other. Our focus will be on two specific settings: one involving interactions between groups over long distances, and another with diffusive interactions between units. Additionally, we'll demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework through applications to both the generalized Volterra system and the Brusselator model. Our analysis will involve examining conditions necessary for pattern formation as well as the relevant time scales for such phenomena to arise. We'll also discuss how our framework's capabilities extend beyond graph theory to capture more complex interactions. Ultimately, we'll discuss potential future directions for our research. Our methodology can be applied to a broad range of systems with intricate interactions and we hope it can serve as a useful tool for understanding dynamics in various real-world systems. Our code is available online for public use at https://github.com/amyjklh/ Hypergraph_nullclines. This code provides a flexible approach that can be adapted to different systems and processes. Additionally, the concept of hypergraphs offers a general representation that can be projected onto graphs when desired. As such, our framework can be viewed as both an extension of existing graph theory to capture more complex interactions and an instance of it in cases where hypergraph projections are applicable. Our work aims to make hypergraphs a more accessible and recognized tool for modeling interactions. By examining the dynamics in our model under different conditions, we found that the emergence of spontaneous patterns often leads to the formation of wave patterns over groups and we've compared these to patterns observed in the Brusselator model. As such, our work relates to existing research on pattern formation but goes beyond it in capturing more complex interactions using hypergraphs. Ultimately, our study offers a new perspective on modeling interactions and provides a framework for investigating dynamics in complex systems and testing hypotheses about pattern emergence. Our analysis reveals the intricate dynamics resulting from the combination of diffusive and localized interactions and the importance of considering the interaction processes themselves, rather than just their effectiveness in leading to pattern emergence. This understanding can be applied beyond our model examples and has the potential to improve our understanding of real-world systems, from group behavior to chemical reactions, and beyond. In conclusion, our work showcases the value of hypergraphs in modeling interactions and invites future research into the resulting dynamics, encouraging researchers to explore new applications and contributions. The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state consisting of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles at 7.65 MeV in $^{12}\mathrm{C}$, has been a topic of interest for a long time. The question of whether this system consists of three weakly-interacting $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital is crucial and can be answered by analyzing the decay paths of the Hoyle state. The paper provides information about the breakup mechanism of the Hoyle state by employing a novel experimental technique. The investigation of the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay of the Hoyle state, rather than through the $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$ ground state, can be performed through an advanced analysis of the energy distribution of the three $\alpha$ particles from the decay. Using beta-delayed charged-particle spectroscopy with high resolution, the researchers discovered a 20-30 keV window around the non-resonant 3 $\alpha$ decay energy of 7.65 MeV where direct decay occurs. The direct decay ratio to the non-resonant state is 0.13 and is consistent with previous studies. The breakdown of the decay dynamics into orbital angular momentum states of the final three $\alpha$ particles was also determined through a convolution technique. The results indicate that the most probable L-values are L=0, 2, 4, with a ratio of 6:3:1, which is consistent with the concept that the Hoyle state consists of highly clustered $\alpha$ particles in the 0s orbital. The second most probable L-value state, with a contribution of 21% to the decay width, may contain a cluster of two $\alpha$ particles in a rotational state of $^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ in the 2s orbital. The conclusion is that the decay of the Hoyle state of 7.65 MeV is described as a superposition of two $\alpha$ cluster states, i.e., the 2s state of $^{6}\mathrm{Li}$ and the 0s state of $^{8}\mathrm{Be}$. The research provides a new insight into the long-standing problem of the structure of the Hoyle state. Moreover, the method used to investigate the direct 3 $\alpha$ decay can be applied to other key issues in nuclear physics, such as the decay of the 0v$\beta$-decay mode of double-beta-decaying nuclei. Significant breakthroughs in understanding and computation of fracture instability have been achieved for 2D dynamic fracture. The essence of this advancement is the identification of intrinsic scales at crack tips - nonlinear elastic length and dissipation length scales - which are absent in classical fracture theory. Studies have shown that in brittle materials at high crack speeds, an oscillatory instability emerges, characterized by a wavelength directly proportional to one of these intrinsic scales, which has been observed in line with experiments on glass. We have extended this by developing a theory for impact-induced fracture in 2D heterogeneous and dynamic systems. The linearized stability analysis revealed a diverse set of modes in such systems. Nonlinearity plays a vital role in causing a transition from a low-speed regime where none of these modes are stable to a higher-speed regime where many are stable. At very high speeds, an oscillatory instability also occurs, but we found a sharp boundary where the wavelength changes abruptly. Beyond a certain point, an oscillatory mode causes the crack face oscillations to change from being in phase to out of phase. The presence of nonlinearity causes this phase transition to happen abruptly at a velocity that depends on the material's other intrinsic scales. The observed phase and oscillatory instability transitions have been cause for speculation on the crack speed oscillations observed in the fracture of iron, as reported over a century ago in the context of fracture mechanics. The findings of this research also open up the possibility of controlling crack propagation in materials that are nearly linearly elastic through carefully manipulating their nonlinear elastic behavior or dissipation mechanisms at the molecular level in order to influence fracture dynamics. The results of this research have been recorded in a series of movies that accompany the paper's supplementary information. They offer a visual representation of the crack speed variability in different regions of a nonlinear, dynamic fracture problem. The movies also showcase the nonlinear elastic behavior and crack face oscillations at very high crack speeds, as well as the rapid approach of a crack face by a impacting particle. The movies further document the primary results of this research, as described above. The crack speed variability has been observed to change from a gentle gradient at lower speeds to an abrupt phase shift at higher speeds. The rate of this phase shift increases with increased nonlinearity in the material, as quantified by the intrinsic scales of the material. The nonlinear elastic behavior and crack face oscillations at very high crack speeds have also been observed to change from a gentle gradient to an abrupt phase shift within a narrow velocity range, as quantified by the intrinsic scales of the material.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels with respect to feedback, aiming to establish a broader understanding of this concept. By utilizing a mathematical model that incorporates feedback, we are able to determine the achievable rates for this class of channels. However, the inverse problem of identifying inputs that nearly achieve these rates becomes computationally complex, even for basic cases like memoryless channels. We address this challenge by developing an approximation algorithm that generates input sequences with high probability, which, when used in a randomization approach, ensure rates close to the channel capacity are attained with high probability. The performance of this approach is quantified through an analysis of its convergence rate and sublinear convergence rate constants. To illustrate the efficiency of our proposed method, we demonstrate its application to a variety of specific channels, including erasure channels, Gaussian channels with quantization, and binary symmetric channels. We compare our findings with existing methods, such as convex programming and brute force exhaustive search, to gauge their computational speed and accuracy. The numerical results show that our proposed method excels in both aspects, yielding fast computation times and high accuracy levels. We also explore the potential extension of this approach to multi-user channels with feedback. We begin by analyzing a pair of related problems: superposition writing and the transmission of binary files. We employ optimization techniques and a two-step file division strategy to achieve rates close to the channel capacity for superposition writing, covering various channel types including erasure channels, Gaussian channels, and binary symmetric channels. For the problem of transmitting binary files, we discover an interesting relationship between this task and the problem of superposition writing over binary symmetric channels, enabling us to devise a transmission strategy that nearly achieves the channel capacity for both problems. We then apply our developed algorithm to achieve rates close to the capacity of feedback channels with memory. Interestingly, the computational complexity of this problem rises exponentially with the channel memory length. We illustrate the efficiency of our proposed method by achieving rates close to the capacity of several specific memory channels, including the binary deletion channel, the binary inspection channel, and erasure channels with delayed access. We also examine its applicability to various practical communication scenarios, such as transmitting pictures and other binary files over these channels. To gauge the effectiveness of our proposed method in more complex situations, we conducted experiments using actual pictures and measured the performance of our approach against existing methods, such as convex programming and brute force exhaustive search. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established a phase diagram for this system, showing both B-phase and SS-wave superconductivity in proximity to a semimetallic state. However, an applied Zeeman field reduces the semimetallic region and suppresses B-phase superconductivity while enhancing SS-wave superconducting regions near the Fermi level. Ultimately, the presence of Rashba coupling and Zeeman field can cooperate to enable s-wave superconductivity in this model. Moreover, under approximate neglect of interband excitations using a reduced Hubbard model, we found that the B-phase superconductivity could also be realized, displaying opposition to both spin-orbit effects and Zeeman fields but exhibiting a different phase cancellation response compared to the s-wave superconductivity in the full Hubbard model. Due to significant non-equivalent contributions from interband and intraband excitations in the reduced Hubbard model, the superconducting gap shows distinct variations from the B-phase and s-wave cases. Hence, it is crucial to consider the complexity and richness of many-body states in tackling spin and charge related degrees of freedom, semimetallic transitions, and superconductivity in such systems.}

This study focuses on understanding and interpreting tables, requiring the ability to recognize their structure and compare cell information effectively. To address this challenge, we introduced a new dataset for SemEval 2020 Task 9: SEM-TAB-FACTS, aiming to verify factual information and locate supporting evidence within tabular scientific data. The comprehensive dataset comprised 981 manually crafted tables and an automatically generated collection of 1980 tables, encompassing over 180,000 statements and more than 16 million annotated evidence references. This task comprised two primary sub-tasks. Sub-task A required participants to verify whether a statement was substantiated, contradicted, or remained inconclusive relative to a given table. Meanwhile, sub-task B involved pinpointing the specific table cells that served as evidence to support the given statement. Ultimately, a total of 69 teams entered the competition, with 19 and 12 submissions successful in sub-tasks A and B, respectively. We are about to present our results and findings from this competition. Due to COVID-19 related constraints, a virtual workshop was held instead of a physical one, where the outcome of sub-tasks A and B were published in a companion paper. For sub-task B, a benchmark with reference solutions and evaluations was made available on the SEM-TAB-FACTS website. Additionally, a collection of unlabelled data drew significant interest from 17 participants, who developed 12 publication-quality systems across both sub-tasks, consistently surpassing the previous best benchmarks in performance. In the evaluation process, the top-ranked system on sub-task A achieved an F1 score of 0.472 in verification and 0.414 in evidence localization, marking the first time this task has been successfully addressed in the SemEval competition. We are set to release the remaining unlabelled data and will update the benchmark with new solutions periodically. Moreover, a new set of data with 987 labelled tables and over 207,000 statements will soon be made available for download on the SEM-TAB-FACTS website. This updated dataset will exclusively benefit the winners of sub-tasks A and B to facilitate further research and development. Consequently, the expanded dataset is expected to support more sophisticated systems in both verification and evidence localization processes. As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing neural network applications on simulated neuromorphic systems requires significant computational power, making it a crucial benchmark for evaluating different architecture designs. To speed up simulations, leveraging the multi-core capabilities of host systems is essential. This paper proposes a parallelized simulation environment based on SystemC for RISC-V multi-core platforms that incorporates multiple computing-in-memory accelerators for neuromorphic computing. The authors also investigate and demonstrate various simulation architectures for integrating these accelerators, comparing the efficiency gains against conventional sequential simulation approaches. The proposed parallel strategy is applied to a range of neural network workloads, achieving significant speedup improvements of up to 9.4 times on single-core systems and 11.2 times on 4-core platforms. The developed simulation framework serves as a valuable resource for evaluating and comparing different neuromorphic computing architecture designs, offering guidance on how to effectively integrate and test neural network applications against alternative solutions. The related technical details and simulation results are made available on an online repository for reference by the community. https://github.com/adl-jcu/SerialParallelSimSC. Deploying machine learning in practical scenarios can often present challenges due to limited data, uncertain outcomes, or problematic assumptions, which conventional methods usually can't effectively tackle. In response, we introduce the concept of Indecision Trees as a revised version of Decision Trees designed to address these issues. Unlike conventional models, Indecision Trees are capable of providing solutions in scenarios involving missing data, imprecise outcomes, and inconsistent instances. We'll examine several techniques for handling uncertainty and data inconsistencies, along with a framework for inducing and evaluating Indecision Trees. We compare their performance to that of existing models, such as Decision Trees and random forests, in a range of simulation-based exercises, as well as a few real-world case studies. The experimental results indicate that Indecision Trees exhibit superior performance when data is sparse or outcomes are imperfect, while both competitive and inferior results are observed in scenarios with dense data. The source code for Indecision Trees is accessible at https://github.com/jxrl/IDT. Further details on our method, along with the experimental protocol, can be found in the supplementary materials at https://arxiv.org/docs/2102.10264.pdf. The technical discussion is presented in a broader context in the accompanying thesis: "Handling uncertainty and data inconsistencies with enhanced decision trees." Additionally, a preliminary version of our work was presented in the paper "Indecision Trees for addressing missing data and imprecise outcomes" [1]. To overcome this, some strategies involve halting DTW early or omitting its computation in advance, tailored to nearest neighbor search scenarios. Nonetheless, PrunedDTW introduced an innovation in DTW's development. Building upon PrunedDTW's capacity to eliminate unproductive alignments, it was later integrated with early abandoning. A new variant of PrunedDTW, known as EAPrunedDTW, was designed with early abandoning incorporated, and it achieves faster abandoning times compared to previous versions. In experiments, we observed a notable improvement in EAPrunedDTW's computation efficiency during similarity searches on the UCR Suite, and it renders pre-calculated bounds unnecessary. Moreover, we found that abandoning paths with the top pruned distances suffices in approximately 90% of cases, and computing these pruned distances amounts to less time than gaining an optimal search time advantage with bounds. In contrast, EAPrunedDTW's design remains versatile and may also benefit classification and clustering tasks without requiring additional development. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has overlooked. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork rather than structured testing methods. Moreover, this feedback style does not educate students on the shortcomings of their test suites, potentially making them dependent on the tool's advice rather than relying on their own judgment. As a more effective approach, inquiry-based learning has the potential to promote student autonomy by reinforcing key testing concepts through feedback. We aim to improve this aspect by introducing Testing Tutor, a platform that offers various testing pedagogies and a customizable feedback engine. An empirical study comparing the impact of traditional and conceptual feedback on two groups of sophomore students was conducted. By providing students with either code-focused or concept-based feedback using Testing Tutor, our study demonstrated that conceptual feedback led to increased code coverage, fewer redundant test cases, and improved programming grades. Additionally, a survey revealed that students prefer conceptual feedback and believe it enhances their understanding of testing principles. Based on these results, we recommend using Testing Tutor as a teaching tool to promote student empowerment through concept-based testing education. In particular, the instructor can use the built-in testing pedagogies and customize the feedback engine to tailor the learning experience to their specific testing curriculum. In a typical 50 or 75 minute lecture, students can learn a new testing concept and then apply it using Testing Tutor, providing them with instant feedback to reinforce their understanding. In this setup, Testing Tutor serves as a "coach," helping students to think critically and make informed decisions about their testing strategies. In the context of on online courses, where human feedback may not be feasible, Testing Tutor can serve as a "virtual coach" with nearly 30 seconds of average response time, making it an appealing solution. To further reduce its impact, a statistical analysis was conducted, revealing no significant differences between these groups in the instructor's graded assignments and the course performance in terms of grades. Therefore, we have made the source code of Testing Tutor available at \href{https://github.com/improve-and-efficiency/testing-tutor}{github.com/improve-and-efficiency/testing-tutor}, encouraging further modifications and improvements to enhance the educational experience. Ultimately, we are seeking feedback from the SE education and tool community to help us refine Testing Tutor and provide more effective learning experiences for students.
