Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Furthermore, our cross-influence model reveals a 10-20 year delay in the public's interest in climate change in response to scientists', policymakers', and economists' interest. However, our findings also highlight the public's interest in climate change as more sensitive to changes in scientists' interest compared to policymakers' interest. Lastly, our research also includes a thorough sensitivity and Monte Carlo analysis to assess the reliability of our results. Our study provides a comprehensive, long-term view of the influence of climate change among distinct groups and highlights their individual contributions to shaping the public's interest in the subject. Our ultimate goal is to inform effective climate change communication by highlighting the significant role that scientific research plays in captivating the public's attention, while also showcasing the public's ability to adapt to changes in experts' interest over longer time frames. Our findings also underscore the importance of collaborative effort between scientists and the public in order to achieve mutually beneficial goals through meaningful community engagement and mutual support. Our ultimate objective is not only to advance climate change communication but also to inspire new strategies for achieving a sustainable future by leveraging the public's interest in the subject. Our research has significant practical implications in this realm, as evident from our discussion of the practical implications in the conclusion section. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility, flexibility, and ease of use. A key challenge in using them, however, is a reliable model that can predict whether an object can be successfully grasped by a given gripper design within a specified grasp width. Current methods are either very realistic but slow, or fast but less accurate. They typically require extensive work to adapt them to new grippers. Our contribution is a two-stage method that first generates soft grasps and then determines their feasibility. We use these results to develop a real-time object grasping prediction model that is both accurate and efficient. This model can be applied to novel grippers with a quick adaptation period. Our study also includes an evaluation of existing soft gripper designs using our method, providing valuable insights for future research and development in the field. The code is available at https://github.com/alexchupin/object_grasping. Our method allows for real-time object grasping predictions with an average error rate of 10.8%, providing 98.2% accuracy within a 100ms processing deadline. The approach can be adapted for use in augmented reality for physical interaction, notably in electronic design. As a result, the performance of existing soft grippers can be quickly assessed and potential improvements identified. Our method indicates that significant enhancements are possible for the Rayo and Robosoft grippers but less so for the Softas and the Soft Gripper by Rubin. Our study demonstrates the practical value of real-time object grasping predictions for various applications in soft robotics. The integration of this technology in augmented reality for physical interaction appears promising. The potential benefits in teaching and learning soft robotics are also explored. The current limitations of soft robotics in teaching and learning are discussed, along with the potential advantages of using real-time object grasping predictions, and suggestions are provided for incorporating this technology in soft robotics education. It is hoped that the approach will contribute to the development of more effective learning environments in the future. The integration of this technology in soft robotics can lead to various applications in research, development, and learning. As a case study, a simple example of using the approach for educational purposes is presented to illustrate its utility in various tasks and to demonstrate how the predicted grasp width can be utilized in object grasping. The example shows the steps for designing a suitable grip for a particular object and reveals that the existing soft grippers have significant room for improvement in terms of the types of objects that can be grasped within a specified grasp width. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, yielding an enhanced 92.1% AUC on the lung cancer dataset. Furthermore, this study addresses the challenge of low-resolution medical scans by introducing an innovative, multi-scale image-upscaling technique within the network framework. Additionally, to facilitate fair evaluation and comparison, this research puts a textual modality-based ProSENet model into practice on various public datasets, including those for lung, breast, and brain cancer. Moreover, the study makes all code and model weights publicly available on the GitHub platform. In terms of future work, this research proposes an integrated engine for disease prognosis and diagnosis, which could serve as a comprehensive tool for medical experts. In conclusion, this study successfully leverages multiple data types to inform survival time predictions in lung cancer, achieving enhanced performance and fair comparison with established methods. In particular, this work highlights the potential of combining text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions with improved accuracy. A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the potential for future datasets to surpass the accuracy of our best results. Once developed, these machine learning tools can process large datasets within a day, making them suitable for near-future surveys. With anticipated future improvements in spectrum quality and available computational resources, we anticipate reaching an error precision of 0.5% in the future. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to consistently
maintain assigned roles during human conversations. Achieving this involves
defining a role specification with specific criteria for stated features and
policies on allowed types of utterances. To build this system efficiently, we
propose a framework for collecting data that leverages few-shot learning from
large language models, rather than relying on extensive role-based dialogue datasets.
Our model processes role specifications as a conditional text generation task
that enables it to maintain role-related attributes, such as persona and style,
throughout the conversation. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our
approach in maintaining role specifications for both persona and style attributes
based on a single model, while a comparison of our model's performance in terms
of coherence and safety metrics shows that it consistently outperforms a model
trained on role-based dialogue datasets. Our model's source code is available at
https://github.com/samanloghmanat/role-constrained_ODDS. Our dataset can be
accessed at https://github.com/samanloghmanat/role-constrained_ODDS/tree/main/

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: firstly, determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions (collision avoidance reformation), and secondly, effecting this reformation while minimizing the time and energy spent by the drones. To resolve the first challenge, a cellular automata-based method is utilized to identify efficient formations that evade obstacles while reducing time and energy consumption. To tackle the second issue, a near-optimal reformation strategy after successful collision avoidance is realized through a temperature function reduction technique borrowed from the point set registration process. The objective of this reformation process is to rapidly eliminate disturbances, thus minimizing the time required for the swarm to reach its destination and ultimately lowering the energy consumption of this process. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated power consumption, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers continuously. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents an SRAM-based TRNG that can sustain long periods of operation. To accomplish this goal, we introduce a novel approach, termed TuRaN, which utilizes a lower supply voltage than recommended to cause SRAM access failures, then applies the SHA-256 hash function to these faults to create high-throughput random numbers. We validate the practicality of TuRaN through SPICE simulations on diverse process nodes and assess its reliability through real-world experiments. Moreover, we demonstrate the high quality of the random numbers produced by TuRaN using the NIST standard randomness tests and note its exceptional performance in comparison with existing SRAM-based TRNGs. Lastly, we evaluate the throughput and security of the proposed TRNG, observing an substantial enhancement in throughput over present SRAM-based TRNGs while maintaining robust security against well-documented attacks on random number generators. In particular, we estimate the NIST entropy rate of TuRaN to be at least 147.4 Kb/s.  All the experimental results are made available at https://github.com/supervA1/TuRaN.  This detailed analysis confirms that TuRaN is an efficient and trustworthy solution for extracting randomness from SRAM arrays. As a result, it presents a suitable and economical solution for embedded systems requiring a continuous and high-quality random number generator.  Additionally, the proposed architecture is adaptable to various application scenarios, as illustrated in detail in the supplementary document. The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this thermal analogy does not hold; while an uneven gravitational force induces specific energy flows, a comparable uneven temperature has little to no effect in systems that exchange energy with their surroundings weakly. Additionally, the similarity between an external electric charge and the system's internal energy potential is also invalid under these circumstances. In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity. Our results offer insights into how geometric complexity is controlled during training and suggest new directions for studying the optimization processes involved in deep learning. Furthermore, we show that regulating geometric complexity is essential for achieving geometrical and categorical separability in our two-digit MNIST classification tasks. A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice. Additionally, this technique can be applied to other $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ decays such as $B^0\to rho^0\mu^+\mu^-$ and $B^+\to phi\mu^+\mu^-$, and may also be adapted for future Belle II or NA48/2 experiments. Furthermore, this unbinned method can be used to investigate other physical observables and provide new insights into $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$. Lastly, this approach can be extended to the quark sector to study semileptonic processes and serve as a potential tool in the measurement of CP-violating phases in the quark sector. Therefore, this technique has significant potential to contribute to our understanding of the flavor sector and ultimately the search for new physics. Moreover, this unbinned maximum likelihood method can also be used for the direct determination of the CKM angle gamma by means of a combination of several observables, taking full advantage of the information contained in experimental measurements, and potentially yielding the least sensitive constraints on gamma. As a result, this technique can further significantly reduce the uncertainty on gamma. Finally, this approach can still be further improved by also incorporating the information from angular distributions to study gamma with even greater precision, and potentially achieve the least sensitive constraints on gamma. Therefore, this technique can potentially lead to the least sensitive limits of gamma. In addition, this direct determination of Wilson coefficients can be used to investigate possible tensions between the measurements of the Wilson coefficients by the different experiments and their potential New Physics implications, by comparing the results obtained from the analysis of the $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays with high precision, and taking into account the correlations between the observables that may contribute to such experimental discrepancies. Consequently, this technique can provide valuable information towards the understanding of the anomalies in the flavor sector, and the potential presence of the New Physics in the flavor sector. Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past successes suggest that similar breakthroughs may occur in the future as researchers continue to explore and adapt established NLP advancements to automated essay grading.  This report presents an automated essay scoring system developed for a standardized 12-point scale used in English language assessments in Colombian high schools.  Our model is based on pre-trained transformer models, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, which are combined with a novel data enhancement strategy employing paragraph swapping to create stronger performance.  Through paragraph swapping, the size of the model's training data can be increased, thereby enhancing the prediction capabilities of the model.  Our findings indicate that the integration of paragraph swapping leads to notable improvements in model accuracy across multiple metrics, with our top model achieving a 0.94 Pearson correlation when tested on hidden test data.  Our research demonstrates that the effective application of transfer learning and data augmentation can result in a single institution's significant advancements in automated essay grading performance.  Ultimately, our model enables the development of highly reliable and automatic tools for the evaluation of student performance, thereby facilitating teaching and assessment processes at our institution and potentially others.  This report concludes with a demonstration of a fully functional web platform for the deployment of automated essay grading at https://iasi-ucaldas-ases.webapp.io.  Our hope is that our work inspires the work of other researchers, in addition to the implementation of this innovative technology in actual teaching and learning settings.  In line of this, our code is available at https://github.com/UCALDAS-ASI/tree/main/ases-bert-rbert.  Our web platform was built using Flask, a common web framework, in addition to other relevant libraries such as pandas, scikit-learn, and transformers, among others, as shown in the appendix at https://iasi-ucalds-asi.github.io/ases-bert-rbert/web-platform/. Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research paper addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus. This updated scheme, Hebrew UD, is specifically tailored to fit the needs of modern, informal Hebrew. Alongside the corpus and annotations, the project also provides a new Hebrew UD repository, complete with data and evaluation scripts. This repository serves as a hub for the Hebrew UD ecosystem, offering resources for further research and development. This paper details the research behind the corpus, its creation process, updates the existing UD HTB, and showcases promising future applications of Hebrew UD to UD NLP tasks. Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to shared knowledge and collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new task generally necessitates a comprehensive retraining, also impairing performance on past tasks. Consequently, cooperative learning often demands duplicate effort when multiple researchers or teams work on similar but distinct tasks. To address this issue, the authors developed a continuous learning framework where the network learns one task at a time, and each task is encoded in a separate block. Notably, the network uses a dynamic routing mechanism to select the relevant task-dependent training data, and a regularization technique to stabilize the network's internal weights structure during training. Experimental evaluations on standard computer vision datasets indicate that this mechanism successfully prevents interference between tasks and achieves satisfactory accuracy on both the current and past tasks. Moreover, the network's architecture allows for efficient task adaptations, requiring minimal retraining when encountering new tasks. The results show competitive performance compared to the current best practices in continuous learning methods. The authors' work provides an innovative solution for cooperative learning, demonstrating the feasibility of'share-and-share-curl' models and opening up new collaboration opportunities between researchers or teams working on different tasks. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. We also observe a correlation between the average degree of LDPC code nodes and the maximum error tolerance, which could lead to the development of unequal error protection methods. By combining degree-degree correlations and non-uniform variable node impairances, we propose a versatile unequal error protection framework that adapts to various channel conditions. We also demonstrate the creation of LDPC ensembles that are close to the maximum-likelihood decoding bounds on the binary erasure channel, both with and without edge endpoint awareness. Furthermore, our research examines the link between degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles and the dynamic behavior of spin glasses, revealing the existence of a glass transition phase in the erosion of LDPC ensembles. We quantify this transition phase and propose a novel method for determining the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes based on the thermodynamic glass transition temperature. By applying this temperature-based scaling factor to LDPC ensembles, we achieve a significant reduction in the maximum error tolerance and approach the maximum-likelihood decoding bounds on the binary erasure channel. Additionally, our research examines the performance of degree-degree correlated LDPC codes over the AWGN channel and proposes a technique to enhance the error tolerance of LDPC codes based on the thermodynamic glass transition temperature. This paper focuses on enhancing the traditional model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design by incorporating a new control signal strategy that significantly reduces the computational burden associated with its implementation. This improved MPSF design achieves higher safety and efficiency through the utilization of the area of dominance (AoD) approach. A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's size doesn't guarantee in-context learning to emerge. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus composed of multiple domains may yield mixed outcomes. Lastly, a pretraining corpus focused on a specific domain is more likely to result in in-context learning, especially when that domain matches the origin of the downstream task. Our research provides initial answers to the corpus-related concerns surrounding LIL and can serve as a foundation for future investigations. Additionally, our analysis offers guidelines for optimizing the pretraining corpus to boost the likelihood of in-context learning to emerge. Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. These fragments act as nuclei, fostering further condensation through processes including Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, thereby nearly doubling the cold gas within a 75 million-year period. Cloud expansion appears to be determined by factors such as density and localized heat-producing mechanisms that either cause the clouds to shrink and crumble or continue to grow in size. Magnetic fields are found to have a moderating effect on the cloud's evolution, slowing down and fragmentation processes, with certain fields even leading to the revival and increased complexity of certain structures; this could explain the observed correlation between magnetic field strength and cold gas content in certain galaxy clusters. Ultimately, our simulation suggests that galaxy clusters possess a greater capacity for storing cold gas than initially thought, with much of this gas being confined within structures less than 5 kiloparsecs in size. This hidden, localized cold gas could play a crucial role in enhancing star-formation activity in galaxy clusters, possibly by reconfiguring the existing virialization shocks to produce more porous surfaces that facilitate cloud penetration. Based on this, we speculate that galaxy clusters with greater cosmic web connectivity and irregularities in electron density could experience increased fragmentation and star-formation activity. Nonetheless, it is essential to keep in mind that our results are contingent on the assumption that the initial, intricate structures of these formations are preserved and adhered to over time. If this assumption is breached, the likelihood of localized star-formation being an regular occurrence in galaxy clusters could significantly decrease. To better understand this, we suggest the use of more sophisticated hydrodynamic simulations that incorporate physical processes on a diverse range of scales and lengths. On a separate note, our simulation indicates a potential relationship between magnetic field strength and density, with the former being more sensitive to this relationship than the latter; this could be utilized in constructing statistical models that incorporate magnetic field strength for determining galaxy cluster scaling laws. Lastly, our study emphasizes the importance of incorporating physical processes and incorporating physical processes and incorporating magnetic field strength into statistical models of galaxy clusters. The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of text input to speech. To overcome this challenge, researchers divide speech into its basic components and model them separately. Although current frameworks rely on a pre-defined unit segmentation, which can be impractical for languages with limited unitization resources, our work focuses on automatically determining acoustic units from raw speech signals. To achieve this, we develop an end-to-end unit selection-based zero-speech synthesis system that identifies and models speech units separately. To ensure the accuracy of speech unit segmentation, we introduce acoustic feature-based speech unit cost modeling, which enables more effective speech unit selection. Experimental results indicate that our proposed approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of speech quality and naturalness. To validate the accuracy of speech unit segmentation, we also conducted an evaluation of speech unit segmentation based on human judgment. Our study demonstrates that the automatically determined speech units can be comparable to human-selected units in terms of their natural occurrence and independence. Our work aims to contribute to the development of unit-based non-parametric speech synthesis systems, particularly in languages that have limited resources available for unitization. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to apply automatic speech unit selection to English, a language that was previously modeled using a pre-defined unit segmentation. Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot. Video recordings of these experiments can be found online at https://youtu.be/namX359P8C8, https://youtu.be/TPpG KsV7MOA, and https://youtu.be/NgB7OVSvI4M. Our open-source implementation is accessible at https://gitlab.grncpa.com/gnrc/optimization/-/tree/hybrid_optimization. We're planning to present this research at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA'24). As a supplementary material, our results are available at https://grncpa.github.io/papers/hybrid_optimization.pdf. Additionally, a conference presentation is anticipated. Our method performed comparably to existing optimization techniques in simulated environments, yet consistently outperformed them in real-world tests, sometimes by a substantial margin. Moreover, our hybrid strategy yielded notably better outcomes than plain evolutionary strategies, underscoring the significance of incorporating specialized parameters. To determine the optimal locations for actuated joints on multi-limbed robots, we utilized an optimization method developed earlier, which treats these joints as semi-actuated, thus facilitating faster computation times. Our study found that minimizing the mass of these joints, while maintaining a fixed position, didn't notably affect their estimated optimal parameters. Consequently, we applied the same parameters to both unactuated and semi-actuated models, which in turn reduced the computation requirements for generating gait cycles. Our research further reveals that optimizing force distribution across the digits of a hexapod, while maintaining posture constraints, triggers unstable gait cycles in the resulting models. However, a simplified single-stage optimization, which disregards these constraints, yielded more stable outcomes, thus supporting our hybrid optimization approach. Our analysis indicates that improving robot stability often comes at the cost of increased posture discrepancies. We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental rule for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a particular resource, and then created two approaches to determine whether this transformation is possible within the prescribed resource constraints.
The first method involves extending the existing convex geometry methods used in classical resource theories to the quantum realm, and applying them to conduct a comprehensive analysis of the resource theory of quantum coherence.
The second method is based on a more general framework that works even in scenarios where the underlying protocols are non-trivial and interact with the quantum system in an unpredictable way.
This framework was successfully applied in the resource theory of quantum information to calculate the quantum gain ability, which represents the ability to transform a quantum state into another with higher purity.
Furthermore, we used a previously established relationship between the quantum information gain ability and the classical information gain ability to calculate the classical gain ability in terms of the quantum information gain ability. 
The results obtained using this new framework were compared with those derived from geometric methods for multiple resource theories, and we found that the quantum theories of coherence and information exhibit properties beyond those predicted by the corresponding classical theories. 
The computational efficiency of our methods was validated by calculating the quantum gain ability for various complex quantum systems. 
The outcomes of our study show that the quantum technologies offer more versatile functionality than the classical systems. 
The methods developed in this research can be used to identify and quantify the quantum properties essential for achieving specific practical objectives in the applications of quantum information processing. 
Furthermore, the classical gain ability obtained from the quantum information ability serves as a lower bound for the classical information gain ability computed using the convex geometry methods, underscoring the idea that the quantum realm offers extra value beyond what is possible with classical resources. 
Ultimately, the value of the quantum resource can be quantified by measuring the ratio of the geometric measure to the classical information measure, and we use this quantity to evaluate the quantum information gain ability in various scenarios. 
The outcomes of our study demonstrate the efficacy of the quantum realm in enhancing the functionality beyond what is possible with classical resources in multiple resource theories. 
The methods developed in this research can be used the identify and quantify the quantum technologies needed to achieve specific objectives in the applications of quantum information processing.

This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. With increasing dataset size, DR-DSGD outperforms DSGD, yielding a larger gap in convergence rate, underscoring its broader application and robustness. With decentralized systems rapidly growing usage, we anticipate a broader impact of our DR-DSGD method. With proper regularization, DR-DSGD guarantees an optimal level of performance, thereby ensuring fairness and achieving state-of-the-art efficiency in communication rounds. To the best of our knowledge, DR-DSGD makes breakthrough contributions in robust decentralized optimization with data distribution uncertainty and regularized fairness. With growing concerns over model bias, our study sets a new benchmark in decentralized optimization with an added regularizer, thereby ensuring an optimal level of fairness. To validate the robustness and performance of our DR-DSGD method, we conducted extensive experiments on various data distributions and test platforms, comparing it to the original DSGD and other leading decentralized optimization methods. Notably, regularized DR-DSGD achieved an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy across different data distributions. Moreover, it outperformed DSGD in up to $20\%$ fewer communication rounds, demonstrating greater communication efficiency and a lower requirement for communication frequency. With increasing dataset size, DR-DSGD exhibited a larger gap in convergence rate to DSGD, thereby ensuring a broader application and robustness. To evaluate the performance of our DR-DSGD method, we analyzed its communication efficiency and convergence rate in comparison to DSGD, while also testing its robustness across various data distributions and test platforms

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma. A detailed description of our energy release model, which integrates perturbative parton dynamics and hydrodynamics, is presented in a companion paper (arXiv:2102.02428). Both studies are an extension of, and were initially developed in, the thesis work described in the accompanying Ph.D. dissertation (arXiv:2002.11316).

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error, which ultimately enables comprehensive compensation and performance restoration. It is acknowledged that within a safety zone, certain thresholds can accommodate minor deviations from ideal conditions, thereby allowing for safe system operation. In this context, the primary objective is to develop a nonlinear control strategy, referred to as balanced performance safety backstepping (BPSB), addressing the combined challenges of saturation, filter error, and performance degradation due to destabilizing factors. A key innovation involves introducing a major backstepping step that rectifies filter-related distortions and leverages the remaining degrees of freedom to actively mitigate within-safety-threshold saturations, thereby ensuring system reliability. A detailed numerical case study validates the efficacy of the proposed BPSB control approach. This research is funded by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. 2002735.

By applying these estimates and tables to specific situations, it's possible to gain a deeper understanding of how different influences affect the object's path and make informed decisions based on that analysis. We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We demonstrate that a properly configured dipole-based model achieves a level of accuracy comparable to first-principle simulations, both in terms of optical transitions and collective excitations. In contrast, a TB model utilizing the velocity gauge must be perfectly gauge invariant to produce accurate results. We also apply a mean-field scheme to investigate strong light-matter interactions and extract single-particle properties from the fully interacting states. The application of gauge invariant velocity-based models may still generate reasonable approximations for certain collective excitations. In such cases, the difference between the TB model and first-principle simulation is primarily attributed to the inherent nature of gauge invariance rather than an imperfect velocity-based representation. Nonetheless, the dipole-based model provides a more general, effective, and gauge-invariant approach that supersedes the velocity-based model, resulting in a better agreement with first-principle simulations for both optical and collective excitations. The improvement achieved through the dipole-based model translates to reduced computational costs, as fewer basis states are required to reach a specified accuracy level. In specific cases, this meant a 5-fold reduction in computational costs. The results of this study validate the potential of TB models in accurately describing both weak and strong light-matter interactions in low-dimensional materials, suggesting their applicability in numerical modeling of optical phenomena in systems like spiro compounds. The improved efficiency and accuracy offered by these models may also facilitate the application of numerical TB models in the broader context of optical excitations in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. In conclusion, the enhanced gauge-invariant dipole-based model represents a more reliable method for describing light-matter interactions within numerical TB models, offering an improved accuracy and efficiency. We introduce a general point cloud registration framework called PCRN, which serves as a foundation for developing unsupervised registration networks. This framework incorporates two essential modules: a feature extractor module and a classifier module. Unlike existing methods that solely rely on feature extractors, our approach leverages a classifier module to refine the feature extractor, effectively enhancing its performance. Additionally, our method innovatively incorporates a keypoint detector to identify crucial points for registration, rather than relying on all keypoints, as well as uses a keypoint descriptor module to prioritize keystone points based on their relevance. This customized prioritization enables our registration method to achieve improved robustness, specifically in the presence of partial occlusions. As a result, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised registration methods, according to both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Further details about PCRN can be found in our paper at [arXiv:2202.13043](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.13043). A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose the nilpotent quotients $\Gamma_{n,c}$ as semidirect products of finitely generated abelian groups, and we identify which invertible matrices can be extended into automorphisms of $\Gamma_{n,c}$. Ultimately, we conclude that $\Gamma_n$ has the $R_\infty$ property and determine its $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree to be 2. Furthermore, we extend this result to BAUMLag-Solitar groups $\beta_n$ and show that $\beta_n$ also possesses the $R_\infty$ property with a $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of 2, provided n is greater than or equal to 3. We also demonstrate that infinite direct products of finitely generated groups possessing the $R_\infty$ property have the same property. Consequently, we find that infinite direct products of non-trivial Baumslag-Solitar groups possess the $R_\infty$ property and determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degrees for two of these products. Higman's partial generalization of Krull's abnormability theorem is also utilized in our research. In addition, we outline additional methods for determining the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degrees of potentially infinite groups possessing the $R_\infty$ property. Faethe's theorem, stating that infinite solvable groups possessing the $R_\infty$ property are linearly solvable, is also employed. Finally, we propose two open questions regarding the potential linearity of groups possessing the $R_\infty$ property with nilpotency degree higher than 2. In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location. Furthermore, an algorithm is introduced to create a signal representing the ground sound that corresponds to a realistic perception of the impact, and this signal can be optimized for a particular set of parameters by utilizing a genetic algorithm. A demonstration of the effectiveness of this algorithm is shown through a comparative analysis of the ground sound produced by a 7.3 kg steel sphere striking a 0.90 m thick layer of pine at a 30 degree angle, under three different conditions: when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, when the ground is perfectly rigid, and when the impact occurs directly in front of the listener. In this comparison, the ground sound can be discernible from the sound produced by the impacting object, the sound produced by the transient vibrations of the impacting object, and the sound produced by the ringing of the impacting object. Additionally, an idealized ground sound effect is created that corresponds to a weight of 700 kg, which can be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. To create a set of realistic parameters for a typical adult, the mass and thickness of the ground surface are set at 700 kg and 0.51465 m, respectively. Applying the optimized algorithm to this set of parameters yields a ground sound effect that corresponds to a weight of 700 kg. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy has been a long-standing challenge. A popular approach in these applications is the application of Principal Component Analysis followed by K-means clustering. However, this method falls short in capturing the dynamic behavior of many systems, leading to inaccuracies in clustering and loss of valuable insights. In this study, a new method for clustering time-series data is presented, taking into consideration the dynamic state of each individual within a system. This is achieved by treating the data as a trajectory in a high-dimensional space over time. The study reveals that when the underlying dynamics of a system are captured, clusters can be accurately defined. A comprehensive analysis of this method is performed, comparing it to traditional techniques in terms of clustering capabilities and computational complexity. In addition, this method is applied to a an equation-based simulator for a model atmospheric CO$_2$ pollution system, as well as to real-world data from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. The results show promising agreements with existing knowledge in the latter case. In conclusion, this approach offers a valuable contribution to the field of data-driven science, enabling the identification of clusters that reflect distinct physical states in complex systems and providing new insights that can inform and validate existing understanding and legislation. The code utilized in this study is openly accessible at https://github.com/sjyotik/dynamic-clustering-for-climatology. This code has been successfully tested on Ubuntu 18.04 and Windows 10 platforms. Additionally, the data employed in this research are available at https://doi.org/10.5065/D3F49TP3, along with relevant information for replication of the results. Furthermore, the figure content used in this study can be found at https://doi.org/10.5065/D6TC3X7N. Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a concept more commonly associated with modern differential geometry.  This paper seeks to reconcile Arthur's position by highlighting similarities between the latter framework and that of Bonnet, Bernoulli, and Euler, all of whom employed an algebraic system grounded in Leibnizian concepts.  This study also addresses common criticisms of Leibnizian calculus, such as its supposed lack of clarity regarding operations like differentiation and integration, and demonstrates how the system's coherence can be established through axiomatics.  Ultimately, the study defends Leibnizian calculus as a well-defined, innovative framework in its own right.  While the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework may serve as the most faithful representation of Leibnizian concepts, it is difficult to overlook the significant advances made by the early pioneers of Leibnizian calculus.  This paper thus seeks to rehabilitate their contributions, acknowledging both their historical and ongoing significance within the mathematical community.  In particular, the study reevaluates the role of formal rigor in the scientific method, a notion recently supported by the work of Michael Hallett, to argue that Leibnizian calculus exemplifies a mature, rigorously applied mathematical methodology.  This defense of Leibnizian calculus is essential not just for its intrinsic value, but also for its potential to illuminate essential conceptual distinctions underlying the relationship between mathematics and science.  In particular, the study highlights how the algebraic coherence of Leibnizian calculus, along with its distinctiveness and innovativeness, can be productively analogized to the distinction between physics and mathematics as characterized by Einstein, where physics is marked by empiricism and mathematics by the freedom to establish fundamental principles and criteria for evaluation, a notion in turn echoed in the distinction between Leibnizian calculus and its subsequent philosophical interpretations.  In this context, the study advocates for a Leibnizian model of the relationship between mathematics and science, in which the former serves as a means to establish fundamental principles governing physical reality, and the latter represents an ongoing effort to interpret and apply these principles in accordance with reality as witnessed in the transition from Leibniz to Newton, and later from Newton to Einstein.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of these models over the 315-665nm wavelength range using cross-dispersion spectrographs, which have an accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. By comparing various models in detail, we're now in a better position to inform the development of improved ADCs for the future, and advise against relying on the Zemax model, especially when blue spectrum accuracy is critical. Instead, we suggest using the Kyodo model, which we've also adapted for use in the presence of air pressure variations. To facilitate this, we've inserted the effects of temperature and pressure into the kyodo code, providing a practical option for researchers working with spectrographs. We've applied this updated adaptation to data from the AGS, a 3.5-meter telescope at the Gunma Astrophysical Data Center in Japan. We've used this corrected data to calculate stellar radial velocities with a greater degree of accuracy, reaching an overall precision of 18.4 milliarcseconds. We've successfully applied this updated adaptation to data from several spectrographic observations made off-axis, which had previously been considered uninterpretable. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this correction on data from various spectrographic observations, including that of SDSS, and displayed improved results across multiple spectra. We've shown a significant improvement in the precision across various spectra, ranging from 18.4 to 16.4 milliarcseconds. We've also used this corrected data to calculate SDSS's atmospheric dispersion, reaching an average accuracy of 18 milliarcseconds. We've achieved a total accuracy of 18.3 milliarcseconds for the atmospheric dispersion calculations across all spectrographic observations. We've successfully validated our corrected ADC model, which we've made available for use in third-party spectrographic observations, such as that of the SDSS. We've used this corrected data to calculate a scale factor of 1.000151, which we've applied to spectrographic data from SDSS. We've used this corrected scale factor to re-determine the pair-wise radial velocity difference between SDSS's observations of HD 220333 and HD 180948, which we found to be -28.6 km/s

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Notably, PILE's enhancements are particularly evident in low-resource scenarios and high-precision searches. Our source code is available at https://github.com/searchenginewebpile/searchenginewebpile.

A detector can therefore look for these low-frequency fluctuations, rather than just its high frequency oscillations, and is not limited to finding frequencies that are easily within its range, but can actually be searching for much larger and unexplored ranges of frequencies. A network of sensors, by cross-correlating their measurements, can detect these low-frequency fluctuations, and is not limited by bandwidth because low-frequency fluctuations will occur simultaneously at a range of frequencies. In this way, existing sensor networks can be used to experimentally explore the unexplored ranges of the parameter space of this bosonic dark matter. We outline how to carry out this low-frequency search for ultralight bosonic dark matter using existing seismic sensors, and describe the relevant mathematical framework that would be used to implement this search in practice. Furthermore, because the cross-correlated sensor measurements will also be sensitive to gravitational waves, this low-frequency search for bosonic dark matter can be used as part of a method to detect an important class of supermassive black hole rings that are thought to form around supermassive black holes. We therefore suggest calling this low-frequency search for bosonic dark matter "The Hum" search, and propose that calling it "The Hum" search rather than just a low-frequency search for bosonic dark matter can help to clarify its role in detecting not just bosonic dark matter, but also an important new class of objects in the universe that can be found by cross-correlating seismic sensor measurements. The proposed recovery algorithm is based on a stabilization technique for a continuous linear operator, which is a method established in [Balan 2011]. The study begins by providing a detailed mathematical description of the given data and the proposed operator, which seeks to recover the original measure from its low-frequency Fourier components up to Kc. The analysis focuses on the uniqueness and solutions of the inverse problem by considering several cases of completeness and compact support constraints on the measures and Fourier representations. Furthermore, the solutions are characterized within the same classes of measures and Fourier representations. Additionally, the operator is shown to be continuous and well-defined on the given data space. P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. Compilers for high-level languages like C, C++, and Java often rely on static analysis to optimize code, check constraints, and identify potential issues. This work utilizes these concepts to develop a framework turning P4 programs, the hardware architecture, and specific constraints into scenarios describing the performance of programs, constraints, and hardware realities. This framework enables multiple uses: (1) validating program correctness against hardware and software limits, (2) performing static analysis to pinpoint runtime issues, and (3) creating realistic workloads to test hardware and software performance. A demonstration of ALOHA shows how this framework can identify runtime issues during packet processing, give warnings for non-executed instructions, and suggest microprogram revisions. Additionally, it highlights the deployment of optimized P4 programs on actual hardware, comparing their performance to hypothetical hardware microprograms. The source code for this research is available at: https://github.com/tda-sec/aloha. The presentation material can be found at: https://github.com/tda-sec/aloha-presentations. In terms of related work, there is an existing compiler system known as v1model-p4-switch-compiler, developed by the P4 organization for mapping P4 programs to V1Model architecture resources, but it lacks the ability to perform static analysis for checking constraints, optimizing code, and creating realistic workloads, unlike the proposed framework, which can also be integrated with this existing compiler to perform enhanced checks and optimizations. The main components of this framework are the hardware model, the static analysis system, and the generators of workload scenarios. It utilizes graph data structures to represent the performance of programs, constraints, and hardware realities, allowing it to perform static checks, create realistic workloads, or map P4 programs to V1Model resources. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, this choice often results in suboptimal convergence of scalar quantities, such as vorticity or stream function, because they are derived as fluxes or averages across elements. We introduce a novel approach to directly compute high-order moments of vorticity using continuous scalar functions on a grid. These functions are represented by continuous finite elements within a suitable space that outperforms standard Raviart-Thomas methods. We test this method in two scenarios: a straightforward case and one with increasing complexity, involving both a simple rotating domain and a realistic simulation of a rotating Earth's atmosphere and ocean. The results show that the method can achieve a convergence rate of O(H^k) with a high-order (k=2) approximation of vorticity moments, surpassing the convergence rate of standard Raviart-Thomas methods (O(H^1). Additionally, high-order moments of vorticity are found to be resistant to numerical errors introduced by using lower-order approximations of the stream function. These streamlined expressions for computing vorticity moments reduce computational costs by minimizing the cost of computing stream function. This method is particularly beneficial when vorticity is the primary variable of interest in simulations, as it also facilitates the convergence of optimized methods for solving partial differential equations and reduces the computational overhead by a factor of ten. Ultimately, high-order approximations of vorticity moments lead to significant savings in computational time, from O(N^alpha) to O(N^2), with N representing the total number of degrees of freedom. In addition to optimizing convergence, our approach also offers an efficient solution strategy for solving partial differential equations and computing high-order moments of vorticity, these results are further demonstrated in relevant applications involving geostrophic and beta-plane approximations. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. A few examples of continuous HBVMs are introduced, including variants based on Gauss-Legendre and Runge-Kutta schemes, and their underlying theoretical connections are explained. It is demonstrated that these continuous methods inherit the properties of their discrete counterparts, such as energy conservation, and are discussed in the context of energy-based applications. Most importantly, it is shown that continuous HBVMs can be efficiently implemented in a straightforward manner in existing code, allowing for a simple substitution of the original problem's matrix Jacobian with its gradient's structure. This fact facilitates the application of these methods, especially in problems involving structured stochastic differential equations and partial differential control problems. The effectiveness of these methods is confirmed through a series of numerical experiments. A key aspect of these methods is their ability to preserve a modified Hamiltonian format, even in the presence of stabilizing potentials, as evidenced by a range of conservative numerical integrations for various problem types. This structure also enables the development of an efficient approach for determining optimal control problems, as shown in a few illustrative examples. Further research is suggested to extend and confirm the findings of this study. A related software package is available online at a specified URL for reproducing the reported results. Additional technical details are presented in a series of appendices. A few promising areas for further research are suggested. First, the potential for reducing stage numbers in HBVMs, including their continuous variants, could lead to improved numerical performance. Second, the structure of these methods suggests they could be interpreted as specific realizations of implicit multistep methods, providing a potential path towards increasing their order. Third, the continuous nature of HBVMs presents an opportunity for integrating them into the popular Newmark numerical method for solving partial differential equations. Finally, the ability of HBVMs to preserve a modified Hamiltonian format could be used to develop an efficient approach for determining the optimal parameters of these methods in various applications. The fourth possibility listed is particularly significant, as confirming the numerical stability of HBVMs would significantly enhance their practical application in solving a wide range of problem types accurately. This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe. We will begin with the basic components of star formation: the conversion of gas into stars and the influence of turbulence and external factors within the process. We will then move on to the structure of young, unstable stars, known as young stellar objects (YSOs), following that with the formation and expulsion of planetary systems and the properties of proto-stellar disks. By looking at the remnants of star formation, we will gain insight into the system that regulates it and its connections to the larger galactic environment, allowing us to reach from the stars to the universe itself. The authors' approach to the subject draws from the broad range of research known as "star formation 2017", while incorporating recent developments up to early 2021. We seek to provide a clear and organized understanding of the complex topic of star formation and make no claims of comprehensively covering it. Rather, we aim to create a foundation and provide pointers to the numerous studies that have contributed to our understanding, while emphasizing key findings and making connections between different aspects of the process. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by our study, where we suggest deploying these classifiers on cloud-edge networks instead. Specifically, we propose a framework that distributes computation between the cloud and edge systems in an optimal manner based on their available resources. We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to the effective conversion of the quantum dot's electromagnetic dipole into a mode within the cavity. However, we discovered that our specific design could only achieve a high Purcell factor for a limited range of wavelengths. Therefore, we modified the nanobeam's width to accommodate two distinct single-photon source designs, each operating at a different wavelength: 678 nm and 890 nm. Both designs exhibited high source efficiencies and notable Purcell factors of 30.8 and 26.5, respectively. Furthermore, we observed that our optimized design at 678 nm displayed outstanding single-photon purity, making it exceptionally suitable for applications in quantum information processing and optical communication. Lastly, we successfully proposed and evaluated the planar integration of the single-photon source onto a chip, thereby facilitating its application in the generation of non-classical light within photonic-chip-based quantum communication and computation systems. \\

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of rules governing the properties of the deposition matrix, revealing that in most cases it has a specific characteristic frequency dependent on the system dimensions and inherent wave speed. We also discover cases where the matrix is featureless apart from a shift in frequency, and derive a mathematical formula for this frequency in terms of system parameters. This understanding enables a deeper analysis of the matrix's properties and potentially holds significance beyond optimized energy deposition. To illustrate the matrix's complexity, we present detailed calculations for two specific scenarios - a hollow sphere and a solid sphere - and reveal that despite our intuition, the matrix frequencies cannot be explained through simple dimensional analysis. This study marks the first foray into systematically investigating the deposition matrix and could pave the way for future applications. Overall, our findings provide a comprehensive overview of the matrix properties, highlighting the challenges and ambiguities associated with optimizing scattering systems, and suggesting novel approaches for optimized energy delivery and targeted heat generation. We also provide a theoretical explanation for the positive scalar rule and demonstrate the scalar rule's efficacy in multiple scenarios, while raising questions about the matrix's properties and its potential for achieving certain goals, such as confining energy within a specific layer or achieving a perfectly uniform distribution. To address these uncertainties, we present a detailed analysis of the matrix properties for a flat slab and a solid plate, and test the scalar rule's validity in scenarios involving non-reciprocal waves and different types of waves. This study opens up new avenues for optimized scattering systems and showcases the matrix's complexity through various examples, thereby enhancing the general understanding of the matrix and its applications. Moreover, we have also implemented the MATLAB code to calculate the deposition matrix frequency for a given system and its associated mathematical expressions are also provided to facilitate code optimization. This study is versatile and can accommodate various types of waves and systems for calculating the deposition matrix frequency. Furthermore, we have also used the MATLAB code to plot the phase plots of the deposition matrix for different cases and showcased the matrix eigenvalues for different types of waves and systems. This code is highly adaptable and can be applied to different types of waves and systems. To validate our theoretical findings, we have also compared the matrix frequency obtained numerically with the frequency obtained by solving the generalized eigenvalue problem, and our results reveal that the two frequencies coincide under certain conditions. This study has also been extended to explore the properties of the deposition matrix

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully created and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed from low-cost ROHO substrate with a thickness of 2.5 mm, the design exhibits an wide beamwidth of 120 degrees in the E-plane and 40.5 degrees in the H-plane along with good agreement between simulated and measured results. Notably, the gain of the antenna averaged 5.74 dB, rising to 6.04 dB when measured at the center frequency of 36.5 GHz. The research lays the groundwork for the creation of highly integrated, low-cost mm-wave planar array antennas. The design's versatility also enables it to be potentially applied in various applications such as radar and data link systems operating at mm-waves. The wide beamwidth makes it suitable for applications requiring significant spatial immunity like adaptive array radar systems. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Our research also spans the boundaries between coding theory and artificial intelligence, with potential applications extending beyond quantum computing. Furthermore, the value of the learned solver can be quantified using a metric called code value, which could serve as a useful criterion for evaluating various decoding methods. Our findings confirm that machine learning-based surface code decoders can perform competitively when compared to established standards, while achieving similar levels of efficiency with reduced computational complexity. We also explore the potential for extending this approach to develop their own algorithms. To facilitate future research, we provide the source code and relevant tools on GitHub so that researchers can replicate our results and contribute to the development of new, learned surface code decoders.
