A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with networks initialized using a comprehensive feature set, allowing even basic models to achieve improved performance. On one hand, this rich representation provides an effective starting point for the optimizer, while on the other hand, it incorporates a beneficial bias towards handling OoD scenarios.

This robust feature set is generated using the Rich Feature Construction (RFC) algorithm, also known as Bonsai, which comprises a sequence of iterative training episodes. The algorithm is comprised of discovery episodes where a multi-objective criterion is optimized, followed by regularization episodes where an entropy-based criterion is optimized using adversarial training. 

Using the Bonsai feature selector, we initialize the networks at a heightened feature of excellence, enabling the optimizer to converge more swiftly and the generalization to be enhanced. The Bonsai-based initialization technique is readily integratable into any existing model and can be used in tandem with various regularization techniques for handling OoD scenarios. 

The Bonsai-based initialization technique yields the most favorable results when combined with deep ensemble models, yielding state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. 

The Bonsai approach can also be applied to feature selection in scenarios where a comprehensive feature set is present, yielding a more efficient and scalable selector. 

The Bonsai feature selector is openly accessible at the URL https://github.com/jindalYB/Bonsai.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index. The unpredictability of these mediums makes it challenging to control the path of light that attempts to focus or travel through them. The widespread applications of disordered systems, such as biological tissues and solar cells with irregular surfaces, necessitate a thorough examination of their light-scattering properties and effective techniques to control light as it interacts with these systems. To address this need, we present a novel approach called the "scattered light modulator" (SLM) that enables the synchronization of waves scattered within disordered systems. Our proposed method employs an innovative technique of "global phase modulation" (GPM) to adjust and control the phase of scattered light waves. This GPM involves modifying the phases of scattered light waves by incorporating their average phases, as measured from the detector, into an optimization algorithm. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in forming intricate structures and focusing light at depths of up to 20 times the transport mean free path in two-dimensional disordered systems. Furthermore, we successfully extended our technique to 3D systems, achieving the formation of intricate structures 30% deeper within such systems. The concepts outlined in this study can be applied to the control of light within and through various disorder systems at greater depths, as well as enable the enhanced detection of fluorescent signals emanating from deep sources within biological tissues. Additionally, our method has significant implications for the development of more efficient and advanced photovoltaic devices featuring irregular surfaces. To summarize, our study offers a practical approach for deep and controlled access to information within and through disordered systems. Our method is straightforward to implement and can be easily integrated with existing techniques for regulating scattered light, as well as detection mechanisms for capturing light signals emanating from deep sources within biological tissues. Furthermore, our approach can also be applied in the development of advanced photovoltaic devices featuring intricate structures. In this final section, we outline potential avenues for further research and demonstrate the extended duration over which our optimized pulses of light can continue to propagate within disordered systems, as well as the enhanced levels of diffusive transmission achieved through our method. These findings are particularly significant in the context of deep-penetrating biomedical imaging and photovoltaic conversion systems. To facilitate the application of our method in the near future, we detail a concrete strategy for its extension to three-dimensional disordered systems on a large scale. Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of our neighboring planet, Jupiter.  Despite recent technological advancements, a significant barrier to successful planet detection remains.  Even with advanced instruments, the distortion caused by the atmosphere is typically the major obstacle to planets farther than 10-15 astronomical units from the telescope.  A significant improvement is needed to expand the detection range.  Research suggests that a new generation of exoplanet detectors requires not only more effective atmosphere correction but also a more stable and dynamic signal-processing system.  We present a new concept for a new, more sophisticated system that utilizes machine learning and a novel image-processing technique called a spatial scanning pyramid wavefront sensor.  This innovative sensor, combined with a neural network, can effectively mitigate the distortions caused by the atmosphere in a dynamic and adaptable manner.  Our team used a controlled laboratory setup to test this concept, and the results demonstrate a significant improvement in the stability of the system, with a wavefront error reductions of up to $57\%$ across various artificial scenarios.  In a related application, this innovative sensor can also facilitate the alignment of the telescope's focus of interest with the target planet, an issue that could soon become critical in planet-imaging systems.  Our research successfully detected a mock planet 20 astronomical units away, thereby pushing the detection limit further than it currently is.  Our study offers a new and promising approach to enhancing the performance and flexibility of advanced exoplanet detectors.  The potential for expansion to not only exoplanet detection but also other applications in adaptive optics is also explored.  The advancements presented in this research can be used in the current 340i camera system, and the future development of the camera system will greatly improve the effectiveness of the algorithm. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In such scenarios, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however these may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  In order to improve the performance of robust estimators when dealing with small sample sizes, two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed.  Both estimators work by adjusting the estimated residual variances using only the diagonal entries of the hat matrix, resulting in asymptotic equivalence to previously proposed estimators such as the bias reduced linearization method.  This new approach is demonstrated in a simulation study on real world data, with particular application in bivariate meta-regression though it may also be utilized more broadly.  The impact of correcting standard errors on the bias and precision of confidence intervals has also been evaluated.  The proposed estimators have been implemented in an available R code and can be utilized through the metaBMA package.  The usefulness of this new package is illustrated through evaluation of its performance in a meta-analyses of financial markets data correlated over time.  The implementation of its package can be utilized for analysis of correlated data, such as that found in the study of financial markets.  The package metaBMA is available for public use at https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/metaBMA/index.html. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for its accuracy and efficiency, and found that increasing the time gap between fluid and particle time steps has negligible effects on the overall simulation. Our model enables optimal selection of time steps based on the desired level of simulation detail, and offers significant performance enhancements up to 100 times for large-scale simulations. Our algorithm also maintains high numerical stability, and achieved results comparable to traditional models for a wide range of simulations. Our method's accuracy was confirmed through comparisons with both experimental data and simulations using traditional models. Our algorithm offers great flexibility in its application to various fluid-particle simulation models, and can be used for a range of simulation cases including turbulent flows, gravitational settling, and particle collisions. Our method's efficiency and accuracy make it an apt choice for extensive simulations of complex scenarios such as drag crises, saltation, and complex collision phenomena. Our algorithm has the potential to significantly speed up the calculation of complex fluid-particle flow problems in engineering and geoscience applications. Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm. Our analysis suggests that the commonly held "particle absorption" theory underlying Hawking radiation requires revision. Instead, Hawking radiation is hypothesized to arise from a thermal force acting on the black hole due to its interaction with the thermal atmosphere, with the thermal force being powered by energy drawn from the black hole's mass. The thermal force is in turn caused by the rapid acceleration of geodesic transfer of angular momentum from the atmosphere to the black hole. Our theoretical framework provides a new physical perspective on the origin of Hawking radiation and the nature of black holes. Furthermore, our model offers potential connections to quantum electrodynamics, serving as a potential link between the geometric approach to black holes and the standard quantum field theory on Curved spacetime techniques used to investigate the Unruh effect. The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially in cases where rapidity is in the forward direction. Additionally, model consistency with ALICE measurements is found across various centrality levels. Nonetheless, models exhibit discrepancies when compared to LHCb data, revealing a notable divergence of approximately one order of magnitude in some cases. Further analysis involves calculating nuclear modification ratios and demonstrates that models tend to generate ratios in the range of 0.5 to 0.8, although some variance exists. Finally, the impact of coherent scattering on nuclear broadening is explored and reveals that it produces a noticeable effect, particularly in central events and at low transverse momenta. Coherent scattering is accountable for up to 20% of the observed broadening and largely contributes to the upper limit of the dispersion observed. In conclusion, the relationship between nuclear broadening, parton saturation, and transverse momentum variations is clarified, thereby facilitating the differentiation between coherent and incoherent scattering processes. This distinction is crucial for understanding the scattering of prompt di-leptons off nuclei. In consequence, the present analysis offers implications that extend beyond the scope of cold QCD to a broader context of perturbative QCD. In addition, the present cold QCD analysis may find applications in future measurements involving the Z-boson production in nuclear collisions. Ultimately, the present results are intended to guide researchers towards a potential resolution of model discrepancies and encourage the performance of further theoretical and experimental investigations. In this context, the present study is expected to foster communication between theoretical and experimental researchers, thereby promoting a deeper understanding of nuclear broadening phenomena. This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. Specifically, the first method involves a systematic examination of the parameter $n$, while the second method utilizes a systematic examination in a related number system. Additionally, it is demonstrated that pairs of relatively prime positive integers $a$ and $b$ can be found such that the expression $a^2-a-b$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$. Similar findings have been previously reported for the prime number $3$ in a corresponding study. However, it is noteworthy that the approach employed in this article relies heavily on unique properties of the prime number $7$. Consequently, this raises the inquiry: can the results presented in this article be extended to other prime numbers? Finally, an attempt is made to find pairs of relatively prime positive integers $a$ and $b$ such that the sum $a+b$ can be factored as the difference of two consecutive square numbers, $q$ and $q+1$. A corresponding study previously reported the existence of pairs $(a,b)$ where $a<b$, while an alternative method presented here finds pairs $(a,b)$ where $a>b$. Ultimately, the largest known pair of relatively prime positive integers $(a,b)$ such that $a+b$ can be expressed as the difference of two consecutive square numbers has a value of $191/3$. However, it is $3$ itself that plays a crucial role in this expression; consequently, it is once again open to question: can results presented in this article be extended to other prime numbers? \bigskip

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, as data in these caches may be lost in the event of a crash, necessitating an explicit flush into the main memory to guarantee data integrity. In this study, a new algorithm-based approach is proposed to guarantee data consistency and correctness for high-performance computing applications in systems using non-volatile memory. This method introduces only a minor runtime overhead, allowing developers to leverage the properties of algorithms to verify data integrity after system crashes. Our proposed approach demonstrates significant advantages over traditional checkpointing methods in terms of runtime efficiency while maintaining the ability to correct errors with minimal reprocessing costs. Our comprehensive evaluations, carried out across multiple test scenarios and algorithms such as an iterative solver and dense matrix multiplication, have consistently yielded a correction time that was just a tiny fraction of the original runtime, averaging less than 0.03%. Furthermore, our solution also accommodates parallel computing by dividing the verification process across multiple processes, thus further minimizing its impact on runtime efficiency. Our proposed strategy offers an attractive alternative to traditional fault-tolerance methods for high-performance computing applications, as it requires no modifications to either the application code or the underlying architecture. Our novel paradigm has the potential to inspire future innovations in fault-tolerance design. Our comprehensive fault tolerance analysis, encompassing over 180 different fault scenarios, has yielded an error correction rate of 100%, thereby solidifying the reliability of this fault-tolerance strategy. Our simulation model, open-source fault insertion tool, and numerical results are available online for replication purposes. First and foremost, our study aims to promote the understanding of non-volatile memory technology and its practical applications in high-performance computing systems. Our proposed algorithm-based approach has the secondary benefit of removing the underlying hardware complexity, thus simplifying the design of reliable parallel algorithms. Our study has also led to the development of several useful parallelization techniques for executing sequential algorithms, thus contributing to the advancement of reliable high-performance computing applications. Our most notable contribution is the creation of a fault-tolerance design framework, capable of automatically generating reliable parallel programs from existing sequential algorithms. Our study showcases the applicability of non-volatile memory in high-performance computing systems and highlights the challenges associated with its volatility, particularly in system crashes. Our proposed algorithm-based approach has the ability to guarantee data consistency and correctness without requiring changes to the application

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation of such structures from text is an understudied challenge. Existing methods often rely on hand-coded associations between words or their statistical similarities, but these approaches fall short in handling novel or unrelated terms. To address this limitation, our research proposes a more principled method for creating topic-based information hierarchies from large corpora of unstructured text. This method employs unsupervised topic models to extract meaningful themes and subsequently clusters related topics into a hierarchical structure through both graph partitioning and embedding techniques. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we compared our method's performance with that of state-of-the-art hierarchical topic model and a semantic network-based method, using three benchmarks and three additional real-world datasets. The results show that our approach surpasses existing methods in assigning relevant documents to each topic and the overall topic hierarchy achieves a higher internal consistency and external validity compared to other methods. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the lowest level of our hierarchies often corresponds to distinct semantic categories and the top levels tend to separate topics based on more general criteria such as time, geographical location, and domain. To facilitate the reproduction of our results and provide a reference point for evaluating automatic information hierarchies, our code and derived hierarchies are publicly available for download. Additionally, the study's findings emphasize the importance of manually evaluating the accuracy and coherence of computational models, and the benefits of an iterative improvement strategy are also discussed. To gauge the practical utility of our approach, a case study is conducted to demonstrate the potential of our information hierarchies to support semantic search by acting as a bridge between abstract queries and specific documents. The outcomes of this study confirm the feasibility of our method for organizing complex information and effectively supporting concrete applications such as semantic search. To conclude, our work makes three primary contributions: the integration of graph partitioning and word embeddings for clustering, the examination of hierarchical topic models, and the assessment of the coherence of automatically constructed information hierarchies, which are crucial for determining their utility in practical applications. The outcomes of this study offer insights into the characteristics and performance of our approach compared to existing methods, and the practical utility of our information hierarchies in supporting semantic search. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the ratio of escape times to orbital periods, and the distribution of Mergers of unbound pairs as new stars form. Our results showed significant agreement between these measures and existing theoretical predictions for non-hierarchical two-body mergers. Nevertheless, in contrast to general relativity's predictions for hierarchical three-body systems, our findings revealed the probability of escape, anisotropy of escape directions, and the ratio of escape times to orbital periods to be indistinguishable from isotropic, uncensored versions of their respective general relativity counterparts. However, the exponent representing narrow escapes and the distribution of Mergers of unbound pairs as new stars form deviated substantially from the predictions of general relativity. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the probability of escape is not solely influenced by the system's eccentricity but rather interacts with binding energy in a more complex manner. In addition, we discovered that the mass ratio of the interacting bodies affects the probability of escape and anisotropy of escape directions. Our exhaustive examination of non-hierarchical three-body systems provides a deeper understanding of the statistical properties of disintegrations and their connection to the formation of new stars. Our findings are also applicable to the interpretation of future gravitational wave detections and the modeling of stellar disruption in the vicinity of black holes and neutron stars. Additionally, our work may be used to improve the modeling of various astrophysical phenomena by incorporating the statistical properties of disintegrations into the modeling of these systems. Lastly, our analysis highlights the significance of further exploring the statistical behavior of disintegrations in the context of stellar disruption. Although our examination focused primarily on the disruption of main-sequence stars, our results can also be generalized to the disruption of other types of stars. In the future, an extensive examination of the disruption of white dwarves is needed to describe their disintegration according to the predictions of general relativity. In contrast to the findings of our study, the disruption of white dwarves is expected to follow the predictions of general relativity more accurately due to the greater importance of gravitational forces in this scenario. When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up. Our study compares
the effectiveness of various CPU optimization techniques for regression testing.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data utilizing advanced deep sequential models. These datasets contain disparate time-stamps and incompatible sampling rates, posing difficulties for previous studies. A novel ecological modeling approach is developed to synchronize analysis with the two datasets, taking into consideration the distinct observation periods. Results indicate that the combined predictors yield superior performance over individual predictors, with an 8.1% enhancement in F1-score. A proposed Ecological Momentary Assessment-aware model is also introduced, addressing biases stemming from EMA sampling and variable observation durations. The research validates the superiority of this model over independent EHR and EMA predictors, demonstrating significant improvements in forecasting accuracy. The Ecological Momentary Assessment-aware model exhibits superior performance in functional datasets and real-world applications, with enhanced predictive accuracy observed in 82% of such instances. The findings indicate that integrating EHR and EMA data using deep sequential models offers significant advantages in forecasting suicidal ideation. The proposed Ecological Momentary Assessment-aware model offers superior outcomes and can be utilized as a benchmark in comparable suicidal ideation forecasting studies. The code for replicating this study's results can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/qzhenergy/DeepEcologicalModel. In terms of practical applications, the integration of EHR and EMA data appears to offer a favorable risk-benefit profile for forecasting suicidal ideation, with 93% of variables and 88% of Ecological Momentary Assessment-aware models exhibiting enhanced or equivalent performance. Consequently, the recommended course of action is to incorporate Electronic Health Records and Ecological Momentary Assessment data in suicidal ideation forecasting studies. The approach is found to be beneficial in a diverse range of ecological variables and forecasting outcomes. The research highlights the importance of carefully aligning analysis with the two datasets and considers their distinct observation periods. To achieve this, the Ecological Momentary Assessment record that is most closely aligned with the Electronic Health Records is identified, with subsequent records then being sampled at consistent intervals. The developed Ecological Momentary Assessment-aware model is then used to forecast suicidal ideation on the basis of this synchronized data. To handle issues arising from variable observation durations in Ecological Momentary Assessment records, the Ecological Momentary Assessment record with the shortest duration is selected as the reference point, with subsequent records then being sampled at consistent intervals. The Ecological Momentary Assessment record with the shortest duration is designated as t=0, while subsequent records are assigned timestamps relative to this reference point

Our findings show that the sound velocity of dense matter is directly influenced by its adiabatic index and surface gravity of the quark star, consistent with the expected behavior in the high-density range. In addition, we observe that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition if it displays a distinct behavior in the density range of 5-10 times nuclear saturation density. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be an additional mechanism explaining the origin of U galaxies. Our findings demonstrate that U galaxies play a key role in the transition between S and S$^+$ galaxies. The magnitude of the nonlinear magnetoelectric effect is determined by the dynamical charge of fermionic excitations and their correlation time. Additionally, this paper builds on earlier results (Messen and Mies, 2019) by extending stochastic lambda calculus to include a shared register for context sharing and stable values, while ensuring that the derived sound and sufficient semantics remain compatible with the core features of the programming language. Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving a satisfactory classification rate of 0.88 within a dataset and 0.80 across different datasets. Additionally, we explore three practical applications of design mining: automatically categorizing discussions, identifying design-related issues, and informing design documentation. The benefits of improved design mining methodology extend to these uses, leading to more accurate and consistent results. This research was conducted using eight large open-source projects under 1 million lines of code, with further analysis showing that, even with existing data, small enhancements to the model can yield significant improvements in reliability. Long-term, this leads to a more trustworthy design mining process, empowering practical applications to consistently inform software design through comments, thus facilitating meaningful design evolution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not feasible in general. A compelling approach to resolve this limitation is to use a variational inequality that is inherently linked to the problem's optimal solution, offering a standard framework that can work universally. In specific contexts, the variational inequality can be replaced with a more interpretable linear system, which is applicable to several prominent problems such as the k-median, flow-based models, and combinatorial optimization tasks. We present a method that combines the strengths of proximal algorithms and these variational inequalities, allowing for the simultaneous improvement of solutions and problem structures, and, in many cases, identifying the optimal solution without the need for explicit regularization. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. A key aspect of our approach is the utilization of a few auxiliary variables to accommodate the desired structure, which reduces the burden on memory usage. Judiciously selecting these variables is possible by formulating a corresponding subproblem. To optimize the choice of these variables, we propose a simple yet effective strategy. The proposed method is comparable to state-of-the-art algorithms for k-median and flow-based models in terms of performance, and, in many cases, outperforms or matches the results of established methods. The source code for our approach is available online. It is worth noting that our approach is intended for offline optimization, as it is not suitable for real-time applications due to its computational intensity. Nonetheless, the proposed method shows great promise for solving various optimization challenges. An interesting direction for further research is the development of a flexible and general approach to determine the desired structure without the need for explicit regularization. Another area of interest is the extension of our method to handle structured sparsity, which is a valuable area of study in its own right. The proposed method is also general enough to be applied to a wide range of problems that are not entirely nonsmooth in nature, as long as they possess a nonsmooth component and a smooth component with shared underlying structure. Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While countries like Japan have
introduced more cost-effective and accessible smartphone-based solutions for
automated road condition monitoring, many other countries continue to search for
efficient alternatives. To address these issues, this study contributes in
several key ways. Firstly, it examines the suitability of Japan's approach for
global implementation. Secondly, a modified version of Japan's method is
developed to enhance accuracy and simplify usage as a global model. Thirdly,
emphasizing the importance of training data for successful model performance, a
system is created to automatically identify and mark road damage for learning
algorithm precision. Fourthly, a comprehensive framework is established to
evaluate the effectiveness of Japan's method in accurately identifying road
damage. Lastly, this study formally presents a detailed evaluation metric known
as ADemRE, which measures automated road damage identification and estimation
performance. These contributions are validated through thorough experiments using
over 10,000 road images, along with nearly 300,000 labeled segments. Our
research indicates that Japan's method excelled in terms of estimation precision
though fell short in damage detection, while our enhanced model demonstrated
excellent all-around results with a success rate of 93.5% for both detection and
estimation tasks. Additionally, results obtained from multiple other evaluation
metrics confirm the substantial improvement achieved by building upon Japan's
approach. Ultimately, this study presents a groundbreaking solution for
municipalities worldwide to evaluate road damage using just a smartphone. By
leveraging a vast collection of labeled images and a trained model, a
smarter, more efficient, and more accessible road damage evaluation process is
realized, one that also empowers further innovation through AI services for
roads, including improved maintenance, more efficient traffic management, and
increased driver safety. Our research also opens doors for integrating road
condition monitoring into a broader range of intelligent urban governance
applications, which could lead to more advanced services like optimized logistics
and navigation systems. To replicate our findings, refer to our step-by-step
implementation guide and data sets provided in the supplementary materials.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes and for which we have access to demonstrated expert behavior.  Current imitation algorithms often rely on in-domain data for training and can fall short when presented with out-of-domain data.  This paper presents an alternative, the Functional Gradient Imitation (FGI), that draws upon the Zero-Shot Transfer framework and treats imitation as a classification problem.  FGI analyzes the impact of state and action function transformations on behavior and proposes a gradient imitation algorithm that leverages this understanding.  The algorithm has been successfully tested on two challenging domains, the continuous control of robots and image classification, and outperforms existing imitation algorithms while achieving zero-shot transfer capabilities.  The code for FGI is available at https://github.com/alecjp/fgi.  The research has been partially supported by grants from the National Science Foundation and the European Research Council.  Further information can be found at https://as4sam.github.io/pubs/FGI.html.  Contact the author at a.pasquale@ed.ac.uk for additional inquiries. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to 1000 years following the initial protostar formation. To represent the protostars and their magnetic field structures, we utilized a stiff equation of state approach instead of the conventional sink particle technique. In nine out of ten locations, gas accretion either slowed or stopped within the area where the magnetic field was highly amplified. Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. We establish a deduction calculus for each of these concepts, show how to create the smallest possible bases, and also examine redundancy with multiple association rules. We fully dissect the case of redundancy involving two partial premises. We illustrate our approach with various numerical examples. We showcase how the smallest basis of non-redundant association rules can be computed using independent parameter values, specifically when rules have the same support value. We explore optimizations for computing the smallest basis of non-redundant association rules with arbitrary parameter values. We compare existing approaches to determining non-redundant association rules and propose new strategies for achieving this. We examine the problem of finding non-redundant association rules with multiple parameters and discuss the possibility of solving this problem in linear time. We conclude by highlighting potential future areas of research. We make our methods available to the public through our website. We fully document the algorithms used in our code. We also provide an implementation of our proposed algorithms in Python for the benefit of the Data Mining community. To our knowledge, our approach to determining the smallest basis of non-redundant association rules with independent parameter values is the first time this has been computed successfully. We measure the performance of our approach through extensive experiments on publicly available datasets. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed methods and the strength of the Deduction Calculus for the two concepts of redundancy. We also investigate the behavior of our approach as parameter values increase from sparse to dense scenarios. We wish to encourage the use of multiple parameters for association rules to facilitate data analysis. We showcase the applicability of our approach to determine non-redundant association rules with multiple parameters in various real-life scenarios, including sales transaction data and image analysis. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  Specifically, every dollar spent on mental health treatment generates between $1.40 and $3.57 in crime cost savings.  The study relies on a difference-in-differences assessment, employing both a linear model and a propensity score matching technique to control for potential biases in the data.  The analyzed population totals 2,632,499 offenders, with 10,398 receiving mental health treatment and 304,989 eligible comparators.  The research indicates mental health treatment as part of probation sentences not only improves public safety but also generates significant crime cost savings.  These findings align with the growing body of research advocating court-ordered mental health treatment as an effective and financially beneficial strategy.  The data suggests that increasing the probability of receiving treatment by 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 percent would decrease recidivism rates by 1.7, 3.4, 5.1, 6.8, 8.4, and 10 percentage points, respectively.  Consequently, such an increase could potentially cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing mental health treatment.  The projected crime cost savings range from $9 million to $18 million for every 10 percent increase in the probability of receiving treatment.  Ultimately, the study's findings strongly support the strategic use of court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation sentences and the associated crime cost savings that can be achieved through such an approach. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework by accounting for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, and demonstrates that utilizing an inverse multiplicative factor in the privacy parameter $ε$ maintains the desired privacy guarantees while increasing data utility. The proposed solution is empirically validated through the analysis of real-world energy usage datasets. Experimental findings indicate that the one-sided differential privacy framework yields substantial enhancements in data utility when compared to traditional approaches, thereby facilitating the creation of accurate and informative visualizations while maintaining dependable privacy protections. The findings of this study indicate that one-sided differential privacy is conducive to supporting various data visualization tasks, including visualization of historical data trends and actionable insights into recent and past system anomalies. Notably, the process of converting raw data into a suitable format for visualization does not compromise the privacy and utility of the processed data under the one-sided differential privacy framework. As a practical example, the paper showcases how one-sided differential privacy enables the development of informative and non-compromising visualizations for building energy usage analysis. The resulting visualizations effectively capture system-wide and system-component-wise historical trend, allowing for prompt and accurate identification of past and recent anomalies. In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough at 88 au that overlapped with the PAH emission peak, and we observed no gas substructures beyond this point.
Our model recreated the observed gas substructures by incorporating a customized dust model that accounted for the effects of radiation pressure and the vertical hydrostatic pressure gradient.
However, this model also failed to replicate the PAH emission distribution, suggesting that it is influenced by large dust particles and specific chemical conditions, ultimately dependent on the disk's structure and composition. 
Our findings imply that the gas substructures in AS 209 are likely attributed to a stable disk configuration with minimal influence from disk winds or the planetesimal belt. 
This understanding of the gas substructures in AS 209 offers a fresh outlook on the gas disk geometry and its relation to planetary building blocks in protoplanetary disks. 
Our model can serve as a baseline for future studies of gas substructures using upcoming mid-infrared spectrometers. 
Our study highlights the value of multi-species observations for understanding the gas disk's structure and composition, and 
our analysis suggests that gas substructures are optimal for discovering similar substructures in proto-planetary disks.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls. As a byproduct of our analysis, we establish the uniqueness of the Lagrangian function under a weaker constraint. We demonstrate that the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls can be restricted to depend only on the common part of their measures when the measures are concentrated on a common path, effectively simplifying the dependence. This outcome leads to the existence of an equilibrium in a mean field game involving controls with velocities, a setting frequently applied to study free boundary problems, dynamic systems with phase transitions, and the behavior of crystals in solidifying materials. Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. Furthermore, we found that these structures' ages, when compared to their actual age spread, appear excessively large. It is also worth noting that these structures, while seemingly homogeneous, can exhibit identical characteristics if composed of stars from different groups, stars moving independently, or stars from groups that originated from different sources. Based on our findings, we suggest that these structures are actually dispersing groups, not physically connected objects as previously thought. We propose that these structures could provide valuable information when analyzed in relation to the broader stellar distribution in the Milky Way galaxy. On the other hand, we believe that "groups of strings" are actually the result of overlapping multiple structures and may hold further insights into the galaxy's composition. Ultimately, we recommend a more conservative approach in scientific literature to both these structures and groups, avoiding language that implies a shared origin for their members, and instead describing the Gaia detected structures more accurately as "strings" and "groups of strings". We propose this linguistic shift in the scientific community to reflect our proposed definition and the corresponding evidence. In the context of our research, we choose to refer to these structures as "strings" and "groups of strings". We hope that our proposed definition and the corresponding evidence can initiate a broader discussion on this topic. On a different note, we would like to emphasize the significance of the Gaia mission in the historical context of astrometry and its continued impact in the era of space-based astrometry. Additionally, we would like to acknowledge the ongoing contributions of the First President of the IAU Division F, Dr. Philippe Kunkel, to the field of stellar structure and constitution, while also expressing our sadness at not being able to celebrate his achievements in person. Philosophically speaking, our findings raise the query of whether the concept of "constellation" should be reevaluated, not just in the context of space but also in the realm of human imagination. This thought experiment will undoubtedly continue to resonate in the future

This research introduces a novel method to calculate the visual similarity between clothing items by analyzing their stylistic attributes such as style, fit, and quality. The proposed method leverages style nets, which are learned from large datasets of fashion items, to map individual items to a common visual space. Thereafter, the aesthetic compatibility of garments in an outfit is determined by computing the distance between their visual representations. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses traditional human assessments in outfits consisting of two or more items. Additionally, the study shows that visual similarity is more crucial than human perception in determining outfit coherence. To facilitate research, the code and trained style nets are freely accessible on the repository hosted at https://github.com/twospotmetals/outfit-coherence. The research extends existing work on visual compatibility, which primarily focused on two items, by exploring its implications for multi-item outfits and establishing baseline benchmarks for future studies. Moreover, the codebase contributes to the growing literature on visual aesthetic analysis in fashion, which holds significant potential for enhancing e-commerce platforms and fashion recommendations. In particular, it may inform the development of computer-aided fashion advice and help reduce fashion misfits during online purchases by recommending visually compatible garments. The code also has potential applications in generating CoCo, the output of an outfit coherence prediction task. The generated CoCo can further be utilized to improve the quality of the output by performing iterative expectations, as initially proposed by Hakeem and others. The code also contains an implementation of the vae multinomial model for generating multinomial outcomes. The research also explores an alternative strategy for outfit coherence prediction by leveraging visual similarity and human assessments in two-item outfits as prior information for predicting the aesthetic compatibility of multi-item outfits. The findings show that visual similarity and human prior assumptions can be utilized as soft constraints in optimizing the aesthetic compatibility of multi-item outfits. The code implements the constrained optimization problem for predicting outfit coherence, as well as the visualization techniques for generating CoCo. This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators. Additionally, we identify connections with existing polynomial function calculi for one-dimensional operators and the $M^p$-function theory for $p$ in the range of $1-2$. We also explore applications of the newly introduced calculus across multiple domains, including linear differential equations, the functional calculus for commuting operators, and spectral theory for (possibly) non-self-adjoint operators. Finally, we outline potential avenues for further research. Throughout the work, we strive to maintain clear, approachable exposition and illustrative examples. As a supplement, we have included a brief survey on recent developments in functional calculi for groups and measures. In particular, we have included a discussion on the function theory for arbitrary measures introduced by the authors of [J. Oper. Theory 2020], set against the backdrop of a decade of research focusing on functional calculi for groups.**}

To better understand these mechanisms, we've developed a simulation model combining principles of fluid dynamics and particle movement, which we use to study cases where the rate of expansion either slows down or accelerates continuously. This means our results can be applied to a wide range of situations, including those caused by cooling or consumed from the inside out. The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride-based electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. We performed detailed computations utilizing the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation to calculate the hole mobility of GaN, revealing that a specific matching material results in an significant increase in hole mobility. Notably, this effect can be utilized to decrease the series resistance in GaN-based transistors. We also found that a particular orientation of the crystal lattice is beneficial for achieving optimal results. Furthermore, our results suggest that aligning the GaN/crystal lattice axis could lead to higher hole concentrations and reduced series resistance. Consequently, matching GaN to a certain II-IV nitride materials may present a novel strategy for improving gallium nitride technology. Moreover, our study indicates that strain-induced modifications to the 2p valence band structure can have a substantial impact on the hole mobility. We discovered that compressive strain in the growth direction causes hole bands to shift toward the $\Gamma$ point, resulting in increased hole mobility when matched to certain materials. Conversely, tensile strain has the opposite effect, potentially rendering it more challenging to achieve optimal hole mobility. Nonetheless, matching GaN to a particular material with minimal lattice mismatch appears to successfully modulate the hole mobility. Consequently, our theoretical findings may inspire new approaches for managing series resistance in GaN-based transistors. We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region. Building on this analysis, we derive a specific set of transformed patches for a particular surface, and use this example to illustrate how these transformations address a long-standing problem involving the consistency of the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Our findings also lead to the creation of four new explicit surfaces. Finally, we use the Calapso transformation to generate a surface that satisfies a unique geometric condition, thereby resolving a problem that had been challenging to solve up until now. \\

Notably, we demonstrate the existence and estimates of Hilbert--Schmidt operators enabling reliable computation of $P$. Additionally, we tackle operators $T$ such as $\mathbb{E}[Y^2] \cdot \mathrm{id} - T$ and prove conditions for inverting $T$ without requiring smoothness assumptions on $P$. These findings are relevant to variational projections and relevant to random linear operators, as well as the study of random matrices. The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded degree. The generated Y retains the same local spectral expansion as X and has the added benefit of having a significantly higher number of simplices.

An important aspect of Y's structure is the presence of groups that act on its covers; these groups can be identified as finitely presented abelian groups containing a specific element of infinite order. By varying the parameters of our algorithm, we are able to create a continuous spectrum of high dimensional expanders, offering different trade-offs between the size of Y's simplices and its local spectral expansion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the beta-transformation associated with any such group has a point of view as a section of an expanding map, and also show that the shift map on the inverse limit of a chain of covers in C^2 has a point of view as a relatively symmetric orbit under a group of hyperbolic isometries. Lastly, we discuss an independent proof by Sahlsten that proves the entire spectrum is discrete, a fact first observed by Bell and Boston. Our study shares similarities with the work of Kadouharov, Sahlsten, and Shlykov in the expander graphs setting. 

Additionally, it is worth noting that the concept of high dimensional expanders can be viewed as an extension of expander graphs, with both share similar properties. Our research builds upon this connection, while also drawing parallels with the works of Kapranov and Gromov in the realm of high dimensional expanders within the context of metric spaces. 

Our initial intuition for our algorithm was inspired by the works of Meshulam and Roth, who used a related idea at the level of graphs, and also by the works of Kapranov and Bertram, who used an idea at the level of simplicial complexes in an unrelated setting.

Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope has been formally verified to be correct through a detailed proof and has outperformed existing systems in both accuracy and computational complexity in real-world experiments across diverse datasets. The outstanding performance of DataScope is attributed to its ability to integrate the parallel computation of relational algebra queries with the incremental recalculation of K-nearest neighbor classifiers. DataScope has been further extended to handle non-canonical pipelines, which consists of multiple relational algebra queries, each followed by a K-nearest neighbor classifier, utilizing a novel approach to segment the pipeline into canonical sub-pipelines, thereby guaranteeing scalability and practicality in real-world applications. DataScope has been empirically shown to be the first system to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples in a complex pipeline that integrates data transformation, feature design, and model training. DataScope has been made publicly available at https://github.com/programminghistorian/DataScope. This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices. The applications of discrete invariants to the study of sparse polynomials, parametric combinatorics, and the feasibility of systems of equations or linear constraints are particularly significant. Moreover, a fundamental concept in the realm of algebraic statistics, the Berinstein-MacDonald invariant, is linked to a fundamental concept in the realm of enumerative algebraic geometry, the Gromov-Witten invariant, as well as to the degree of a sparse polynomial, thus revealing a connection between these invariants. We present a unified framework that integrates discrete invariants across all these fields and illustrate the complexity of this theory through examples. Lastly, we outline promising avenues for future research. The provided documentation is suitable for researchers who wish to apply and extend the theoretical concepts described within. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant internal rearrangement, notably a rotation of the equilibrium order parameter $\phi$ from 55° to 180°. Our pressure-induced resistometry measurements confirm that the anomalous resistivity exhibits a significant increase rate of 1.7 T% per GPa within the low-pressure regime, aligning with in-plane lattice contraction. The Hall signal intensity undergoes an intriguing phase transition across the pressure range of 1.3 to 1.8 GPa, exhibiting a Hall intensity ratio of 3:2 within the high-pressure phase. Our density functional theory analysis reveals that this critical transition is characterized by a substantial increase in carrier mixing between Mn sites along the a-axis. The experimental and theoretical findings concomitantly show significant modifications of specific heat, spin Hall conductivity, and Rixs spectra. An accompanying spin model indicates that the transition is a deconfementization process, in which magnetic dimers are established at a certain critical pressure. Our research thus bridges the gap between transport behavior and microscopic antiferromagnetic arrangements within Mn$_3$Sn. The anomalous Hall effect is found to cease at pressures exceeding 1.8 GPa, as corroborated by our theoretical predictions and an empirical AHE scaling formula. Conversely, a substantial transverse magnetization remains evident in the high-pressure phase, in accordance with our experimental findings. Additionally, a substantial Kerr rotation is observed at pressures exceeding 1.8 GPa, providing an alternative method for detecting phase transitions in Mn$_3$Sn. Our research provides pivotal insights into the connection between pressure-induced antiferromagnetic rearrangements and the Anomalous Hall effect. The resulting Kerr rotation could yield significant applications in the development of spintronics and optoelectronics within triangular antiferromagnetic compounds. Furthermore, our study may inspire the creation of innovative and efficient spintronics and optoelectronics devices by integrating similar triangular antiferromagnetic materials. For example, when a pressure-induced phase transition is applied rather than an external magnetic field, as in Mn$_3$Sn, the resulting material may maintain its robustness against temperature increases, thus holding promise for the creation of a new class of spintronics and optoelectronics devices. Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as the
prevalent approach for RE. In particular, the reliability of DNNs in the forms of
supervised and distant supervision methods makes them nearly universally trusted
solutions for RE. This article serves as an introduction, offering an in-depth analysis
of DNNs for RE from three key perspectives: related work, techniques for feature engineering, 
and models used for RE. This comprehensive examination serves as an accessible entry
point for researchers new to RE who can benefit from the discussion of existing approaches,
as well as a convenient reference for seasoned researchers to assess the current state
of the art in RE. Furthermore, the article addresses key challenges and possible future
directions, along with highlighting prominent gaps in RE research. Finally, the article
provides a detailed classification of existing RE work, facilitating future evaluation
and assessment of the field by the research community. This comprehensive survey
distinguishes itself from earlier RE surveys by its DNN-centric focus, incorporating
insights from prominent knowledge graph conferences (KGC), a separate examination of
distant supervision methods for RE, and an in-depth analysis of recently introduced
evaluation and analysis tools for assessing DNN-based RE methods. The final version
of this article was completed in February 2021. Following the submission, further
research was conducted and new findings were incorporated in April 2021. Additionally,
the repository containing the survey https://skep.me/re/ provides open-access to
all relevant information discussed in this article.

Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download. Furthermore, we demonstrate the broad applicability of our work by successfully applying it to the analysis of two groundbreaking datasets, one for adverse drug-drug interactions and another for gene interactions within cellular co-localization systems. health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies
within medical images. This requirement has made anatomical information analysis
a crucial area of study within medical computer vision. Previous methods rely on the
use of annotated structures to locate and identify human anatomy, disregarding
anatomical context in the images provided by doctors' reports. This leads to
suboptimal results, as the relationship between images and reports is unconsidered.
In an attempt to resolve this, researchers have introduced a new system that uses
anatomical information from reports to guide medical computer vision tasks. This
system allows for the generation of highly accurate and detailed mappings of
anatomies within medical images, simply by utilizing clinical reports as guides.

information in reports, as well as by anatomical structures in images, allowing it
to correctly locate and interpret variations in anatomical contexts. In experiments
conducting 2D and 3D anatomical structure mappings, it was observed that the proposed
system notably outperformed current state-of-the-art methods. In addition to
improving mappings of anatomical structures, the anatomy-mapping model was also
applied to a range of other computer vision tasks, such as the detection of lesions

anatomy-mapping model was both highly accurate and intermediately fast, as
determined by tests. All of these findings indicate that the anatomy-mapping
model could be developed into an highly effective tool for a range of medical
computer vision tasks. Furthermore, it provides the foundation for which future
research can be conducted on a range of other medical image-to-text tasks. This

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model, a procedure known as 'covered interest arbitrage'. The outcome of this study reveals a significant boost in the efficiency of cryptocurrency price formation dynamics between 2016 and 2020, a boost that surpasses that of the financial markets during the same period. Our research provides strong evidence for the medium of exchange stability of cryptocurrencies. The findings presented here can be utilized to strengthen the case for cryptocurrencies as reliable investment opportunities and as a foundation for further in-depth analytical studies. Additionally, the methods employed can be transferred to the analysis of other emerging markets and assets. Finally, the idea of 'covered interest arbitrage' presented here could be developed into an automated trading strategy. In contrast to previous studies, which primarily based their analysis on Bitcoin, our research offers a more comprehensive insight into the stability of major cryptocurrencies as a group. The outcomes achieved through our analysis may serve as a foundation for further in-depth studies on specific cryptocurrencies and their potential as investment opportunities. The findings presented here provide the strongest evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a group since 2016. The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the Hall effect. These theories are substantiated through the examination of associated electric field data. For the sub-ion range, one of the theories implies the presence of Hall modes, supported by observed magnetic field alignments. However, the absence of certain ion spectrometer measurements forces an alternative interpretation of the observed density patterns as being related to the Hall effect. These findings emphasize the need for ion data in understanding the compressive plasma turbulence, specifically at sub-ion scales. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications. The modified approach maintains low pulse energy fluctuations and retains high pulse stability. The method demonstrates great promise for achieving attosecond pulse generation directly from high-energy SASE FELs, thus streamlining experimental workflows and increasing the accessibility of attosecond physics research. Furthermore, the improved performance of the chirp-taper technique can also be applied to other SASE FEL schemes, such as the undulator-based solution and the waveguide FEL device. Waveguide FELs, operating at higher gain values, may achieve the same level of performance with fewer undulator periods, while the ideas presented can be transposed onto other SASE FEL schemes, such as the undulator-based solution.
