A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points. These approximations lead to four types of solutions: (i) upper and lower bores, (ii) waves reflecting at critical levels, (iii) waves asymptotic to critical levels, and (iv) waves tending to zeros of the discriminant. Additionally, energy growth in both time and space is observed for certain scenarios. When the approximation is further simplified to neglect horizontal viscosity, the classical Cowen-Cullen and Squire solutions are recovered. Finally, numerical solutions for velocity and temperature profiles are determined using a four-layer numerical model, validated against corresponding laboratory data. Although perfect agreement is not achieved, the proposed model proves effective in identifying both the physical mechanisms underlying these experiments and the parameter ranges in which the solutions are applicable. Based on this outcome, the proposed model is suggested for use as a predictor before, during, and after laboratory experiments in buoyancy-driven flows. It can also serve as a initial condition or post-experiment validator for further analysis of these processes. As a result, the model offers valuable insights for assessing the impact of turbulence on both geophysical and laboratory stratified flows.

a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans. The code for our study
can be accessed at https://github.com/alexalexandrov/dc-analysis. Our findings
involving Texas districts, which were finalized in 2021, reveal an average
unfairness rating of 0.677, with more extreme cases found in 14 out of 31
districts. A comparison of our method with traditional approaches confirmed its
efficiency, running approximately 5-6 times faster on a standard desktop computer.

accurate enough for the purpose of gerrymandering detection and analysis.

individual voters whose addition to or removal from a district could significantly

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. By incorporating an additional mechanism into existing frameworks, we enable them to identify the key object underlying each target description before initiating navigation. This mechanism employs unsupervised feature learning via self-supervised training of the convolutional network, leveraging optical flow and rigid transformations. We experimentally determine that goal-related object detection enhances the navigation system's robustness in diverse scenarios. Additionally, we integrate this mechanism into two existing navigation frameworks to evaluate its effectiveness. The results indicate significant performance improvements of up to 3.6% in terms of success rate and 17% in terms of average navigation distance in challenging scenarios. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside outside of galaxies, alone or in binary systems, and have a tendency to wander due to kicks from supernovae explosions, eventually entering nuclear star clusters at later times. Specifically, about 10% of systems with a primary mass greater than 15 solar masses will merge in clusters at z>5, although this percentage increases to 30-50% for those with masses between 3 and 15 solar masses. Our analysis indicates that systems with primary masses less than 3 solar masses predominantly reside within galaxies and experience less movement compared to more massive systems. Nuclear star cluster mergers of these lighter-weight systems occur more frequently, but at lower redshifts. Our findings suggest that Population III binary remnants have the potential to form the seeds of the earliest detected black holes, particularly in nuclear star clusters hosting central black holes. These lighter-weight systems could develop into the heavier-weight systems seen in the first detected black hole events, ultimately forming the most massive black holes observed. Our study also shows that the rate of Population III binary system entry into nuclear star clusters should be observable in future studies with the James Webb Space Telescope, specifically in programs aimed at detecting the gravitational wave echo of these mergers. Our analysis indicates that the gravitational wave echo of these Population III binary system mergers should occur at a rate of 0.1-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3, within a distance range of up to 10-100 Mpc for z<5. Our study suggests that the gravitational wave echo of these Population III binary system mergers should be detectable in a program aimed at finding the gravitational wave echo of these events across all accessible redshifts. We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces. Additionally, the paper presents a full exceptional collection for any smooth quadric, which has implications in the study of spherical objects and the category of singularity-free sheaves on these quadrics. Specifically, the result enables the construction of a Spherical Hilbert polynomial and yields a complete classification of Spherical objects among line bundles on smooth quadrics. Furthermore, the research extends to other classes of varieties - stutsum hypersurfaces and rational normal scrolls - for which full exceptional collections can be found, leading to new insights in the field of spherical objects and reflecting symmetry in the morphology of these varieties. Specifically, the result implies that any line bundle on a smooth quadric can be expressed as a tensor product of a Spherical object and another line bundle, whose Spherical counterpart exhibits symmetrical properties in the context of the variety's Chow ring. The consequence of this finding extends to other classes of varieties - stutsum hypersurfaces and rational normal scrolls - where the same property applies, as proven in the presented research. 

In the course of the study, the paper also identifies full exceptional collections for any smooth quadric, which has independent significance. Specifically, the result shows that for any smooth quadric, full exceptional collections exist, which can be obtained by combining line bundles from two distinct Chern roots. Similarly, the result holds for any stutsum hypersurface and rational normal scrolls - for which full exceptional collections can also be obtained through a combination of line bundles corresponding to distinct Chern roots. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of utilizing text-based games in research is the lack of readily available, high-quality platforms for testing AI agents, leading to few agents being trained and tested on these environments.
To address this, we develop PearPedia, an extensive library of text-based games based on Wikipedia articles, allowing for the diverse range of questions found in Wikipedia to be utilized in game development.
By employing Wikipedia's advanced search functionality, we identify a vast selection of questions suitable for text-based game creation, along with their corresponding action descriptions and Wikipedia page links.
As a result, PearPedia offers over 382K unique question settings derived from Wikipedia, encompassing more than 51M unique transitions and actions, providing a substantial platform for AI training and evaluation. Moreover, the platform facilitates the comparison of agent performance across different environments, as well as the analysis of agent successes and failures in a practical context.
PearPedia serves as a platform for ongoing research, as well as a resource for the community to test and evaluate their AI agents in real-world scenarios, with opportunities for contribution and collaboration through our repository of game questions and summaries. PearPedia can be accessed at https://github.com/apla/meadow. If you are interested in using the platform, please feel free to reach out to [sheng.zhang@ed.ac.uk](mailTo:sheng.zhang@ed.ac.uk) for further information.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, the transfer of this information from human to robot systems has been overlooked. This research aims to bridge this knowledge gap with a new method to transfer manipulability information from one robot to another with a different kinematic structure. Since these ellipsoids are based on symmetric positive-definite matrices, they can be treated as points on a specific geometric manifold. This work offers the first approach to transfer manipulability by leveraging the technique of point cloud registration. To achieve this, it employs an algorithm combining parallel transport with Iterative Closest Point. The method also uses an adaptive geometric matching heuristic to find corresponding features in manipulability ellipsoids. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated through simulation data and a real-world experiment involving teaching a Puma robot human-like motion through an iRobot Arm. The latter involves aligning the two robots' manipulability ellipsoids while they perform a pick-and-place task, resulting in a trajectory that mirrors the original human motion. Code for this research is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/soomekh/manipulability-transfer. The associated video can be found at https://youtu.be/6kZyc-XE3UI. A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection and feature matching methods yields surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimations in such video footage. The proposed method, which consists of two stages, initially learns a canonical pose from multiple videos, followed by a model for predicting object poses in a single view. In contrast to existing top-tier models, this method performs competitively without relying on explicit 3D pose annotations during the training process. Additionally, we present the Accidental Turntables Dataset, a set of challenging images depicting 41,212 car scenarios with complex backgrounds, motion blur, and varying lighting conditions, serving as a new benchmark for 3D pose estimation. The proposed method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on two benchmark datasets, with significant improvements reaching up to 25.6% in terms of key performance indicators. Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes on an attosecond timescale, while also ensuring low emittance to focus attosecond pulses spatially for enhanced sensitivity. Secondly, establishing a platform for generating XUV pulses with higher stability and controllable properties would facilitate rapid, sequential exposure to different atomic and molecular environments, thus necessitating a parameter-controllable source. We outline a groundbreaking approach to achieve both objectives by leveraging the capabilities of a plasma-based soft X-ray free-electron laser with a short-wavelength undulator, integrated with a cutting-edge grating monochromator. This innovative setup enables the simultaneous production of a high-photon-flux, low-emittance attosecond source and a highly stable, pseudo-constant XUV flux for repeated exposures, thus laying a solid foundation for a next-generation attosecond science platform. We also highlight the pioneering role such an integrated platform can play in driving advancements in both X-ray and FEL research. As such, we recommend its implementation as a central component in the upcoming European strategy for attosecond physics. These systems have broad applications, as seen in stochastic realization theory, state estimation in noise-disturbed dynamic systems, and simulation of dynamic systems. This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through KNN search. This insight drives the simplification of multiple KNN searches within GCNs. Secondly, rearranging the sequence of feature aggregation and multilayer perceptron operations yields equivalent results. Based on these findings, we refine the computational procedure for GCNs. Experimental results demonstrate the optimized networks enjoy lower computational complexity, reduced memory usage, and accelerated inference speed while retaining comparable accuracy for point cloud learning. The source code will be publicly available at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git. Our research further introduces a set of benchmark datasets for point cloud learning at https://github.com/ofsoundof/EfficientGCN.git to facilitate replicating the experiments. We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in a predetermined set as trigger points. This set can be tiny, consisting of just a few unique images, and the attack can produce a vast array of fake backdoors, far exceeding the number of trigger images. This innovative threat can evade detection using conventional methods based on neural network behavior, and we showcase a practical demonstration of this attack on a dataset of medical images. Additionally, we propose an efficient and robust countermeasures strategy, which can effectively prevent this type of Trojan attack. This countermeasure works by analyzing the patterns in poisoned data and blocking any unusual or anomalous cases that contain backdoor signals. This approach can be applied more broadly as a general-purpose classifier, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on multiple datasets, including ImageNet and Flirter. This study highlights the need for more sophisticated methods to detect and prevent Trojan attacks and suggests a new research direction in this area. A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition for this purpose, which is referred to as devolatilisation. In this research, we explore devolatilisation in mixed steam-rock atmospheres within the habitable zones of Sun-like stars. We created a model combining conservation principles, equilibration of atmospheric gases, and a parameterized description of atmospheric processes, which we applied to various cases with varying atmospheric pressures, temperatures, and initial water fractions. The results show that, compared to models limited to pure rock compositions, excess gases in the atmosphere are produced when both rock and water components are considered, up to 17 times more gas in certain scenarios. However, this devolatilisation effect has a cooling effect on planets, which can lead to a 30% reduction in devolatilisation and new estimates placing this process at 1% when considering a temperature range of 250-300 K. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN. The findings indicate that incorporating an attention module within the DNN enables the selective learning of crucial features from noisy CSI, thus enhancing localization accuracy. The attention-based approach achieves enhanced results, particularly under channel agitation and in complex environments with limited training data. The constructed model demonstrates high adaptability and can serve as a robust foundation for localization in the presence of CSI perturbations. Moreover, the designed attention-based DNN can be applied to other MIMO systems with ample antennas. The research suggests that the attention mechanism can effectively mitigate the impacts of CSI perturbations on deep learning-based localization systems. The developed model can serve as a robust foundation for localization in the presence of CSI perturbations, thereby addressing a significant drawback of traditional DNN approaches and demonstrating improved generalization capabilities across diverse scenarios. The computational complexity of the implemented approach was found to be comparable to conventional DNN methods. Specifically, for a centralized massive MIMO system with 64 antennas, the attention-based approach exhibited a higher accuracy without sacrificing computational efficiency. The developed approach is anticipated to have numerous applications in localization tasks involving MIMO systems with numerous antennas. COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser. Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It offers a basic model upload feature and a server-loaded model option, providing web access to existing models. Users can access ShinyCOPASI at http://shiny.copasi.org/ and the source code at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI. For web-based model management, please contact the corresponding author. Additionally, ShinyCOPASI is listed on the Bioconda package repository. Further details are available in the user manual at http://manual.copasi.org/ ShinyCOPASI/. High-level functionality is documented there, with more advanced information provided through issue tracking on GitHub at https://github.com/copasi/shinyCOPASI/issues. To report issues or suggest improvements, please use the GitHub repository issue system. Ultimately, ShinyCOPASI serves three main purposes: 1) providing web access to existing models, 2) allowing users to upload their own models for sharing and preservation, and 3) offering a platform for web-based model development and interaction. By leveraging ShinyCOPASI, users can access and utilize COPASI tasks without needing to install COPASI on their local system, thereby expanding the potential uses and applications of COPASI. It is expected that ShinyCOPASI will enhance user collaboration and the exploration of biochemical network models. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and inverse problems using uncertain data and models. In this study, we seek to address these gaps by investigating the feasibility of solving partial differential equations and inverse problems using uncertain data and models and demonstrating the feasibility of proposed methods on exemplary problems. Additionally, the proposed methods are compared with established techniques that incorporate Bayesian uncertainty, focal loss, data augmentation, and data filtering. This research was presented at the autumn school on fundamental aspects of deep learning for physics and engineering at the University of Pittsburgh. Some relevant results were also presented at the 2021 International Conference for materials and information technology. In this research, we explored the application of deep neural networks to solve partial differential equations and inverse problems. In particular, we considered the Hestenes and Carleman estimates methods for solving the latter, while proposing the use of Hestenes methods for the former. Our numerical experiments confirmed that these approaches are capable of reducing solution inaccuracies resulting from noisy data and overfitting. Furthermore, we observed that incorporating uncertainty into the loss function and using Hestenes methods for partial differential equations and inverse problems, respectively, yielded accurate results and provided insight into the uncertainty associated with solution values. This research has far-reaching implications for the use of deep neural networks in physics and engineering applications. In particular, we propose the use of Hestenes methods for partial differential equations and inverse problems, the utilization of focal loss for reducing solution inaccuracies, the incorporation of uncertainty into the loss function, the use of data augmentation to increase data quantity, and the utilization of Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property-based techniques to optimize model performance. In the future, we intend to apply these methods to practical problems in physics and engineering, while also exploring new techniques for uncertainty quantification. Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a high number of value function evaluations required for each iteration. Concurrently, the surge in large-scale reinforcement learning tasks necessitates an efficient approach to policy evaluation. We address these challenges by utilizing a Monte-Carlo based expectation-maximization algorithm for policy iteration, which translates to multiple instances of the EM algorithm for state evaluation. Our approach leverages the benefits of both policy iteration and EM, resulting in a faster convergence compared to other online policy iteration algorithms. Furthermore, our method shares similarities with the EM algorithm used in structured policy iteration, but takes a more general form that doesn't rely on a specific function approximation method. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a large-scale simulation test, highlighting its superior performance over other online policy iteration methods, such as the natural policy gradient, state action elimination, and the EM algorithm for structured policy iteration. Our code is available at https://github.com/argentcaum/MC_PIEM. Our results indicate that a Monte-Carlo based PIEM can achieve faster convergence than both PIEM and structured policy iteration methods in both stationary and non-stationary environments. We attribute this performance to our method's ability to simultaneously compute action values and policy updates, as well as its capacity to handle large-scale Markov decision processes. We also observe that while our method performs well in the presence of non-stationary dynamics, it doesn't come with a guarantee against potential data corruption in its theoretical formulation. We verify the empirical robustness of our approach by comparing its performance against other existing online policy iteration methods under non-stationary and dynamic environments with data corruption. Our empirical results confirm the theoretical expectations, demonstrating our method's and the NTPE's robustness in the presence of data corruption. We observe the NTPE's knowledge gradient to be sensitive to noise, but our approach remains robust due to its ability to utilize past data. We further analyze the implications of data corruption on the Monte-Carlo based PIEM by examining its behavior in the presence of various levels of corruption. Our results indicate an inverse relationship between the level of corruption and the convergence rate of our method. We verify the empirical validity of this observation through additional simulation tests. Based on our analysis, the Monte-Carlo based PIEM appears to be a robust choice for policy iteration, especially in the presence of data corruption. Additionally, our method's convergence rate can be accelerated by minimizing the level of corruption. We verify the empirical validity of this observation through additional simulation tests. For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly transitioning at a point around 3 GeV. This study is the first to demonstrate alterations in parton (dominated by quarks) showers traversing the QGP with a known initial trajectory, also offering a controlled comparison to calculate transmission coefficients for quarks and gluons. Additionally, the results provide a means to investigate path-length effects of the QGP, assuming quarks have a greater tendency to stop within the quark-gluon plasma, potentially offering further insights into its high temperature and density. The results have also been compared to theoretical models describing a quark-gluon plasma, such as viscous-textured hydrodynamics and transport theories. This comparison allowed for the extraction of the quark and gluon transmission coefficients, evaluated at an average temperature of approximately 1 GeV, came out to 0.55 for quarks and 0.91 for gluons, both within a quark-gluon plasma temperature range of 400 MeV. Furthermore, the results have been offered in a framework susceptible to theoretical evaluation, within the block-particle framework, resulting in the extraction of the gluon transmission coefficient, evaluated at an average temperature of approximately 1 GeV, came out to 0.73. Lastly, the results have been offered in a framework susceptible to theoretical evaluation, within the quark-particle framework, resulting in the extraction of the quark transmission coefficient at an average temperature of approximately 1 GeV, came out to 0.55

New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature consistent with the coolest Y dwarfs. Moreover, the object possesses color indices of W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 about 1.6 mag bluer than a typical Y dwarf. New data collected from WISE, Spitzer, and HST for parallax measurement have determined a close distance of $16.3^{+1.4}_{-1.2}$ parsecs and a substantial transverse velocity of $207.4{\pm}15.9$ km/s. The calculated J, W2, and ch2 absolute magnitudes align with the coolest Y dwarfs despite W1-W2 and ch1-ch2 indices displaying a distinct discrepancy. Research suggests that the object is most likely an ancient metal-poor brown dwarf and possibly the initial instance of a Y subdwarf, necessitating further examination through broad-band spectroscopy and photometry using the JWST for validation of the hypothesis. Future studies with Gaia DR3 data, comprising precise parallax measurements, are anticipated to uncover additional analogous examples of this peculiar brown dwarf. We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching. The techniques are suitable for intensive numerical calculations and will be crucial for incorporating NNLO corrections into NNLO DPD calculations. The findings are demonstrated through the numerical evolution of PDFs and DPDs with multiple partons, employing the MRST2003 and NNPDF3D1Z PDF sets. The work also introduces Chebyshev evolution of PDFs, a related field that could contribute to the development of next-generation PDFs. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printing with a binder. Consequently, larger drops tend to form on fibers with high slip coefficients. This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. In this particular study, we classify the braided auto-equivalences of the local modules in categories linked to known type I quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. It has been determined that the symmetries exhibited in this research are all non-exceptional apart from four unique instances, which can be accounted for under the concept of level-rank duality. These exceptional instances include the orbifolds $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{2},16)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_2)}$, $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{3},9)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_3)}$, $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{4},8)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_4)}$, and $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{5},5)_{\operatorname{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_5)}$. Various technical tools have been developed in this research, including a skein-theoretic description of the orbifold quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. This description has the potential for application to braided tensor categories more broadly. Additionally, an expression of orthogonal level-rank duality in the type D-D case was formulated, which facilitated the construction of one of the exceptionals. It has also been revealed that quadratic categories have an unanticipated connection with exceptional braided auto-equivalences of the orbifolds, which enabled the construction of two out of the four exceptional instances. In the follow-up to this paper, we intend to leverage the classified braided auto-equivalences to develop the corresponding type II quantum subgroups of $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. This will be accomplished through local module categories, which will in turn enable a comprehensive understanding of the representation theory of the quantum group itself. It is anticipated that the techniques and connections outlined within this research will contribute meaningfully to representation theory beyond the scope of quantum groups

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown of its conventional interpretation occurs once time surpasses zero, particularly in scenarios involving limited spatial coverage. Nonetheless, a crucial advantage of this solution lies in its ability to approximate exactly the behaviour of solutions with zero-normal distribution for large times, which also extends to solutions with arbitrary positive probability distributions. Consequently, the technique can be utilised for estimating the approximate velocity of invasion or the distribution of traits within a population, given access to the probability distribution of the underlying model. Furthermore, the proposed method is versatile and can be adapted for analysing travelling waves associated with periodic or stationary spatial patterns. Presently, the technique remains effective for modelling scenarios involving multiple species interactions, although potential existing limitations might hinder its further applications in certain species competition systems. The proposed method is also versatile and can be adapted for modelling scenarios involving multiple species interactions, although certain existing limitations might hinder its further applications in certain systems of species competition. The approach is further utilised for calculating the speed of invasion for systems modelling species competition in heterogeneous environments, as well as for systems involving one species against a background of periodic or random fluctuations. The validated accuracy of the approximate solution is examined against numerical solutions of the numerical solutions of the relevant partial differential equations through various statistical measures. The results indicate the efficacy and simplicity of the proposed method, offering a valuable tool for quick estimation and modelling of invasion velocities and distribution of traits within populations, facilitating numerous applications and providing valuable insights into population dynamics, evolutionary genetics, and phylodiversity. The proposed method also successfully estimated invasion velocities and was applied to investigate various biologically significant scenarios, including the invasion of a single species against a background of periodic or random fluctuations, multiple species interactions in heterogeneous environments, and the distribution of traits within populations under the influence of several environmental factors. Furthermore, the simplicity and accuracy of the proposed method make it an ideal and versatile tool for modelling and analysing invasion velocities and distribution of traits within populations, enabling numerous applications and providing valuable and biologically significant answers to questions in evolutionary genetics, population dynamics and phylodiversity. This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, aiming to classify handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen. The challenge involves recognizing mathematical expressions from 15 possible characters written by multiple individuals. To overcome the initial challenge, a combined strategy of neural networks and statistical analysis is employed. Specifically, a dual-binary classifier consisting of an initial character classification followed by a symbol check is used. However, the approach proved incomplete, and further development is required to meet the challenge requirements. Initially, a two-part neural network classification system was designed: first, a 7-way binary classifier determines whether the writing belongs to one of the first 7 characters, followed instantly by a second 7-way binary classification to identify the remaining characters. To enhance classification accuracy for digits 0 and 5, featuring similar forms and thus posing a challenge to classification, a statistical model incorporating Bayesian estimation was developed. To optimize the system's performance, a Bayesian estimation technique was applied to the classification of digits 0 and 5. Although the approach showed promise for these two digits, it proved computationally complex and time-consuming. Consequently, a more efficient Bayesian estimation technique was designed. This new method yields better results for the classification of digits 0 and 5 while minimizing computational costs. To validate the system's effectiveness, a rigorous "leave-none-out" validation process was conducted. The outcome revealed a remarkable 90.1% accuracy for the classification of digits 0 and a impressive 92.5% for digit 5. Consequently, the integrated approach achieved an outstanding overall accuracy of 87.8%. Although the attainment was satisfactory, it fell short of the target of reaching an accuracy of 90% as demanded by the Stabilo UbiComp 2021 Challenge. Consequently, a new strategy of ensemble classification was developed using the differential signals from the DigiPen's time series data to classify digits 0 and 5 separately. To my knowledge, this approach marks the very first application of the use of neural networks in the classification of handwritten mathematical expressions. Furthermore, the success achieved in classifying handwritten mathematical expressions constitutes the very first achievement in the history of achieving this challenging task. Lastly, valuable insights were gained into the dynamics of handwritten writing actions captured by the DigiPen's time series data. This knowledge may lead to new developments in the field of handwriting recognition in the future. The code used for the project can be accessed at the https://github.com/jcjian0/Stabilo

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that median-based durations yield higher quality synthesis than mean-based durations, and the best results come from combining median durations with a mean-based acoustic representation. Furthermore, this approach achieves better synthesis quality compared to traditional methods that model a specific distribution or use a lookup table for each HMM state. We also examine the performance of different recurrent networks and a simple linear model as alternatives to recurrent models. Finally, this paper confirms the benefits of median durations when applied to state-based HMMs, and suggests future areas for improvement. The code and model weights are openly available for replication. It is hoped that this work will serve as a starting point for further research into frame-level duration modelling. Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the fundamental single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive functions for modeling species detection data and estimating species distribution patterns, as demonstrated through multiple case studies. Evaluation of model performance is also simplified by the implementation of several metrics. Additionally, the package includes a set of pre-built datasets that are accessible via data(spOccupancy)). Furthermore, spOccupancy offers a flexible framework for custom model development based on user-specified prior distributions. If a user prefers to specify their own likelihood functions, the package also includes the functionality to create custom models. This flexibility enables users to incorporate external data into the species distribution analysis. For users who prefer a more straightforward approach, the package includes pre-built single and multiple species occupancy models that are optimized for precision and efficiency. By default, the models are configured to handle false positives, autocorrelation, and spatial relationships, as well as a combined model for extensive dataset analysis. The package is fully compatible with the Biodiversity R package, which is also developed with a focus on statistical biodiversity analysis. A comprehensive overview of spOccupancy functionality is provided in the spOccupancy overview document. Additionally, the package includes a set of helpful utilities for conducting species distribution analysis and publishing results. As an example, the package includes a helpful function called ablate() that facilitates the creation of figure panels, as well as other visual aids for presenting findings. The package is fully accessible through the GitHub repository, https://github.com/mattgermann/spOccupancy. Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence, especially in cases of rare malignant skin lesions. The study presents an innovative interactive deep learning system that enables and facilitates the use of AI in clinical practice. The system was successfully tested by 30 medical students and general practitioners who attempted to diagnose skin images before receiving AI-assisted feedback. Compared to their initial diagnoses, participants' accuracy improved significantly and their diagnostic speed was also substantially shortened. The study highlights the potential of the proposed interactive system as a general solution for integrating AI into medical decision-making within the field of dermatology. Overall, the results indicate that the combination of human and machine intelligence can produce superior outcomes. The study's findings will be presented at the IHMW 2021 conference and will contribute to the development of interactive AI systems in the future. To capture the intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics of Type Ia supernovae from global SN spectra time series through probabilistic learning, we integrated Bayesian neural networks and physics-inspired techniques. By incorporating an auxiliary variable representing the physical explosion age in the network, a probabilistic autoencoder variant was trained. This model was trained on a dataset of 34 global SN spectra, including both training and normalization steps, to produce a probabilistic representation of SN spectra. The research demonstrates that this method produces an intrinsic characteristic orthogonal to individual variability, resulting in tighter residual variability. In contrast to previous studies using unsupervised techniques, this intrinsic characteristic was found to resemble the age of the SN explosion, consistent with observational constraints. The resulting model was tested on SNe with data gaps, demonstrating improved denoising capabilities and robustness. Furthermore, an underlying intrinsic characteristic was extracted that resembles the photosphere velocity of SNe, and the model was used to predict time-series data for additional SNe. The research indicates that probabilistic learning combined with physical modeling can effectively separate intrinsic and extrinsic characteristics in global SN spectra, leading to potential improvements in SN cosmology applications. Additionally, the method may be applied to other astrophysical phenomena in the future. The code used in this research is available at https://github.com/malindes/SNPAE. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This new approach leads us to develop novel nonlocal equations of reaction-diffusion type on networks. We then investigate the existence of steady state solutions and show that in certain scenarios, the stability of these solutions can be examined using a parameter related to the graph's degree distribution. Our research indicates that in networks where the average vertex participates in multiple interactions, our proposed models can outperform traditional contact graph models, assuming the average vertex has a relatively low number of interacting partners. We demonstrate the efficacy of these new models through numerical examples and suggest potential applications in the study and control of epidemic diseases. A particular scenario where the average vertex has a relatively high number of interacting partners presents an open research question for the existence of stable steady states, which we address numerically. Upon investigating the relevance of our hypergraph models to real-world disease outbreaks, we propose two potential testing scenarios for future observation and analysis. The first involves examining the progression of the COVID-19 pandemic in a highly connected network, assuming the existence of multiple interacting contacts. The second tests a fictional virus in a network where non-paired interactions are minimal to absent. We anticipate that our hypergraph models and the resulting mathematical framework will contribute meaningfully to the study and understanding of disease spread within networks. This research may also be translated to identify and control critical interfaces in the network to mitigate disease transmission effectively. The mathematical framework developed here can be potentially applied across diverse social systems, akin to the manner in which reaction-diffusion equations have been applied in various social systems previously. The last section discusses the wide range of questions that remain unanswered in this research, offering avenues for the ongoing study of this problem in the future. Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an in-plane magnetization orientation. Their investigation reveals that this ferromagnetic bilayer displays a rich pattern of spin texture within its uppermost valence bands, which arises from two unique spin cants resulting from the interplay of ferromagnetic order with both chirality and electrical polarization. One type of cant is a result of layer stacking asymmetry and valence state polarization, resulting in equivalent canting patterns on both layers. Conversely, the other cant is a consequence of Rashba effect, which in this ferromagnetic case generates oppositely canting components on adjacent layers within the same electronic state. Additionally, researchers found that this ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer will exhibit optical anisotropy due to the difference in interlayer and intralayer polarization. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the outcomes of convective damping and tidal synchronization. To better understand and analyze these processes, we present a comprehensive computational study that explores the effects of rotation and radial diffusion on the internal structure and evolution of anti-solar differential rotation. Our results reveal an inner radial tube, surrounded by an outer convection zone rotation pattern, characterized by the rotation velocity at the tangent photosphere track approximately 0.5 Upsilon. We find that convective damping may still deliver convective energy to the tidal potential, thus potentially prolonging tidal synchronization. Furthermore, we suggest that the characteristic rotation velocity of 0.5 Upsilon could serve as a boundary between rotation regimes suitable for gyrochronology and those exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation. Based on the available observational data, we find it unlikely that solar-like differential rotation may emerge during the main sequence. Conversely, late K and M dwarfs may feature rotation velocities exceeding 0.5 Upsilon, according to observed rotation statistics. If verified, this would mean that solar-like and anti-solar rotation regimes are mutually exclusive, primarily due to differing initial angular momentum content. Finally, we find radial diffusion to have a minor effect on both types of rotation patterns, thus ruling out its contribution to their development. Our study provides new, exclusive information on the effects of radial diffusion, initial conditions, and convective damping on rotational evolution and strives to integrate these aspects into existing literature on these topics.

The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs. Traditional unit and functional tests are insufficient for guaranteeing the proper execution of synchronized code due to its hidden nature, making it impossible to anticipate emergent behaviors through testing. The McSync and McLock checkers utilize kernel-level APIs to verify the correct functioning of multi-threaded programs at an abstract level, focusing on specific synchronization primitives. Although McSync and McLock have proven effective, their limitation lies in their restricted focus on particular primitives, hindering their applicability to diverse programs that employ novel synchronization mechanisms. To overcome this, a new kernel-level API, called McOpen, has been developed with the ability to automatically generate checkers for a wide range of synchronization primitives, including previously un explored ones. The McOpen system significantly expands the scope of McSync and McLock, has been successfully applied in identifying bugs in real-world programs, and provides open access to its underlying technology. The two major components of McOpen are (1) a rich abstract model of thread-local data structures that facilitates the automatic generation of checkers for various synchronization primitives, and (2) its integration with McSync and McLock, enabling McOpen to leverage their developed verification techniques. As a result, McOpen can utilize existing proof techniques and expand the scope of applicable synchronization primitives, significantly increasing its coverage. The McOpen system has been successfully used in identifying multi-threading issues in well-known programs, as well as open-sourced on GitHub under the liberal Apache 2.0 license for public access and modification. The McOpen user guide is available at https://mcopen.cs.umass.edu/. The McOpen paper has been submitted to POPL 2024 for consideration. It's assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the scalars remain heavy compared to the Hubble scale to facilitate single-field inflation.  Additionally, supergravity predicts several non-renormalizable interactions, rendering it an effective field theory that remains valid up to a specific cutoff energy scale, and thus a quantum gravity candidate such as string theory is required to provide a more fundamental understanding of the physical universe and its cosmological implications.  This article will provide an overview of the recent advancements in constructing inflationary models within the framework of supergravity, highlighting both the challenges posed by this theory and potential avenues for research within the field.  A primary goal of this review is to illuminate the intricate relationships among various cosmological models based on supergravity, and to illuminate the challenges, opportunities, and potential avenues for further investigation in this area of research.  Additionally, supergravity offers an effective field theory that may offer a way to describe the early universe and its cosmological implications, and therefore serves as a useful tool for exploring the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework and their related applications in cosmology.  A comprehensive discussion of the recent developments in the cosmological applications of supergravity is provided in Chapter-1; an in-depth examination of the role of moduli fields in the cosmological models based on supergravity is presented in Chapter-2; an overview of the recently constructed modular inflationary models within the framework of supergravity and their analysis is provided in Chapter-3; and finally, supergravity-based axion inflationary models along with an examination of the challenges posed by this theory and potential avenues for further investigation in this area of research are presented in Chapter-4. Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission. As a result, this work in silicon microdisks represents a new method of controlling the mode of light and implementing circulators, routers, and mode converters. Unlike traditional methods using magnetism or thermality, this coherence-based approach can control individual modes of light and enlarge optical communication bandwidth. Additionally, this work includes a full numerical simulation to illustrate how to develop and enlarge the pump's mode conversion and demonstrate a working optical circulation based on coherent photon pair technology. Lastly, this paper discusses potential future applications and developments of coherence-based nonreciprocity. Optical circulation and mode conversion were successfully implemented at the wavelength 1550 nm. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we outline potential future applications of terahertz SNOM for evaluating Josephson junctions and other quantum components. Although initially laborious, such near-field terahertz investigations prove invaluable for understanding and identifying loss channels on small chips comprising multiple quantum components. Furthermore, this near-field technique enables the analysis of local properties within quantum circuits and may facilitate the development of optimized lossless and coherent microstructures. Lastly, terahertz SNOM could be employed to evaluate and identify loss channels in quantum circuits utilizing an unconventional decay rate approach. In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely driven by their trades in commodity futures. But their fortunes have shifted dramatically since the 2010s, with underwhelming returns. One plausible explanation for this downturn may be the presence of short-term reversal traders, who allegedly exploit CTAs for financial gain. In a recent study, an artificial market model was devised by incorporating both a commodity trading advisor (CTA) and a short-term reversal trader (SRT). The aim was to establish whether these SRTs were detrimental to CTA profitability. Notably, the research yielded the opposite outcome - in markets with both types of traders, CTA profitability and activity actually increased. Consequently, a positive symbiotic relationship between these traders may be a more likely phenomenon than initially assumed. Specifically, when SRTs were absent, CTA returns and activity exhibited greater volatility. The presence of SRTs, it appears, facilitates a more stable market environment that benefits these advisors, thereby suggesting a more complex dynamic between the roles of these traders. The study's findings support previous research indicating a potential symbiotic relationship between CTAs and long-term traders and offers valuable insights for the commodity trading advisory industry. This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces operating within the sub-6 GHz frequency range where channel propagation isn't sparse. A high-performance, low-overhead estimation protocol has been developed to minimize reflection power loss without requiring on-off amplitude estimation for each user and channel. A convex optimization framework has been devised to estimate the complex-valued channel estimates separately for each user without needing feedback from the base station. We have also tested various iterative algorithms that refine estimates until convergence, including those based on the alternating direction method of multipliers. An innovative approach called the difference of convex alternating direction fractional difference method has been developed and proven to converge globally to exact solutions. An experimental study comparing our proposed estimator with state-of-the-art estimators has shown that significant performance improvements can be achieved, and simulation results for a 10-bit, 5 GHz communication system have been presented. Furthermore, our proposed estimator has been successfully applied to a live outdoor measurement data set to demonstrate its practical effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Based on these results, we have determined that our estimator is capable of supporting loads up to 128 users per channel. Our study has established that our proposed estimator outperforms traditional and state-of-the-art estimators by 3-10 dB in terms of power loss due to channel estimation. The associated code for our proposed estimator can be found at https://github.com/samermoghadam/CDFD-ADFM.git. This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information. This study highlights the benefits of using online news monitoring to gain deeper insights into public health crises and social inequality. By incorporating user comments, our findings suggest news outlets should adapt to effectively reach and inform diverse audiences during public health emergencies. In light of increasing concerns about fake news and disinformation, our study's findings stress the need for targeting underrepresented populations with trusted media sources in order to counteract the spread of misinformation. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the potential of leveraging local news coverage as a public health indicator that can aid data-driven decision-making at the community level. Overall, this study offers a unique example of using computational methods to explore the complex intersection of public health, media communication, and social inequality. To facilitate further research, we provide our code and the monitored news data, a distinct and valuable resource, for academic use.}

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. In line with the suggestion that infants' brains are initially designed to learn concepts efficiently, we've found a significant inflection point in the learning process of counting. Our study shows that counting can be seen as a Markov decision process, and using numerical data from the UK's Cognitive Development in Middle Childhood dataset, we've identified the critical period for counting development. Our analysis indicates that the inflection point occurs around the age of 3-4 years old. Based on these findings, we've proposed a dynamic learning model that reflects both the steady and sudden progress in learning to count. The model suggests that younger children use striding, an error-correction strategy, to improve their counting skills, whereas older children adopt a more efficient reinforcement-learning tactic. Notably, our results are consistent with the notion that the brain is primarily designed for efficient learning, and the inflection point in learning to count can be attributed to the sudden realization that counting follows a regular rule, marking the transition from striding to reinforcement-based learning. Additionally, the proposed model is versatile and could be applied to studying other cognitive developments where similar inflection points and learning mechanisms might exist. In conclusion, the study offers insights into the intricate relationship between the human brain's design and cognitive abilities. The model developed here can be utilized to analyze, on a large scale, how the transition from striding to reinforcement learning might be a universal mechanism for reaching a steady pace in mastering new skills. Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively. Additionally, we reveal a correspondence between sectional curvature and the asymptotic curvature of Zariski decomposition. This research heavily draws from Tsuyama's work in "Positive Products" and Fan's in "A course in complex analysis and geometric hermitian structures," along with other influential papers from the incursion of convex geometry in algebraic geometry. Our findings are further generalized to the context of noncommutative projective schemes. Lastly, the relationship between noncommutative divisors and convex geometry is explored, leading to the discovery of new geometric inequalities, the division of noncommutative divisor classes, and new constructions of noncommutative Hermitian Einstein metrics. This research opens up new avenues for the study of holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds at the noncommutative level. Our analysis also yields significant parallels between commutative and noncommutative settings. Specifically, the division of divisor classes corresponds to convex geometry's division of mixed divisor classes, while the formation of a cone structure mirrors that of the movable cone of curves. Furthermore, the application of a particular addition technique for divisor classes translates to the addition of curvature tensors, leading to new inequalities and the creation of Hermitian Einstein metrics in both the commutative and noncommutative contexts. Our study also yields an intriguing noncommutative analogue of the second main theorem, along with the view that the application of convex geometry to algebraic geometry may offer new insights into the geometry of complex projective varieties. From a broader perspective, our research suggests the potential for noncommutative geometry to provide novel geometric insights and constructions in the context of projective varieties. A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values. The resulting dynamic price equations combine both types of data and are used to test the impact of various variables on trading efficiency. Specifically, one of these variables is the number of shares traded per unit of time, which is demonstrated to significantly influence the convergence of future prices towards optimal values. Furthermore, a technique called multivariate linear regression is employed to verify the statistically significant impact of several variables on trading efficiency and to quantify their relative importance. The validity of this approach is confirmed through analysis of both established and emerging markets, with a focus on the former. Ultimately, the empirical results reveal that market segmentation has a pronounced effect on trading efficiency and can be accurately modeled using dynamic price equations, with the consequent potential for higher trading gains. However, the application of this approach to emerging markets yields less conclusive outcomes due to greater instability and variability in the market. The research presented here differs from previous studies in its integrated perspective on market analysis, forecasting, and algorithmic trading, as well as its unique combination of past and future price data. The theoretical framework is grounded in the principles of general equilibrium theory and the neoclassical model of economic optimization, with a practical outcome in the form of market-friendly algorithmic trading software. The verified market segmentation hypothesis facilitates the development of trading strategies that can adapt to distinct market segments and enable the consistent application of trading efficiency across all markets. The software demo, accessible at https://www.macrosecurity.com/, demonstrates the practical application of these concepts, with a particular emphasis on the connection between past and future price data and the associated statistical significance of the findings. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning framework that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize DBSCAN with S2PC to cluster the legitimate data majority without acquiring private user data. Concurrently, clients create duplicate models and engage in distance-controlling testing to tailor their local models towards a centralized standard. Our framework is both autonomous and adaptive, as servers and clients require no manual parameter adjustments. Furthermore, it relies on SMPC operations such as multiplication, addition, and comparison, which omits expensive operations like division and square root. Evaluation on standard image classification datasets demonstrates that FLVoogd effectively blocks malicious submissions and precludes data exposure from the server. Flawless results are achieved for clean datasets, while FLVoogd exhibits robustness against a range of Byzantine attack strategies, even in scenarios where there is no majority data present. Our work also highlights that a significant majority of data is not always necessary for model convergence. Thorough benchmarking against existing defense systems reveals that FLVoogd surpasses other approaches in robustness, while also exhibiting faster convergence compared to FL-Tee and comparable generalization performance to FL-Tee and MPC-Fl. We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters embodied intelligence advancements in autonomous driving, by benchmarking the progress in applied autonomy. The Deepracer challenge proved to be complex, especially when translating skills from simulated to real-world settings, so we implemented a two-pronged approach to bridge the domain gap in observation spaces by applying canny edge detection and image cropping techniques. By leveraging a behavioral cloning method using the MLP-MIXER optimization technique, we achieved robust performance despite control noise. Furthermore, our model demonstrated a remarkable runtime efficiency of 2-3 milliseconds on modern CPU architectures, showcasing its real-world applicability. We successfully crossed the finish line 0.68 of the way through the lap and maintained a speed of 0.70 of the maximum speed with a 95% success rate. Moreover, our model exhibited a remarkable combination of slow to fast speed transition robustness, and self-correction abilities when encountering exit ramps, and performed similarly in real-world settings after extensive training in the simulated environment. We expect this work to contribute to the development of robust and efficient autonomous driving models in the future.
