The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being automatically fulfilled by the former, despite similarities in atmospheric composition. Thermochemical grid calculations are combined with the Reynold's number-based transition criterion for the onset of mean flow and turbulence-driven atmospheric loss to establish the mass range within which atmospheric masses of temperate exoplanets should fall, with the transition from quiet to turbulent atmospheres occurring at Reynolds numbers exceeding 4000. We find that for a 1.8 times Earth mass planet at 0.93 solar radii and 500 K effective temperature, Reynolds numbers exceed 10,000, leading to inefficient heat recombination of gases compared to smaller planets of similar gravity, resulting in reduced CO pressure and a cooler stratified atmosphere. This distinctive behavior distinguishes planets with liquid water oceans from those with massive H2/He envelopes, offering a distinctive signature suitable for verification of theoretical models and atmospheric loss mechanisms in ongoing and upcoming transit spectroscopy missions. For example, using primate-based transit spectroscopy data, we find that planets on the turbulent-atmosphere boundary can be differentiated from those with quiet atmospheres at similar wavelengths and optical thickness. Ultimately, mission planners may require additional observing time and higher signal-to-noise ratios to accurately model atmospheric compositions and solve for individual atmospheric masses consistent with the new photochemistry and thermochemistry characteristics. However, mission designers may also consider incorporating specific observational initiatives aimed at detecting atmospheric oscillations and gravity modes, verifiable with space-based spectrographic data of higher spectral resolution. Nonetheless, the improved understanding of atmospheric processes and composition now facilitates a thorough examination of atmospheric dynamics in accord with upcoming mission requirements for characterizing exoplanet atmospheres. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more robust scene text models capable of providing more reliable and innovative applications.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking. To demonstrate the proposed methodology, this research achieves the precise calculation of random equilibrium cycles in the Lorenz system, as well as solution branches and 2-dimensional planes of steady states in the Swift-Hohenberg equation. The findings are compared to existing results obtained through numerical methods. This method's scalability to higher dimensions is discussed, along with potential future applications. This research demonstrates that combining chaos expansions with validated tracking provides a powerful tool for analyzing dynamical systems with uncertain factors and multi-parameter dynamics. The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial systems may exhibit multiple failure patterns, and identifying the primary cause is essential. This work aims to develop an efficient monitoring system for processing high-dimensional data in resource-scarce environments where various potential failures may occur. Our proposed solution incorporates a Multi-Layer Elastic Averages Scheme (M-LeAS) for handling high-dimensional data and detecting abnormalities within subspaces. Since our method relies on a sliding window approach and uses algorithms with optimal time complexities, it ensures real-time performance. Our approach also employs the Elman Recurrent Neural Network (ERNN) as a classifier for accurately identifying and distinguishing between different failure types. Our experimental findings demonstrate that our proposed monitor system surpasses the current state-of-the-art methods in resource-scarce environments due to a combination of lower overhead and higher classification accuracy. We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galaxy growth patterns, is based on exponential infall scenarios and allows for reliable fitting of these patterns. Our analysis led to the discovery of key time frames: 1.01 billion years for GSE to form new stars, while 10 billion years ago, the system experienced initial infall and then maintained its stellar formation for about 1.5-2 billion years. Conversely, the star-formation times for Wukong/LMS-1 were roughly estimated to be 3.36 billion years. Our model showed strong correlation with predicted numerical simulations in multiple areas, such as mass distribution, angular momentum, and mass variation over time. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both end-to-end training and model pruning for CNNs, distinguishing itself from previous work with fine-grained architecture preservation through pattern-based pruning, precise weight estimation, and compiler-optimized calculations. As a result, ClickTrain can deploy high-accuracy and fast-pruned models directly without additional overhead compared to traditional methods, while also minimizing the pruning-after-training approach by up to 2.3 times with similar results and up to 2.3 times with the pruning-during-training approach with both higher accuracy and compression ratios, all under equivalent time constraints. Furthermore, ClickTrain can also adapt to various hardware platforms with accelerated deployment and high accuracy through a 2.3 times faster inference speed on GPUs and a 2.9 times faster inference speed on FPGAs, matching the original model's accuracy without any retraining, hyperparameter tuning, or compiler modifications. Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). However, the optimal policy for a CMDP is often non-intuitive and non-transparent, making it unsuitable for some practical applications. This study proposes a novel transparent policy algorithm, which uses an exact method to calculate the worst-case cost of a valid policy and leverages this calculation in an optimistic reinforcement learning framework. This approach is proven to converge to the optimal policy in the least amount of time compared to other existing methods. This technique is applied to a production planning problem with a constraint on inventory holding costs and yields a transparent policy that significantly reduces costs and meets the constraint. Our results demonstrate a cost reduction of 16.5% and confirm that the proposed method achieves the best possible convergence rate. This technique is now available as a package called T-PPO-CMDP. https://github.com/arunarora98/TPPO-CMDP. Our empirical analysis reveals that the proposed algorithm performs well even when the underlying model is imperfect or unknown. This technique is particularly significant because it can be applied to a wide range of sequential decision-making problems in operations management with minor modifications. One such example is preserving confidentiality in sequential decision-making processes, such as those encountered in supply chain and clinical decision-making. Our results indicate a cost reduction of 16.5% in such scenarios. In conclusion, the proposed algorithm offers a successful solution to the difficult problem of achieving the best results while sequential decision-making and maintaining the confidentiality of the underlying model. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept we introduced between a 7D black hole and superconformal quantum mechanics. The duality holds when the charge of the black hole corresponds to an equivariant locally free sheaf on the resolved space with a given holomorphic vector bundle structure. The first order linear differential equation representation of BPS state degeneracies also undergoes transformation in this duality convention. The 7D black hole area spectrum, derived from BPS state degeneracy growth data, corresponds to the Newton polynomial degrees of equivariant Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on the prequantum bundle of the symplectically resolved space. The transform of this duality convention applies to the Witten Duality, converting it into an equivalence between two self-dual elliptic operators under the symplicial resolution of the hyper-Kahler cone. The duality convention has a consequence that influences the quantum cluster variables of the F-gon basis. The impact of this duality convention is further expanded to apply to the conformal quantum mechanics of one and two particle potentials. We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process using numerical methods. Initially, our findings in two-dimensional networks align with previous research, demonstrating that the impact of network heterogeneity results in a broader range of epidemic occurrences in comparison to homogeneous networks. Additionally, our numerical analysis permits a detailed investigation of the network's role in modulating the system and reveals a more complex interplay between network geometry and epidemic behavior than previously appreciated. Specifically, our results reveal that the presence of clusters within the network has a significant effect on determining the likelihood of epidemics. Furthermore, a comprehensive mathematical model is developed to better understand the relationship between cluster size, network heterogeneity, and disease propagation. This model highlights the significance of degree distribution in determining the prevalence of epidemics and demonstrates that cluster size can influence disease propagation even in two-dimensional networks despite previous claims to the contrary. Our research also explores how cluster size and network heterogeneity affect the system's stability and disease propagation, resulting in a detailed phase diagram that illustrates the complex interplay between these factors. Moreover, our findings are accompanied by a detailed evaluation of the robustness of our numerical methods and the potential implications of our research for understanding disease transmission in biological and social networks. To facilitate further research, a detailed description of our numerical approach and the code utilized in this study are provided. Ultimately, our analysis emphasizes the importance of considering network architecture when developing strategies for mitigating and preventing the spread of diseases. By combining theoretical models of disease propagation and numerical simulations, our research demonstrates that the interplay between network structures and disease dynamics can be effectively explored and understood. This knowledge can be utilized to inform and guide the development of practical and effective disease control measures. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of their respective generators makes practical sense. This paper introduces a novel strategy for verifying the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing a sieving approach to extract all twin primes at their corresponding generator levels. In the context of $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers, $n$ representing the number of primes, we will demonstrate that the difference between two consecutive $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers grows at a faster rate than $n$ itself. Additionally, the smallest possible $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers will be listed and their upper and lower bounds will be established. This paper will also establish the fastest known known sequence of consecutive primes produced by a single generator and verify the Twin Prime Conjecture for all $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers up to their current recorded fastest known sequence. This verification process leverages a combination of existing research and Novikoff's Infinite Prime Sequence Theory. Finally, this paper will derive new upper limits for the gap between the largest and smallest prime numbers, establishing the fastest known known sequence of consecutive primes and setting the lowest possible infinite prime gap at $4\ldots040$. In conclusion, this paper offers a new approach to verifying the Twin Prime Conjecture, providing solid mathematical evidence in support of the conjecture. This approach also offers a new method for verifying the conjecture in specific cases of twin primes and establishes a new relationship between the gap between consecutive prime numbers and their generators. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Moreover, the approach provides an adaptable and future-proof design for sonar-based navigation, encompassing single, double, and triple sensor setups. Although specifically designed for sonar sensors, the concepts presented can be extended to other modalities such as infrared sensors. A key advantage of this research over existing approaches is the modular and future-proof design that accommodates multiple sensor configurations. In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. To study this highly interacting system, we developed a family of multi-band Hubbard models exhibiting exact pairing ground states across all symmetries. Through analytical computations, we discovered that many-body excitations are governed by an effective single-particle Hamiltonian and that a continuum of pairons occupies the flat band. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the Meissner effect is characterized by a pairon dynamics involving particle-hole excitations that are confined to electron pockets, effectively protecting the superconducting symmetry. We demonstrate that the pairing interaction in these compounds can originate from either an underlying lattice structure or electron-phonon coupling, and we analyze the consequences of a flat band superconductivity on the pairing mechanism of the Sr$_3$Ru$_2$O$_7$ material. Our findings also emphasize the significance of flat band superconductor as a unique system for investigating strongly coupled superconductivity, allowing us to distinguish it from conventional pairing phenomena, and potentially yielding novel pairing features, such as a reentrant normal state at pressures exceeding 20 MPa. Lastly, we outline the experimental signatures of this superconducting system that distinguish it from conventional LiFeAs-type superconductors. These distinctive features include reduced pairing energy, broken pairing symmetry under magnetic field, and a reentrant behavior in pressure-temperature space. Therefore, a detailed microscopic analysis of this superconductor is crucial for resolving the long-standing superconducting puzzle posed by Sr$_3$Ru$_2$O$_7$.}

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this, this study proposes a novel data creation approach based on probabilistic models that allows for the integration of domain knowledge. Additionally, a pioneering training method is presented, which relies on a probabilistic model to generate synthetic data, tailored to the specific characteristics of ciphers. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on both synthetic and real-world M85 cryptogram data. The research introduces a unique evaluation metric for ciphers that takes into account the inherent uncertainty associated with the decoding process. The developed model is compared to a conventional sequence-to-sequence baseline and outperforms it significantly. Furthermore, this study showcases the feasibility of utilizing language statistics and domain-specific constraints to develop a viable decoding strategy for M85 ciphers, which yields a 25.9% improvement in accuracy compared to a conventional beam search approach. The presented framework is versatile and may be applied to various other cryptograms and handwritten text recognition tasks in multiple languages. The model and supporting code are publicly available at https://github.com/Imagination-Labs/M85_HTR. Last updated: February 2022.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the entanglement spectrum, as well as localized density excitations and the effects of periodic driving. Hands-on numerical experiments are employed to illustrate key concepts, providing insights into the properties of topological systems. The goal is to equip students with the ability to independently analyze and identify topological properties in a range of models, preparing them for more advanced research in the field. Furthermore, we encourage students to apply the concepts learned to the study of the Majorana system and a model for superconducting nitrogen vacancies, using numerical methods to examine the properties of both systems. This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc. Additionally, it's discovered that the compactness of a composition operator is unaffected by whether it operates on the entire Bergman space or a weighted variant. We also explore the dual consequences of these findings, such as identifying compactness of other operators such as multiplication and Toeplitz operators, as well as establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for the compactness of these operators under specific weight choices. Specifically, this study provides a complete characterization of compact multiplication operators with continuous symbols (limited to their closure) on the Bergman spaces of the polydisc and the taut extremal weights, as well as identifying compact Toeplitz operators with range restrictions and explicit forms. Ultimately, this study offers a survey of compactness and boundedness criteria for several operators, including composition, multiplication, and Toeplitz with weighted Bergman spaces. Key findings include that compactness of a composition operator is unaffected by its symbol's continuity or boundedness and that multiplication operators with continuous or bounded symbols are compact if and only if they map onto the zero space, while Toeplitz operators with range restrictions and explicit forms provide separate and necessary conditions for compactness. Furthermore, this study provides compactness and boundedness criteria for Bergman–El Karoui spaces and identifies compact multiplication operators with weighted Bergman spaces. Specifically, this study finds that compactness of a multiplication operator with a weighted Bergman space is unaffected by its symbol's boundedness but requires certain conditions on its continuity. Conversely, this study discovers that compactness of a Toeplitz operator with a weighted Bergman space is unaffected by its symbol's boundedness but requires separate and necessary conditions for continuity. Additionally, this study identifies compact multiplication and Toeplitz operators with Bergman–El Karoui spaces and provides separate criteria for boundedness and compactness of these operators, as well as other operators such as composition and weighted composition. Specifically, this study finds compactness of a composition operator with a weighted composition operator if and only if its symbol's image includes the zero space, while multiplication operators with weighted composition operators are compact if and only if they map onto the zero space, and Toeplitz operators with weighted Bergman spaces are compact if and only if their symbol's image includes the zero space

To address this gap, we have developed a memory management system and related tools enabling true object-oriented programming on SIMD devices. Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The amount of X-rays absorbed by the material becomes contingent upon the energy flux, giving rise to a unique form of X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES). Researchers can study valence excitation directly without needing to fit XANES data with comprehensive theoretical models of electron dynamics, as the effects of flux vary greatly with the type of material and its excitation density. In particular, excitation of electrons in multi-electron systems appears highly non-linear with respect to the X-ray flux, as evidenced by two case studies involving nickel nitride and potassium: both show significant changes in XANES at fluxes as low as 100 millijoules per square centimeter:  (i) at much lower fluxes than those estimated for interband excitations, (ii) with a much shorter time frame for these changes to occur (on the order of a few femtoseconds) than can be attributed to rapid changes within the electronic system's distribution over 5-10 picoseconds. The distinctive characteristics of flux-dependent XANES make it an invaluable tool for investigating extremely short-lived electronic states within matter. Moreover, the findings suggest that an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse can serve as a coherent scattering agent for creating a new generation of ultra-short laser sources. The research highlights the considerable potential for creating novel, highly concentrated states within matter by interacting it with an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse, which in turn could find applications in developing novel optical materials. The findings also open up new avenues for investigating matters in a yet unknown state, commonly referred to as an 'x-ray-excited state'. Lastly, the research shows that an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse can transform materials in a yet unknown, highly temporary state ('femto-phase'), characterized by unique properties (unique 'color', unique electron density, unique connectivity) that persist for a duration equivalent to the lifetime of the pulse. The application of this concept, however, would necessitate the development of a new class of ultra-fast detectors. Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a different approach is presented to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded method that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. Specifically, the study showcases a system comprising two integrated components: the generation of entangled photons and a method for detecting their links. Firstly, a means of producing entangled photons is demonstrated through a downconversion process facilitated by a type-II optical parametric downconverter, coupled with a method for identifying their polarization links via the birefringence effects of a fiber channel. Secondly, a means of detecting the polarization links is demonstrated through a technique called polarization mode demutation, achieved by applying a control beam to modulate and detect the state of a signal photon, thus highlighting potential applications in quantum communication and the verification of quantum systems. Furthermore, a means of enhancing the entanglement of the system is demonstrated through a method for correcting distortions and noise, thus offering a means of maintaining its quantum connections even in the presence of noise and directional confusion. The research identifies potential limitations in the presented system, a distance of approximately 1 km, beyond which a supplementary means of maintaining the quantum entanglement, a quantum receptor, would be necessary. Ultimately, the distance to which the system can maintain its quantum entanglement connections would ultimately be governed by the level of directional confusion and noise, leading to further investigations of its practical implications in the field of quantum information sciences and technologies. In doing so, the study also raises the query whether the recognition of entanglement, commonly believed to require precise measurement, can still effectively be detected through observations of less precise relationships between quantum connections. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives, with the constraint that its edges have lengths at most 1 + 1/n times the Euclidean distance between those points. We show that the competitive ratio of any such algorithm must be at least Omega(log n / log log n) in one dimension, and at least Omega(sqrt{(d + 1)/n}) in higher dimensions. We also look at the all-pairs problem, where a sequence of points in R^d is given at once, and find that the competitive ratio of any geometric t-spanner must be at least Omega(sqrt(d/n)) in one dimension, and at least Omega((d + 1)/n) in higher dimensions, although these results are improved upon by previous research in some cases. We propose more efficient algorithms for the online all-pairs problem, which give competitive ratios of O(sqrt(d/n)) in one dimension and O((d + 1)/n) in higher dimensions. We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures. The scalability and efficiency of this asynchronous approach are ensured due to the ability to simultaneously update strategies from multiple players. The given framework is versatile and encompasses various problem settings, including differentiable and nondifferentiable games, as well as risk-averse games based on entropy-variational approximation. To further demonstrate its applicability, we present specific applications in the context of real estate and educational matching, formulated as risk-averse games and Pareto-optimal problems, respectively. The latter involves a challenge similar to the former, namely solving Nash equilibrium for a risk-averse game, as well as finding the best worst-case response, which translates to minimizing the maximum expected value of a linear function. For the latter challenge, we propose an alternative asynchronous methodology. Both algorithms are supported by numerical examples and experimental results demonstrating their effectiveness and efficiency in solving various game-theoretic problems. The former algorithm shows a speedup of up to 3 times in comparison to a corresponding synchronous approach, while the latter exhibits a speedup of up to 20 times. A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all this, leveraging the unique properties of a Michelson interferometer and combining it with induced coherence-based nonlinear interferometry, along with the use of a single-pixel imaging method. By doing so, we have successfully performed interaction-free imaging of a structured object using undetected photons, thus pushing the boundaries of quantum imaging to the point where object interaction and photon detection are minimized. This innovation lays the groundwork for utilizing single-pixel imaging to examine delicate samples at wavelengths detectable by standard silicon detectors. Furthermore, we have formulated a matrix-formulated calculation method for nonlinear single-pixel imaging, which will serve as a fundamental reference for future experiments. This technique has also enabled the visualization of two hidden objects stacked vertically, thereby opening up the pathway to single-pixel imaging of multiple objects. Finally, we have assessed the system's sensitivity capability, affirming its potential for low-level light sensitivity and extending its applicability to a wider range of wavelengths, specifically up to 660 nm. This significant advancement holds significant promise for numerous biological and metrological applications. Next steps for further refinement include utilizing wavefront coding technology to enhance the protocol's sensitivity and parameter stability, thereby significantly increasing its practical value in everyday life. In conclusion, we have successfully implemented a groundbreaking single-pixel imaging protocol that achieves all this without the usual light source and object-sample interaction, thus paving the way for a new generation of quantum imaging protocols. This innovative technique not only facilitates the examination of delicate biological samples but also opens up the possibility of using standard silicon detectors to detect a broader range of wavelengths. We hope this advancement will inspire a new era of research in imaging technology. Lastly, we have outlined two potential applications for this technique: utilizing the protocol to enhance the imaging capabilities of microscopy, particularly in the detection of samples at wavelengths normally inaccessible to standard microscopy; and using the protocol in conjunction with existing optical imaging technologies to extend the sensitivity and precision of existing systems, effectively making it an excellent bridge between the quantum world and everyday optical imaging applications. This technique has immense potential for both purposes, specifically the former in the near infrared range

Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders. Based on this criterion, we have established a phase diagram for the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces. This comprehensive understanding of friction behavior may also be applied to non-foam complex liquids. Additionally, we explore potential connections between our findings and the mechanisms of surface slithering and stick-slip motion observed in living organisms. The implications of our research extend beyond the scope of surface roughness, as they may contribute to a broader understanding of the behavior and rheology of complex liquids. The findings of this study may be useful in fields such as surfactants, biophysics, geophysics, and cosmology, as well as in the practical design of surfaces to minimize friction. Finally, we emphasize the significance of observing both the mechanics and morphology of foams during experiments, as the geometric conservation of foams is inherently connected with their mechanical response to external forces. By combining these perspectives, we gain a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between mechanics and geometry in the behavior of complex liquids. The experimental methods employed in this study are versatile and can be applied to the study of both foams and non-foam complex liquids within various fields of research. The key advantage of our approach is the measurement of stresses over rough surfaces with high spatial resolution, which is a capability unique to foam dynamics experiments. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. Specifically, we achieved accuracy superior to all competitors in identifying the outlier class, and our metadata-based model performed equally well to the best competitors. When combining the accuracy of these methods, we achieved a 66.45% overall accuracy, surpassing all competitors with a 5.3% improvement. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of the data and discovered correlations between class distribution and geographic origin. This led to the development of a region-based classifier, which, although seemingly straightforward, was found to be effective with an overall accuracy of 65.21%. Furthermore, we analyzed the effectiveness of various image augmentation methods and determined that performing simple rotations may be more beneficial than employing more sophisticated techniques. Lastly, we highlighted some challenges in using CNN for outlier detection and suggested potential avenues for addressing this issue in future challenges. The code used to achieve our results is available at the link: https://github.com/alents97/ISIC2019/tree/master/code. Additionally, the models used to obtain our results can be accessed at https://drive.google.com/drive/share/D Drive ISIC2019 Models?usap=sharing. Specifically, the ensemble of our models can be found at https://drive.google.com/drive/share/Drive ID ISIC2019 Models Ensemble?usap=sharing. It is intended that this report serve as a resource for participants in the challenge to quickly replicate our results and continue working on this exciting area of research. Furthermore, our code and models may be utilized as a foundation for future research in this domain. Lastly, our report concludes with some future directions and potential avenues for further investigation.

These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected, producing exponential asymptotics approximations. Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two oscillatory contributions, cancelling out under certain mass ratios to produce localized waves, thereby confirming prior numerical and experimental observations on the phenomenon in non-precompressed diatomic chains. Nonetheless, an approach grounded in exponential asymptotics fails to accurately predict solitary wave formation for various mass ratios in precompressed diatomic chains. Consequently, we suggest an alternative method for predicting solitary wave formation, based on a modified Stokes curve, thereby providing a comprehensive and consistent theoretical framework for solitary waves in precompressed diatomic chains. Furthermore, we investigate the effect of system compression on the frequency of solitary waves. Our findings are also applied to a non-precompressed diatomic chain, producing a localized wave formation condition solely based on mass ratio $\mu$, supported both analytically and numerically. Consequently, we suggest an approach for improving the accuracy of solitary wave formations, by incorporating parts of the oscillatory component which are deemed significant, thereby producing improved exponential asymptotic representations of solitary waves in precompressed diatomic and woodpile chain systems. This method is versatile and can be applied to other non-precompressed solitary wave systems. Furthermore, we examine the behavior of precompressed systems where the masses are evenly spaced and take the same value, thereby forming a uniform diatomic chain. Our findings are then used to determine whether a localized wave can form within such a system. This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings reveal that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers and convnets' backbone features in the self-supervised era, due to their robust semantic representation. Notably, self-supervised ViTs outperform convnets in the self-supervised paradigm, and their associated linear classifiers surpass convolutional backbone features in both the self-supervised and supervised settings. Moreover, our research highlights the value of ViT's deep pooling layers in preserving semantic structure, and demonstrates that a ViT model incorporating channel attention has the potential to be the premier image analysis method. Our study also examines the applications of self-supervised ViT models in other tasks, such as object detection, and achieves exemplary results in the self-supervised paradigm. Our research further delves into the advantages of ViTs over other visual backbones in the self-supervised era, and explores their performance as few-shot classifiers. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its marked simplicity, it exhibits all the complexities needed to account for the observed variety in the Hubble parameter. The model's compatibility with the cosmic data is quite satisfactory. We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li. The provided proof is based on a combination of existing results and a demonstration of ill-posed behavior in specific function spaces, which in turn relies on construction of particular smooth vortex distributions. Additionally, our work shares similarities with an earlier study by Colding and Colding in terms of functional analysis and periodicity of discrete groups. Furthermore, the proof involves utilizing an integral transform and examining the behavior of certain function spaces, which in turn requires an in-depth analysis of the properties of these spaces and a demonstration of their ill-posed nature in the context of the Cauchy problem. The provided proof is notable for its simplicity and the fact that it relies solely on existing results, including a study by Christ and Shubin as well as another by Zampieri. The final result has significant consequences in terms of the existence of local solutions to the Cauchy problem and the behavior of smooth vortex distributions. Moreover, the proof also demonstrates the existence of smooth and periodic discrete groups, thereby confirming an earlier conjecture by Colding and Colding. The provided proof is also applicable to other types of Navier-Stokes equations and Euler equations in lower dimensions. Moreover, the proof is almost entirely self-contained, requiring only the incorporation of existing results and making the proof more accessible. Furthermore, the application of the Littlewood-Paley projectors, along with other tools such as the properties of oscillatory integrals and the behavior of Fourier integrals, plays a significant role in the proof. The computational method of estimating certain quantities, such as those related to the Fourier transform, also contributes to the understanding of the ill-posed nature of certain problems. Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks, demonstrating its ability to create high-quality, tailored images and compositions. Additionally, we provide the source code at https://github.com/Alibaba-Seva/Stable-Artist.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. Moreover, our study showcases the utility of uncertainty analysis in assessing the reliability of predictive models. To facilitate the adoption of Bayesian uncertainty analysis by the steganography community, we provide Python-based implementation details on GitHub at the address https://github.com/alsaad99/SteG-Bayes. This resource is designed to be accessible to users who are familiar with deep learning and reversible steganography but lack expertise in the theoretical foundations of Bayesian deep learning. As such, we include a comprehensive theoretical overview and an accompanying code base that can be used for Bayesian steganography analysis. This code base supplements the paper's content and is meant to facilitate the reproduction of our results. Additionally, we include additional resources for the steganography community at the address https://github.com/alsaad99/SteG-Bayes. This code base contains the code used to generate our empirical findings and includes detailed documentation that explains the parameters and techniques used. Specifically, we provide an overview of the following algorithms: the generation of aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties; the creation of predictive models; the creation of SteG-Bayes datasets; the implementation of Monte Carlo sampling; the utilization of Bayesian neural networks; the computation of posterior predictive distributions; the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis to steganography; and the estimation of capacity-distortion metrics. This code base aims to streamline the process of Bayesian uncertainty analysis and we hope that the community will find it beneficial in assessing the reliability of predictive models for steganographic purposes. To our knowledge, this study marks the first instance of the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis to the field of reversible steganography. The integration

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses consider various uncertainties associated with neutrino and dark matter production. Our findings reveal constraints on neutrino and dark matter couplings, which we compare with previously established benchmarks. Furthermore, we discovered that J/ψ decay into invisible matter offers more stringent limits on certain neutrino couplings and a particular dark matter coupling compared to electron and muon decay modes. While J/ψ decay into visible states such as electrons, muons, and gamma plus lepton or quark pairs primarily constrains right-handed current and vector current couplings, the decay into invisible matter also influences left-handed and vector current couplings. Our research demonstrates that J/ψ decay into invisible matter is a valuable tool in exploring light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter, making it an essential component in understanding low-energy physics phenomena. Moreover, the analysis reveals the potential for future J/ψ decay into invisible particles to be a key discovery candidate for a 5 GeV dark matter particle and to set the world's best limits on its coupling with the charm quark. Ultimately, the findings could pave the way for new research opportunities in particle physics. Our study is self-contained, and the associated code and tables are available online at https://www.desy.de/~wfeng/Jpsi_invisible/index.html.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal' stimuli - specific configurations of visual inputs that facilitate either object or action recognition. Unlike existing computer systems, human performance with these minimal stimuli reveals a more nuanced and context-dependent integration of spatial and motion cues. Additionally, modeling human performance with a Bayesian approach suggests that object and action representations interact competitively, but also exhibit 'friendly' interactions that are sensitive to stimulus configuration and prior knowledge. This study provides a new framework for exploring how humans integrate diverse visual information and how prior knowledge influences visual perception. Furthermore, it highlights the complex and delicate nature of visual integration in human perception. This work has been submitted as a conference paper to the 2024 Meeting of the Society for Vision Science.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities confined under electromagnetism. However, the strength of their dark magnetic interactions with ordinary matter is significantly constrained by observations of galaxy halo ellipticities. Furthermore, the ground state of dark monopoles initially stable and chargeless becomes quantum mechanically unstable under an external magnetic field, an instability whose characteristics vary with the scale of the dark monopole mass and kinetic mixing. The resulting decay products include neutrinos, gamma rays, and neutral pions, leading to observable signs such as an excess of cosmic ray muons beyond those produced by the decay of muons and gamma rays. The data from high-energy particle physics experiments, cosmic microwave background measurements, and galaxy halo observations yield the most stringent constraints on the parameter space where the dark magnetic interaction between ordinary matter and a single type of dark particle becomes visible, an effect which may realize a long-sought "messenger" connecting the fermionic sector of the dark matter to the observable sector. The resulting constraint has implications for the understanding of dark matter consisting of two distinct particle types with different properties including masses, while the present model's features vary based on the underlying mass and interaction characteristics of these particles. Specifically, for a situation where one type of particle has a much heavier mass than the other and the dark monopole's lifetime spans from microseconds to hours, the allowed range for the mass of the lighter particle varies broadly from approximately $10^{10}$ to $10^{20}$ grams. Furthermore, the reverse scenario where the heavier particle has a much higher mass also yields similar constraints, an outcome consistent with the current limits imposed by other types of dark matter stability mechanisms. The present model's characteristics include a cross-over phenomenon where the predicted constraints on the dark monopole decay time and mass could either mirror the behavior of the unstable $SU(N)_C$ monopoles studied in a 1987 paper by Arnold and Vilenkin, or even exceed it in certain cases, an outcome stemming from the application of the Pauli principle to the dark monopoles' quantum state. Lastly, the data from high-energy particle physics experiments, cosmic microwave background measurements, and galaxy halo observations may also provide a solution to the problem of the age of the universe in models where the dark monopole decay is slow, an outcome stemming from the application of the reheating criteria to the energy released

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network. Building on existing research into vision transformer architectures, we address the limitations associated with their high computational complexity and data-hungry nature. To achieve this, we propose combining Video Swin-Transformer with a dedicated data augmentation method, and employing a gradual spatial reduction on the encoder and cross-attention on the decoder. The efficacy of our proposed approach was tested on the Weather4Cast2021 challenge dataset, where we successfully predicted 8 hours of future weather frames from hourly weather sequences. After normalizing the dataset for evaluation consistency, our model achieved an MSE score of 0.4750 using training data, and 0.4420 using transfer learning without training data. Notably, our paper presents the first published results for the Weather4Cast2021 challenge, which demonstrates the potential of AI in real-time weather forecasting. Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The outcome of our preliminary analysis indicates that extracting network motifs can reveal meaningful and understandable patterns within the data. This study validates the effectiveness of our motif discovery approach by identifying a complex pattern indicating unauthorized transactions linked to compromised account hacking. We have made our dataset and code available for other researchers to verify our results and build upon our work. The analysis presented in this study has further improved our understanding of banking transaction graphs by identifying trends, such as rare transactions, and those involving large sums of money. Additionally, we have found that when accounting for account balances, some of these unusual transactions are considered plausible. This implies that simply focusing on transaction quantities may not be sufficient for accurate analysis. Finally, we have found that some of these unusual transactions are linked to account hacking, while others have clear explanations, such as those involving tax refunds or transfers to new accounts, which could potentially be flagged as suspicious due to their novelty. Our findings suggest that incorporating account balances and transaction amounts can help filter out some of the genuine, novel, or unusual transactions. This could pave the way for a more effective and accurate fraud detection system. In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern. To simplify the understanding of this process, we also point out an analogy between our problem and the phenomenon of wave radiation emission in the case of a accelerating charge. It is also noted that the energy emitted from the accretion process is mostly in the form of gravitational radiation, contradicting some speculations about high-energy observations. The quantum hydrodynamic model we employed is based on an approximation where we consider quantum effects to be negligible in comparison to thermodynamic effects. However, it is pointed out that, due to the rapidly changing conditions of the white dwarf, this approximation may not be entirely accurate. Therefore, a more precise quantum statistical mechanical model of the white dwarf should be developed in the future to further improve our understanding of this process. Lastly, it is noted that the mass range of the black holes participating in this process is potentially broader than currently expected, extending up to the mass of the black hole observed in the binary system of 16 Lynae, which is potentially a stellar mass black hole. The maximum mass of the white dwarf in our simulation is around 2 solar masses, which is consistent with the current understanding of white dwarf physics. The white dwarf is represented as a quantum fluid consisting of both semiconducting electrons and negative electrons, and its mass is determined by considering the mass range of typical white dwarfs, from 0.6 to 3.5 solar masses. Three-body $\tau$-decays, which involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations, can provide insight into these processes. Studies of weak electromagnetic interactions rely on form factors to describe the hadronic part of the final states, which can be further understood by decomposing the hadronic current into specific orbital angular momentum components. We apply this decomposition to the three-body system, using amplitude equations to describe the interplay between different angular momenta, and provide explicit expressions for specific angular momenta in the orbital part of the hadronic current. This approach could serve as a basis for parameterizing the form factors involved in these interactions. While our focus is on CP violation research, this methodology can be applied to a broader range of studies in strong and electroweak physics. In addition, we outline potential future experimental investigations that could be conducted with larger data sets, including processes involving decay sequences, such as $\tau \to \pi \ell \bar{\nu}_{\ell} \gamma$, and $\tau \to \ell \bar{\nu}_{\ell} \gamma$ in the presence of virtual hadronic effects. \bigskip

We present the results of a theoretical investigation into the structure of hadronic currents in weak electromagnetic decays of the $\tau$ particle. These findings can serve as a foundation for analyzing the hadronic parts of decay processes involving the $\tau$. We have also examined potential applications of our theoretical analysis to experimental studies of weak electromagnetic $\tau$ decays, including a review of past work and suggestions for future investigations that could be conducted with larger data sets in the future. 

In particular, the future experimental study of $\tau \to \ell \bar{\nu}_{\ell} \gamma$ in the presence of virtual hadronic effects could be highly anticipated with larger data sets, as well as the investigation of hadronic effects on the $\tau \to \ell \gamma \ell \bar{\nu}_{\ell}$ process and possible connections with the study of $\tau \to 3\ell \bar{\nu}_{\ell}$ processes once the data sets grow sufficiently large to enable such studies. 

In addition to the applications to the experimental study of weak electromagnetic $\tau$ decays, our theoretical analysis can also be extended to a broader range of studies in strong and electroweak physics, including three-body $\tau$ decays that involve semileptonic interactions with light hadrons and CP symmetry violations.

Additionally, it was discovered that the set consisting of all $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ functions has a more complex structure as a topological space. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning rely on paired synthetic data for training frameworks, which are obtained by manipulating sharp images. These data pairs, consisting of a sharp image and multiple blurs from various directions, are obtained through an optimization process, requiring significant computation time. Furthermore, these pairs are limited to a specific set of blurs and cannot be easily extended to other areas. To overcome these limitations, we propose a new framework that learns blurs directly from video sequences and can handle an unlimited number of blurs within a single training phase. Using regularized optical flow estimation, we leverage real-world video data to learn blurs automatically and efficiently, achieving the first end-to-end motion deblurring method. Our framework outperformed state-of-the-art methods in various benchmarks, both for blurs derived from the paired data and blurs obtained from our end-to-end framework. Our code and blurs can be found at https://github.com/shizeng/End-to-end-Deblurring. We also provide 81 real-world video datasets, available at https://github.com/shizeng/Real-World-Deblurring-Datasets. The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive description of the refined version's properties in terms of the original set's order type. Specifically, we've established a one-to-one correspondence between refined versions of sets of the same order type and have identified which of these refined versions share similar characteristics using established mathematical concepts. Ultimately, we've examined the interplay between refined versions of sets and their original properties, considering both individual and collection-wise scenarios. This research allows us to address a specific query from a 2004 problem set, answering it in the affirmative. Specifically, we've confirmed that for any set, its refined version will always have a one-to-one correspondence with a set of sequences, leading to an extension of a 1985 result initially demonstrated by Benci and Thorngren. We've also discovered a refinement of a 1993 result by Scheepers and Stricker, which involved observing a property within a set of sequences and its relation to the refined version of another set. This relation serves as a source of new examples, explaining an earlier phenomenon observed by Benci, and has far-reaching consequences in the study of refined versions of set sequences. This research combines existing research on refined versions with new findings, offering multiple applications and examples. We've explored two specific scenarios. Firstly, we've examined the refined version of a set that remains unchanged over time and has a constant number of elements, in contrast to a set that changes over time and has a constantly growing number of elements. Secondly, we've compared the refined version of a set that is ordered in a straightforward manner to one of a set that is encoded in a more complex order. This research allows us to address a 2004 problem set question in the affirmative and extends a 1985 result by providing a refined version, in addition to discovering new examples and phenomena while gaining insights into the generalized continuous principles of non-standard models. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that integrates dataset profiling into the model selection process, providing more accurate model assessments. Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where a certain set of its vertices uses every possible color, then that graph must have a complete graph with t vertices within it. This more robust idea has been tested with success for the case of t = 4. This result holds further implications for 5-colored graphs; specifically, we can confirm a revised and more robust version of the original Hadwiger's conjecture, where 5-colored graphs contain complete graphs with 5 vertices within them. This has further implications for 5-critical graphs in the same scenario. This proof relies heavily on previous work done by Robertson and Seymour in re-proving a theorem by Mader, as well as a recent paper by Tangerman. This also holds implications for a more general concept of coloring where certain vertices must be assigned the same color. This more general idea, when applied to 5-colored graphs, contains a complete graph with 5 vertices within them, where a given set of its vertices use every possible color. Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, yields superior results despite reduced entanglement. Our findings have implications for optimizing entangled atomic state production for quantum-enhanced matter-wave interferometry applications. Additionally, they may also be adapted for the improvement of spinor atomic clocks by incorporating the nonclassical properties of entangled states, thereby further enhancing their precision. It is observed that utilizing the trigger mechanism results in a more controllable level of entanglement than the vacuum case, especially when considering real-world situations where only a few of the collisional states are relevant and the remaining fluctuations are unimportant. Therefore, a more versatile approach to trigger-entangled states could provide significant gains in matter-wave interferometry by facilitating wider access to the nonclassical properties of entangled atomic states, thereby paving the way for their use in precision applications such as atomic clocks and metrology. Furthermore, the research suggests an interesting connection between the behavior of entangled states in the spin-changing collision and the coherent population transfer phenomenon found in quantum optics, both of which share a similar underlying physics and both of which can be effectively modeled through the use of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. This link between the two concepts has significant implications for the development of new techniques to produce entangled atomic states on demand, thereby enhancing their potential in a variety of precision measurement and quantum communication applications. Finally, the possibility of utilizing the entangled atomic states formed through the spin-changing collision as resources for quantum key distribution has also been explored, leading to the conclusion that while the levels of entanglement achieved are sufficient for this purpose, they may not be enough to make the key distribution process entirely secure when compared to other quantum key distribution methods. However, the potential of entangled atomic states for this purpose should still be considered significant, as the inherent advantages of matter-wave interferometry could be used to overcome some of the conventional limitations associated with quantum key distribution. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $N$-dimensional space, and a smooth norm $F$ on this space. Specifically, for positive $\beta$ we proved a lower bound for the eigenvalue and for negative $\beta$ we proved an upper bound. Furthermore, for positive $\beta$ we were able to derive a lower bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the anisotropic inradius of the domain $\Omega$, and for negative $\beta$ we were able to derive an upper bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the parameter $\beta$. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This has limited the availability and accessibility of this technology, particularly for resource-constrained communities. To address this issue, we introduce a novel self-training technique that enables the adaptation of neural dependency parsers to new domains with minimal prior knowledge. Our approach embeds domain-specific structural information into the parser's word representations, exploiting the parser's existing linguistic cues to focus on key domain-specific word dependencies. We have extensively tested our method on diverse domains within English and Chinese, as well as cross-language scenarios, has successfully improved parsing accuracy in over 90% of the domains we tested. Additionally, our cross-language results show significant improvements over existing benchmarks in Senna and SPMRL benchmarks. With our self-training technique, these adaptations have become faster, more reliable, and easier to implement, demonstrating an average speed-up of 5-10 times and requiring only a small fraction of the original dataset. Our work suggests that self-training can greatly enhance neural dependency parsing adaptation, empowering users to produce high-quality results quickly and efficiently. Our code and data are publicly available for reproduction. Based on our findings, we recommend a unified self-training framework that integrates both token-level and arc-level training techniques, leading to the best overall results. This integrated strategy has proven particularly valuable in domain adaptation scenarios and is likely to remain an essential tool for natural language processing experts. Our research further validates the effectiveness of token-level training alone, achieving comparable outcomes in numerous cases and often outperforming combined training methods. We intend to explore the potential applications of our token-level training methods in other natural language processing tasks in future studies. With our self-training approach, we have successfully achieved more accurate dependencies by filtering out unnecessary branching relationships in complex sentences. Our results indicate that sentence-level arc prediction methods may not always be necessary and can, in some cases, cause more harm than good for the parser's overall performance. Our studies of sentence-level dependencies have primarily been limited to non-branching relationships, as finding suitable training data for these contexts has been challenging. Our work demonstrates the versatility of our self-training method in handling various training techniques and dependency types, enabling us to achieve superior results in a wide range of scenarios. Our research has primarily focused on the application of token-level training in adapting neural dependency parsers to new domains, as this has been the most practical approach to integrate this technique into existing parser architectures.
