Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality with string theories on orientifolds of type IIA/B, we can determine the actions of these symmetries on the dual gauge theories. We find that the orbifold operation and the mirror symmetry have equivalent effects on the baryonic operators of the dual gauge theories, thus explaining a previously observed duality. We use this duality to construct an LST duality relating three-dimensional tri- and quadri-fecta theories. Furthermore, we can determine the actions of the non-invertible symmetries on the basis operators of the dual gauge theories and demonstrate that the charge under one of these symmetries accounts for the exponential growth of the basis dimensions. We also find that the basis dimensions of the dual gauge theories obey a poly-Time growth pattern. Utilizing the basis elements of the twisted algebra of chiral symmetries, we can rederive the operators of the basis of the dual gauge theories. We find that the operators constructed in this manner match a previously proposed set. Our work also reveals a duality between four-dimensional megafecta and bifecta theories, which can be proven by utilizing an LST duality in three-dimensional tri- and quadri-fecta theories. We propose that this duality explains a previously observed one-loop correction in a theory, thus providing a physical interpretation. Furthermore, we can determine the basis dimensions of the dual gauge theories and propose an LST duality relating three-dimensional pento- and hexa-fecta theories, which can be proven by utilizing an additional mirror transformation. We find that the operators constructed in this manner match a previously proposed set with differing sign. Our work suggests the presence of an additional non-invertible symmetry, which accounts for the difference in the sign of the basis dimensions. We conclude by proposing LST duality relating six-dimensional (2,2s) and (1,1), with a (1,1) theory containing a free orbifolded sector, through an action of the non-invertible symmetry. The dualities presented can be tested by computing one-loop corrections in the gauge theory and comparing the result to the corresponding twisted K-theory correction in the string theory. Furthermore, we can determine the basis dimensions of the dual LST basis and propose an LST duality relating three-dimensional tetra-, penta- and hexa-fecta theories

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the CFT (CPT with function symbols) conjecture, which aims to establish CFT's superiority over CPT. A significant hurdle in studying CPT lies in its limited comprehension of basic numerical functions, as evidenced by the inability to reliably count cycles in its queries, according to specific function symbols' interpretations. A notable advancement has been the development of CFI (CPT with intersection mod n), a variant of CPT capable of using mod n operations on natural numbers in its queries. However, even CFI proves insufficient for certain applications, as seen in its insufficient power for determining adjacency in a cube complex. A key discovery presented here is that, for any fixed n, CFI becomes too powerful and thus separable from CPT on classes of graphs consisting of bounded-degree n graphs and their covers. A significant finding is that the ability to solve the CFI-query is the primary determining factor for CPT-definability on this class of graphs. A general approach is to utilize a variant of path-coding, which allows us to robustly determine cycle counts in a dependent manner. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition with increasing amounts of Bi substitution at the Eu site. To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. Interestingly, Bi substitution unexpectedly led to a significant (20 %) reduction in the radius of the Eu ion. However, the local environment of the Eu 4f electrons remains unchanged, and the surface density of states at the Fermi level exhibits a concentration-dependent evolution, indicating that the metallicity in this series is likely caused by extended states within the gap rather than a simple doping effect. The insights gained from HAXPES measurements facilitate the construction of a phase diagram for the Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 series, providing a framework for the understanding of electron correlations and lattice effects in these materials. Furthermore, the results have implications for the search for Weyl semimetal characteristics in this and similar compounds. The research was conducted at SPring-8's BL25XU beamline with the assistance of an experimental team. The data have been uploaded to the MWO website under ID 202300010101N. The full research paper has been published in Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter [1]. The associated supplementary information and presentation are available at http://j-phys.org/promedia/202300010101N. Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_m(X)$ of compact convex subsets of $X$ of dimension $m$ or less. Our recent joint research with Charles Fefferman established a principle that enables the existence of a Lipschitz selection for $F$, which is a mapping $f:{\mathcal M}\to X$ that satisfies $f(x)\in F(x)$ for every $x\in{\mathcal M}$. This paper presents alternative proofs of the existence of a Lipschitz selection under two specific conditions. Firstly, when $m=2$ and $X={\bf R}^{2}$, and secondly when $m=1$ and $X$ can be any choice. These proofs leverage a simple reiteration formula for the core of a set-valued mapping $G$ that satisfies $G(x)\subset F(x)$ and is Lipschitz in the Hausdorff distance. In addition, the paper presents several criteria that can be used to constructively prove the existence of a Lipschitz selection for set-valued mappings from ${\mathcal M}$ to the family of closed half-planes in ${\bf R}^{2}$. These criteria provide insights into the relationships between core, $\varepsilon$-fidelity, and $\varepsilon$-Lipschitz equivalences of mappings. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that the minimum distance between the core and an $\varepsilon$-fidelity or $\varepsilon$-Lipschitz equivalent of a mapping can be estimated in advance. Furthermore, for mappings from ${\mathcal M}$ to the family of closed half-planes in ${\bf R}^{2}$ with Lipschitz image, the distance to the mapping's core can be found to be exactly $\gamma({\mathcal M})$, where $\gamma({\mathcal M})$ denotes the Lipschitz quotient of the mapping's image. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If an n-tuple satisfies this condition, it is considered a probability vector. We let $\mathcal{C}_n$ denote the set of all possible cyclic n-tuples, where the minimum element is 1/(n+1) and the maximum element is 1-n/(n+1), making it a subinterval of [0,1]. Our study focuses on the specific n-tuples where the sum of all elements equals 1/2, as this is the only instance where there is a direct relationship between cyclic n-tuples and well-known classical examples. We also present an alternative method of generating these probability vectors, explore symmetry and quasibipartitioning within the vectors, as well as presenting open questions regarding geometric representations of the vectors. We aim to demonstrate that these probability vectors have intriguing, counterintuitive applications. We use the term 'cyclic' because of a particularly fitting example. Also, we mention a few recent findings related to the field of probability that are related to this topic. Our goal in presenting this topic is to show that there is a broader universe of counterintuitive phenomena than what has been previously recognized. Our ultimate goal is to encourage researchers to continue exploring this universe and uncover new examples. We also mention potential applications where cyclic n-tuples may be used as the building blocks for other interesting counterintuitive examples. We also present some examples and counterexamples that highlight the difficult process of determining whether a given n-tuple is cyclic. Our study also shows how the concept of cyclic n-tuples may be used as the basis for developing educational thought experiments that challenge students' perceptions of probability. We conclude by presenting some interesting counterintuitive examples of cyclic n-tuples and suggesting potential applications where these tuples may be used as the building blocks for other interesting examples. We also present some common pitfalls in the field of probability that may be used as thought-provoking thought experiments for students and laymen.

In our research, we devised an experimental approach to reduce a system's configurable parameters during compilation and eliminate unnecessary settings on demand. A detailed analysis of the well-known video encoder x264 revealed the positive impact of this approach on the system's efficiency and security aspects, particularly by cutting the system's binary size and improving performance and resilience against malicious attacks. This groundbreaking methodology opens doors for further research in the field of software security and system configuration. This work was previously documented in a paper published by McHigham and Avgerinos in the ACM Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation (PDL) in 2017, using the system's source code to gather insights, whereas our method relies on the system's compiled binary and execution environment, offering a more comprehensive perspective on the role of run-time configurations. Additionally, we developed an automated tool to implement our approach, previously demonstrated on x264, in the Stevens Tool released during the International Symposium on Code Generation and Optimization in 2018. This paper revisits the method and provides an updated assessment of its effects on x264, in conjunction with a recent counterpart tool. In addition, we expand upon our previous research to investigate whether our approach can be adapted to system configurations that utilize dynamic libraries and multiple compilation passes. In conclusion, our method holds significant potential to both reduce system dependencies and improve dependability, promoting a safer and more secure computing environment. Lastly, we outline promising avenues for further exploration into the relationship between system configurations and security, providing a safer and more secure computing environment. Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. This is because they can more easily explain the correct abundance of cosmological matter. However, detecting such lightweight particles directly poses a significant challenge due to the high energy scale required for spin-dependent interactions with target nuclei and the difficulty of achieving sufficient nuclear recoils. Additionally, the predicted spin-dependent structure functions for target nuclei like germanium have limited uncertainty margins. This study explores an alternative approach focused on the direct detection of sub-GeV dark matter using superconducting radio frequency cavities as sensitive nuclear spin detectors. Our initial findings illustrate how SRF cavities can serve as highly sensitive instruments for investigating lightweight dark matter interactions, offering improved constraints on existing models or even discovering new ones not previously detected. The use of SRF cavities as direct dark matter detectors represents a novel and unexplored field of research. It offers the potential for groundbreaking breakthroughs in the understanding of sub-GeV dark matter, particularly when combined with cutting-edge simulations and research dedicated to the enhancing material properties. Furthermore, this approach can be used to investigate other phenomena outside the realm of dark matter, thereby contributing to the broader goals of particle physics research. In conclusion, the use of SRF cavities as direct dark matter detectors represents an innovative and unexplored field of study, thereby promoting new opportunities for particle physics research. It is essential to develop advanced software tools to accurately simulate the underlying physics processes as well as the associated technical limitations inherent in this novel detection method. Ultimately, this research will yield highly sensitive physical process searches, significant improvements in the understanding of sub-GeV dark matter, and the opening of new avenues for investigating unexplored phenomena beyond the confines of existing model predictions.}. direction of the standard Jaynes-Cummings interaction process. The research discovers
that this anti-process also leads to a direct connection between the maximum connected
pairs of states generated through the standard process and the minimum connected pairs
of states generated through the anti-process. The study reveals that this anti-process
occurs in two distinct parts: one part mirrors the standard process and the other part
occurs in a higher energy state. The energy difference between the initial and final states
in this anti-process varies based on the presence of photons and is not fixed. The
anti-process has the potential to be applied in the production of entangled states in
cavity QED systems. Furthermore, the research indicates that this anti-process could
be slowed down by introducing a dissipation mechanism. The study also discovers that
this anti-process can be reversed under specific conditions to form a time-reversed image
of the standard process, resulting in the same connected pairs of states. The time-reversed
image of the standard process can be distinguished from the anti-process through the use

down the time-reversed image of the standard process offers an alternative method for

We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully captures rich, semantically significant representations across languages despite the absence of direct supervision. To facilitate the reproduction of our results, we've made our source code, data, and task representations available at https://github.com/alefthompson/xglue. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our analysis highlights the potential for using multi-task learning
in a model-based reinforcement learning framework, without the need for a bundle of
tightly related tasks. Our code is available at: https://github.com/awheeler3/Dynamics-Shared-Model.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that power generation systems affected by storm surge can suffer prolonged capacity losses, and the damage to lines and transformers is significantly higher when considering both hurricane and storm surge situations. Overall, the study's findings suggest that non-coastal systems may also incur significant losses due to storm surge scenarios. Based on these results, the proposed model can be utilized to estimate hurricane and storm surge-related losses for large power grids in various regions, and is intended to support decision-making activities such as conducting cost-benefit analyses for hurricane mitigation measures. Additionally, the study's results can aid utility companies and grid operators in assessing their exposure to such events, and guide investment in hurricane-related insurance policies. We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system, but possess an additional structure of translation invariant paths, enabling a direct connection to the study of tilings as recognized by Smale. We investigate the geometric constraints imposed by this additional structure, leading to a finding that the intrinsic encoding properties can be fully captured by projecting onto a specific 2D subspace, effectively reducing the dimension for encoding purposes. To confirm our hypothesis, we provide numerical evidence of a specific family of these maps, demonstrating that the topological covering of the space can be accurately modeled within a 2D subspace. Moreover, we connect this model to the study of unstable paths in 3D topological covers, revealing a new structure that can be utilized to analyze the dynamics of certain families of one-parameter level sets of smooth 3D maps with hyperbolic structure, including those resembling the structure of certain Mandelbrot set components, through a process of folding back. This new structure, based on a method of three-directional folding, allows us to explore the hyperbolic structure of these maps by establishing a correspondence between their unstable sets, particularly those exhibiting hyperbolic structure, and a part of the Mandelbrot set that is known to have smooth one-parameter level sets. This correspondence enables us to prove the existence of certain families of maps that are topologically non-trivial and have a hyperbolic structure, thus providing new examples of such maps, along with verifying the smooth hyperbolic structure of certain families of maps that were initially proposed as potential models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. Additionally, we provide insight into the geometric constraints that determine the stability of certain families of maps, including those resembling the structure of certain Mandelbrot set components, by analyzing their distribution within the 2D subspace and showing that there are families of maps that are topologically non-trivial and have a hyperbolic structure, thus providing new examples of such maps. Furthermore, we establish the existence of an infinite family of maps that are smoothly hyperbolic and have a hyperbolic structure, thus providing new examples of such maps, and verify the smooth hyperbolic structure of certain families of maps that were initially proposed as potential models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels. A comprehensive computational framework named SCAFO has been created to optimize the connection between simplified models and collider experiments. Within this framework, SCALOPP is a tool specifically designed for beyond the Standard Model search applications at the interface of particle physics and cosmology. Here, we introduce the SCAFO framework and its component, SCALOPP, highlighting their capabilities and functionality. A detailed overview of their toolsets will enable the simplified model reinterpretation of collider searches and measurements, facilitate matching between model and observable quantities, and facilitate the thorough examination of extended scalar models. Furthermore, we will outline our future plans for developing the SCAFO framework to make it even more useful for model-independent beyond the Standard Model search applications. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data due to the complexities and idiosyncrasies of user preferences. Researchers attempted to overcome these challenges by integrating CF with Biclustering techniques. This research aims to evaluate the efficacy of Biclustering approaches for high-quality recommendations by examining various Biclustering methods and evaluating their performance on real-world datasets for two specific recommendation tasks. Our findings indicate that, at present, Tableau-based Biclustering methods are well-suited for CF applications, offering notable improvements over traditional CF systems in prediction accuracy and overall performance. Nonetheless, our analysis discovers several shortcomings of these Biclustering methods that create opportunities for further innovation in this field, prompting us to propose two potential strategies for future development. Ultimately, the evaluation outcomes serve as a guide to helping researchers and practitioners navigate the complexities of Biclustering methods and select the most appropriate techniques to meet their specific needs. The conclusions of this work are formulated into design principles for proposing novel Biclustering methods, urging researchers to prioritize three key factors: compatibility with existing technology, the attainment of balanced performance in addressing user preferences and data variety, and the simplicity and scalability of the recommended solutions for practical applications. To facilitate the comparison of Biclustering methods and future research initiatives, our study introduces a new framework for evaluating recommendation systems, CF-BiClust, which integrates both CF and Biclustering evaluation metrics. This framework enables researchers to assess the effectiveness of CF and Biclustering methods in addressing the complexities of user preferences within recommendation data while promoting healthy competition and collaboration among research teams. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these indicators from planetary signals, allowing for reliable differentiation between activity and planetary signals. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found significant patterns in the daily variations of these features. In particular, the spectral feature at $\Delta$\lambda $ \approx$ 0.1 $\mu$m, which is easily measurable even with low-resolution spectra, correlates strongly with other activity indicators and allows for their separation from planetary signals with high precision when used in conjunction with existing activity indicators. This finding should enable the reliable identification of Earth-like planets even in cases of intense stellar activity. In simulated data analysis, we found that combining the activity indicator related to this spectral feature with existing activity indicators enabled the gain of up to 80% in precision when detecting planetary signals, and in some cases allowed for the gain of up to 170% when used in combination with other indicators. In addition, we found that using this indicator and engaging in statistical analysis enabled the gain of up to 40% in precision when comparing activity-induced induced noise to the noise produced by random fluctuations. Furthermore, we found that using this indicator and engaging in statistical analysis enabled the detection of Earth-like planets with a much smaller ratio of signal to noise, specifically a gain of up to 30% in planetary parameters, and in some cases up to 55%. In conclusion, this research indicates that using this new indicator can significantly enhance our ability to identify Earth-like planets even in the presence of strong stellar activity. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperature decreases in proportion to $T^\Delta$, non-Majorana-induced peaks exhibit temperature-dependent conductance that is proportional to $T^{-1/3}$. Through numerical calculations, our method has been validated by being applied to a simple model consisting of a gapless spinless Majorana wire in contact with a high-resistance wire characterized by a high Ohm value > 10^3. The predicted behavior of the Majorana peak matches that of the theoretical model, leading to potential experimental differentiation between the two zero-energy peaks. Yet, our study has unforeseen implications in that Majorana modes could be poorly distinguishable from non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks in highly localized systems with long signature segments. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Furthermore, the relationship between shadows and THH enables the calculation of the THH of a group of homotopy classes of maps of pointed simplicial complexes. Additionally, this computation yields an interpretation of the homotopy groups present within the THH spectrum as a generalization of the group in question. Lastly, the relationship between shadows and family representations allows for the formulation of conditions under which the homotopy groups present within the THH spectrum can be expressed as generalizations of the group in question in terms of representable functors from the homotopy theory of simplicial models. This general condition is shown to apply to groups that are either abelian or have vanishing $H_2(G,\mathbb{Z})$. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability, focusing instead on predicting a singular style. Contrasting conventional approaches, our research seeks to harness conditional generative models to capture and manipulate the various styles associated with color grading, enabling more precise control and realistic generating of footage. Building on state-of-the-art U-net models, our method enhances traditional approaches to image processing, preserving the unique characteristics of input images and seamlessly integrating artistic and technical interventions. Thorough evaluations, conducted across multiple datasets including the LIVEMMI dataset with 4000 images and the DIV2E dataset with 1000 images, have confirmed the substantial potential of our approach, as demonstrated by human assessments and quantitative performance metrics. Further details regarding our method's implementation, along with the evaluation data, can be accessed at https://github.com/stevejpapad/multi-style-color-grading. Our technique has been successfully applied in the film industry, as exemplified by the footprint matte creation for the Disney feature film 'Raya and the Last Dragon.' Ultimately, our goal is to enable more versatile image processing operations, allowing artists to explore a broader range of styles and transforming the field of color grading through machine learning technology. The technical underpinnings of our method have significant implications for the application of machine learning in cinematography and visual effects. Our research has also led to the development of an open-source tool for real-time color grading, which has started to inspire creative work within the filmmaking community, as illustrated by three independent projects submitted in response to a call for challenges. The source code for our method and the challenge entries can be accessed at https://github.com/stevejpapad/multi-style-color-grading-challenges. This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon not seen in prior studies. Images captured within the flow patterns show that snowflakes tend to concentrate near the base of vortex formations, moving preferentially downwards. High-resolution footage of these vortex formations provides quantitative evidence of accelerated snowflake speeds. This study provides comprehensive evidence that a phenomenon called preferential sweeping is the primary cause of enhanced snow deposition in the atmosphere's lower layers. As a result of this process, snowflakes are effectively gathered and carried by the flow, leading to more efficient snow deposition and heavier snowfall as a consequence. This research has significant implications for improving the simulation of snow deposition in models of global climate models. Our investigation of the complex relationship between snowflake trajectories and atmospheric turbulence will help advance snow deposition modeling by identifying the key physical processes at play and the parameters that require further examination. Ultimately, this research could lead to the development of a self-consistent model for snow deposition that is essential for accurately simulating the process at the ground's surface. Our most recent findings involve the application of a model that is based on the flow's velocity distribution, an approach that was first proposed by Wang et al. (2015) and is known as the velocity-based model. This model successfully explains the observed connection between the flow patterns, snowflake speeds, and snowfall masses, indicating a high level of accuracy for the ranges of velocities and concentrations that were examined in this study. However, the model was found to be ineffective in accounting for the behavior of snowflakes within the vortex formations and the associated snowfall phenomena that result from that interaction. As a result of this discrepancy, the model was modified to include an additional term that is designed to capture the effect of the vortex formations on the snowflake settling process. The modified model is able to account for the accelerated snowflake speeds, the concentrated snowfall at the base of vortex formations, and the high-speed snowfall phenomena that were previously discussed. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. The results show promising performance comparable to state-of-the-art robotic navigation systems, and more importantly, this approach is based on a more realistic and varied learning environment. Overall, this research validates the idea that learning mental frameworks using deep learning can support active inference. This finding is particularly significant as it opens the door for the development of more sophisticated cognitive agents and also paves the way for incorporating established knowledge and principles of neuroscience into cognitive agent design. Moreover, this work reveals a novel and versatile navigation method that extends beyond traditional robotic systems. The success of this study suggests that a more detailed examination of the relationship between this type of mental framework and the brain's neural architecture could yield valuable insights for cognitive neuroscience. Lastly, this work suggests that a more thorough investigation of the relationship between this type of mental framework and the brain's neural architecture could yield valuable insights for cognitive neuroscience. In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a significant hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of state-of-the-art compression methods and standard image or volume compression techniques yield underwhelming results. To bridge the gap, our research focuses on the efficient use of machine learning for real-time data reduction in real-time data streams. By combining lossless data reduction and lossy data compression, our experiments with various workloads have produced more favorable outcomes than standard methods. Specifically, our results exhibit multiple orders of magnitude improvements in data loss tolerance and compression ratios, thereby manifesting a substantial boost in real-time data capture capacity. Moreover, our approach enables the preservation of raw data on a recording medium substantially smaller than what was possible in the past, thereby greatly simplifying data recovery and enhancing the overall data capture system. Ultimately, this leads to a substantial reduction in the costs associated with data storage and recording technology. To summarize, our findings indicate that real-time data reduction and compression can be used to greatly expand the capabilities of real-time data capture systems, allowing for a larger band-width, higher data capture rates, lower data storage costs, and more extensive data sets, in essence empowering users to capture more data. Our findings reveal that the clusterization of alpha particles resulting from interactions between projectile protons and nucleons within the target has a greater impact than other formation processes, with relative strengths of the nonresidual channels ranging from 10% to over 100%. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios. In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain about a source sequence, under the assumption that the coding system is suboptimal. This problem is linked to the concept of leakage in information theory and is known as $P$ leakage. We are examining the smallest amount of information (and thereby the best suboptimal coding efficiency) that allows an adversary to accurately guess a source sequence of length $n$ within a fixed error probability bound, and this measure is maximized under optimal adversary strategies. This problem can also be seen as a measure of how easily a source sequence can be compressed when an adversary has some level of access to the source sequence and is trying to accurately guess it. We show that the maximum amount of information an adversary can gain in this situation is limited to an fraction of the total information in the source sequence, and this upper bound on information loss applies even when the source sequence is highly structured and nearly completely uniformly random given the adversary's information. This finding applies particularly well to situations in which the source sequence is either completely uniformly random or nearly completely uniformly random, and we are investigating under what conditions the information loss in these situations may approach this upper bound as the length of the sequence becomes very long. We also found that the information loss when the source sequence is binary may approach this upper bound as the length of the sequence becomes very long under specific conditions, and we were able to determine the exact information loss when the source sequence is either completely uniformly random or binary and completely uniformly random. A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at points A and B. A key aspect of this method involves identifying the intersection points of the secant line with each ellipse, which can be accomplished through the application of Cramer's rule to a system of linear equations derived from the elliptical equations. Once the intersection points are identified, the area between the secant line and the two ellipses can be calculated using the formula for the area of a triangle, scaled by a correction factor that accounts for the ellipses' curved shapes. The proposed method has been successfully implemented in a programming language and compared with established methods for calculating overlap areas, including separation detection and the Liu method. The results have been normalized into a C++ library called LIBOVERLAP, which computes the overlap area and separation distance between two ellipses in a single unified function. The validation of the proposed method involved comparisons with both experimental and numerically computed values, including analyses of edge cases and scenarios of nearly touching or overlapping ellipses. The calculated overlap areas were also utilized to determine the separation distance between the ellipses, as well as the likelihood ratios for overlap areas less than and greater than a predefined threshold value. The theoretical limits of the proposed method have been estimated through the application of both Lagrangian multiplier optimization and point process theory. The method has been tested on a variety of elliptical shapes, including standard cases, such as circles, and less standard variants, including nearly touching and overlapping ellipses, as well as those in contact. The computational efficiency of the method has been assessed by measuring the processing time for a large number of random ellipse pairs. The proposed method has significant practical applications in a wide range of sectors, including (i) geometry teaching and assessment; (ii) medical imaging and phenotyping; and (iii) industry, particularly in the production and design of car parts. The method's impact extends to a broader range of topics, including edge cases, separation detection, and likelihood ratios for overlap areas. The results obtained through the method have been further utilized to develop multiple comparisons tests using the likelihood ratio criterion, including scenarios with up to six ellipse pairs, as exemplified by the analysis of coffee cups and standard elliptical shapes. The method's extension to a larger number of ellipse pairs has been tested through the computation of overlap areas for ten pairs of standard ellipses

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and introduce the term "instantaneous advantage rate function". Our analysis leads to the development of two value functions: the "q-function" and the "continuous Q-function". Both functions are shown to have stochastic differential equations representations and their relationships with the instantaneous advantage rate function are investigated. Furthermore, we discuss the conditions under which the continuous Q-function recovers the traditional Q-function, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our results through numerical simulations. Lastly, we provide a path-integral approach to the continuous-time Q-learning problem, and establish a relationship between the current path-integral rule and the traditional Q-learning equation. Our results in this study generalize the theoretical outcomes of Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning. The proof strategies employed here are critically different from their work. We also attempt to provide physical and biological interpretations of our results. Due to the broad applicability of our results, a vast array of potential applications could arise from them. From a practical standpoint, our results offer a potential route to solving the reinforcement learning problem in continuous time. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. To achieve this, we developed a novel and multi-stage vertebral segmentation network (MVS) which dynamically adjusts its focus on different vertebral features across various spinal locations. By implementing three dedicated blocks in the MVS, we effectively filtered out non vertebral objects, and then refined the model's focus on vertebral features, or adjusted its focus away from similar features in non vertebral objects. This unique multi-stage structure allows the model to accurately distinguish between close vertebral features and non vertebral objects through adjusted feature focus. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the MVS in achieving superior performance compared to alternative methods, specifically with respect to vertebral feature recognition and focus adjustment. Additionally, 3D- MVS was applied to accurately identify vertebral bodies in CT images afflicted by artifacts from metallic stimulation. What's more, his lack of mathematical prowess may have contributed to his breakthrough in kinematics, with his focus shifting from standard mathematical techniques to a more novel, less mathematically sophisticated method. This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.  The course covers various challenge scenarios and provides a framework for designing intelligent systems that are tailored to the unique needs and capabilities of their human partners, while also exploring a range of design choices and intelligent system architectures that balance the interplay between human and machine intelligence.  The course concludes by investigating how these digital assistants can be used to develop patients' cognitive abilities and deliver personalized medical treatments in the future.  The course is designed to cater to the needs of systems engineers and designer-developers who want to develop intelligent systems that are in sync with their human counterparts - including biomedical and cognitive engineers and users of general interests.  The course is rich in examples, has a week-by-week delivery pace, and combines online lectures with assigned readings, design activities and weekly forums for discussion and feedback.  The course is evaluated through individual projects and a final project that showcases the intelligent design of a digital assistant that learns from its experienced human counterpart.  The course is rich in supplemental materials and is now fully available on the Stanford University platform for free.  The course is the result of a collaborative effort between R holden Stanford University and K Pugh - a renowned cognitive scientist and long-time colleague.  The course is the culmination of nearly 1000 hours of dedicated time and a comprehensive approach to creating intelligent systems that are in harmony with their human partners.  The course is an extension of a 2015 mini-course that successfully reached over 20,000 users and sparked a wide range of individual projects - now revised and expanded into the current 7-week format to better serve a wider audience and provide the necessary framework for designing intelligent systems that are in sync with their human counterparts.  The course is an invaluable resource for creating a new generation of intelligent systems that are tailored to the unique needs and capabilities of their human users
